| Frame allocation (JavaScript heap per steady-state frame) | Measured by the check `npm run test:frame-alloc:browser` ([frame-alloc-browser.mjs](../scripts/frame-alloc-browser.mjs), scenes in [tests/fixtures/frame-alloc](../tests/fixtures/frame-alloc/main.js); run by `check:merge`). RTX A6000 desktop, Edge 156 headless with `--enable-precise-memory-info`: `performance.memory.usedJSHeapSize` read once per frame, 600 warm-up frames (one of them, 60 before recording, late on purpose: a 200 ms stall, so the floors hold for the steady state after a late frame) then 600 recorded, frames with a garbage collection left out, the median frame, largest of three runs, at the item 53.1 commit (`perf(core, shadows, post)`, 2026-10-29). Per frame, before and after (two steps, item 53.1 parts 1 and 2): three lit meshes 1,428 B to 340 B; 10,000 moving instanced boxes 1,076 B to 292 B; the same room with cascaded shadows and eight moving casters 26,920 B to 860 B; with SSAO, Bloom, tone mapping and FXAA 5,116 B to 1,528 B. The room plus 10,000 `DynamicInstances` boxes (@margoengine/culling), every row rewritten each frame through bulk writes and `update()`, measured 396 B in three runs at the item 53.2 commit (56 B over the room alone, among them the 16 B wrapper of its compute pass). The check fails when a median frame passes these floors; they are only ever lowered. | Every byte a frame allocates is a byte the garbage collector must sweep later, and a collection in the middle of a frame is a stutter. Margo reuses its arrays, descriptors and callbacks from frame to frame instead of making new ones. | Not 0 B, and it cannot reach 0 B: every WebGPU call that returns an object (the command encoder and its finished command buffer, each render pass, the canvas's current texture and its view) hands back a new 16 B JavaScript wrapper from the browser, and V8 stores the fractional frame time it passes to frame callbacks and plugins as a heap number. Shadows and post-processing add passes, so they add wrappers. Measured and left as they are: the frame-resources view set clears about 120 B per frame in the post scene (a fix changes the protocol between copies of the resources, judged risky for a frozen core), the SSAO scene walk makes an iterator and an options literal, the fixture setters box about 216 B in the shadowed scene, and each returned WebGPU object costs 16 B. Core's changed-row upload walks its dirty-row words 16 bits at a time, so no tier boxes a full 32-bit word (it cost 3,744 B a frame for 10,000 moving rows until 2026-11-11, KB0378); `tests/frame-alloc.test.js` fails it over 0 B a call at the baseline tier and at Maglev. Edge 157 reads the instanced and shadowed scenes 12 to 20 B over their floors on the RTX A6000 (open in docs/known-bugs.md). Number boxing in V8's middle tier (Maglev) is gated too: `tests/frame-alloc.test.js` fails a core frame over 780 B, shadows over 620 B and the cascade fit over 128 B there on V8 14 (Node 26) and newer. V8 13 (Node 24, the minimum Node) passes the core limit (628 B) but its Maglev calls Math.sqrt with a boxed argument and result, 32 B a call, so it has its own row for the other two: shadows over 1,120 B (measured 1,081 B, 704 B of it 22 square roots) and the cascade fit over 256 B (measured 242 B, 224 B of it 7 square roots); a square root in JavaScript arithmetic with the same bits would cost every engine more time. Node 22 has no Maglev by default, so the middle-tier probes skip there. A late frame once deoptimized core's frame loop (its delta clamp first ran a compare on a frame past `maxDelta`, with no type feedback), and the loop then ran its next thousands of frames in a tier that boxes numbers: 24 to 84 B more per frame in every scene, seen only when `check:merge` loaded the machine. Fixed in core, and gated twice: the browser check's late warm-up frame, and `tests/frame-alloc.test.js`, which fails when a late frame leaves the loop unoptimized. The Node probes compile on the main thread (`--no-concurrent-recompilation`), so a package build running beside them cannot make them measure a lower tier. `npm run test:frame-alloc:nodes` runs the test on every Node it finds; the probes leave out windows in which V8 collected garbage. In these runs 0 to 3 of 600 recorded frames held a collection. On the WebGL2 compatibility layer (`MARGO_COMPAT=1`, the check installs the layer in its pages) the check measures the same scenes against the same floors, and the layer is within them since 2026-11-18 (KB-COMPAT-FRAMEALLOC1, ten parts): median frames on the layer, Edge 156 on the RTX A6000, basic 252 B, instanced 228 B, shadowed 800 B, post 1,464 B, dynamic 264 B (15,652 B, 12,684 B, 154,856 B, 155,712 B and 497,716 B when it was first measured, 2026-11-16). The layer's objects WebGPU returns per call are a browser wrapper's size or near it (a pass encoder and a default texture view 16 B, an encoder and a command buffer 20 B); its present makes one 16 B ImageBitmap a frame, the zero-copy way to show a WebGL2 frame on a page canvas. | Keep your own `onFrame` callbacks allocation-free (the check's scenes keep their clock in a `Float64Array`). `node scripts/frame-alloc-browser.mjs --profile --source` names the functions that allocate per frame. |
| Moving transforms per frame (CPU budget) | Measured by [transforms-budget.mjs](../examples/package-benchmarks/transforms-budget.mjs): every mesh sets `position.y` and `rotation.y` through the setters each frame, one shared geometry and material (one instanced draw), all in view, Node v26.12.0 on an AMD Ryzen 9 9950X (32 threads), a stand-in GPU device so the figure is the CPU work only (the onFrame callback, the Wasm kernel tick, instance patching, the renderer's frame). 120 warm-up frames, 300 timed, the median frame, a binary search for the largest count within 4 ms (a quarter of a 60 Hz frame). Result: 14,500 moving transforms per frame (record: [transforms-budget.json](../examples/package-benchmarks/results/transforms-budget.json), item 53.1 part 2 commit). Three runs on a machine busy with other checks gave 14,500, 16,000 and 17,700; the lowest is the figure. | A scene can move this many objects every frame before the engine's own CPU work passes a quarter of a 60 Hz frame. | The count at 4 ms depends on the CPU, the Node and browser build, and on what else is running; it is the engine's CPU work only, not GPU time, culling of hidden objects or your own callbacks. | Move fewer objects per frame, or leave resting objects untouched: only a changed transform is patched. Run the script on your machine. |
| Voxel worlds and render distance | Measured ([voxel-sandbox-bench.json](../examples/package-benchmarks/results/voxel-sandbox-bench.json), RTX A6000 desktop, Edge 155, 1920 × 1080, 4x MSAA, quiet-gated, `examples/voxel-sandbox` seed 1): render distance 8 (1,379 chunks loaded, 602 with quads, 1.18 M quads, 14.5 MB of quads on the GPU, 15.9 MB of chunk data, 322 draws) fills in 1.06-1.22 s with frame CPU 0.7 ms median, 1.1 ms p95; render distance 16 (5,579 loaded, 2,435 with quads, 4.84 M quads, 59.5 MB, 64.1 MB, 1,170 draws) fills in 3.59-3.67 s (8.8-9.2 s before 2026-10-20) with 1.7 ms median, 2.2 ms p95 right after the third fill (1.3 ms median once settled, about 4 s later). While the world fills (the sandbox joins 2 ms of chunks a frame then) frame CPU is 4.2 ms median, 8.8 ms p95 at render distance 8 and 6.6 / 11.1 ms at 16, worst 15.8 ms. Flying at 11 blocks/s while chunks stream in: frame CPU p95 3.7 ms (render distance 8) and 5.0 ms (16), worst frames 6.8 and 10.2 ms; back to back with the code before 2026-10-20 at 16: 4.2 / 8.1 ms before, 3.9 / 7.4 ms after. Voxel GPU time from timestamps between passes is rough: 0.39-2.56 ms median at render distance 8 and 0.72-1.51 ms at 16 over three runs. Laptops and phones: not measured. | Each loaded chunk keeps its block palette and light on the CPU; each chunk with faces keeps 12-byte quads in one GPU pool (`maxQuadBytes`, default the device's storage binding limit, 128 MiB on a default WebGPU device); generation and meshing run in workers, joining and light on the main thread spread over frames (`chunksPerFrame`, `frameBudget`); chunks above a column's ceiling, when the generator gives one, load as air without a job. | Filling the range takes time in proportion to the chunks in it, about 1,550 chunks a second here with a 2 ms join budget (about 680 with the default 0.5 ms, which keeps frames light during play). A full quad pool leaves far chunks undrawn until near ones free pages; `VoxelRenderer.stats.poolFull` is true meanwhile. Far from zero, pass `origin` (a `FloatingOrigin`) to every `VoxelRenderer`: chunks draw relative to a base snapped to 1,024 cells near it, so every float32 value the GPU reads stays within about 1,500 cells of zero, tested at 2^24 blocks (packages/voxel/DESIGN.md, decision 4). Without `origin` a world wider than float32 precision (about 100 km) jitters. Bounce light (`/gi`) and RGB light (`/light-rgb`) follow their renderer's origin; smooth terrain views, objects, models and debris take the same `origin` option, tested at 2^24 blocks. Debris with physics takes no origin: physics simulates in world coordinates (docs/known-bugs.md KB-VOX-ORIGIN2). | A smaller `distance` on `VoxelStreamer`; a larger `frameBudget` and `chunksPerFrame` while a loading screen shows; a larger `maxQuadBytes` (up to the device's storage binding limit); more `workers` for the mesher and streamer. |
| Voxel translucent order and merged-quad edges (`@margoengine/voxel`) | By method: translucent quads (glass, water) are drawn in an exact back-to-front order for every quad on a cell face (`sortQuads`): cells in descending grid distance from the eye's cell (Frieder, Gordon and Reynolds 1985), chunks likewise by chunk, so along every ray from the eye the farther of two quads draws first; translucent faces are never merged, one quad per cell face. Quads inside one cell (a lowered or waving liquid top with a slab's inset face, a stair's parts) draw by centre distance; the two quads of a cross block cut each other and have no order. A chunk is sorted again when the eye's cell changes against it, at most 4 chunks a frame, nearest first. With `bevel`, chamfered translucent triangles and quads sort by centre distance. Merged opaque and cutout quads have their edges moved out by 1/128 pixel to close T-junction cracks, where 1/512 closed every crack of the browser check on the Intel Arc 140V (D3D12 snaps vertices to 1/256 pixel). | Exact order needs one cell per quad, so a wide water surface is one quad per block instead of one merged quad. A general order of overlapping polygons needs pairwise depth tests and splitting (Newell, Newell and Sancha 1972); the grid gives the order directly. | A large translucent area costs one quad per block face. A sort lags the camera by a frame or more when more than 4 translucent chunks need one at once. A rasterizer with only 4 subpixel bits (some mobile Vulkan GPUs, untested) can open slivers up to 1/32 pixel at T-junctions. | Keep translucent blocks out of cross shapes when their order matters; leave `bevel` off for exact translucent order. |

| Far voxel levels (`@margoengine/voxel/lod`, 2026-11-07) | Enforced: 1 to 12 levels, `radius` 2 to 32 nodes, `scale` a power of two to 4,096. | Smooth far levels (`@margoengine/voxel/smooth-lod`, 2026-11-15) | Enforced: 1 to 12 levels, `radius` 2 to 32 nodes, `skirt` (cap depth) 0 to 32 cells, a material 0 to 255. | Voxel-edit undo history (`@margoengine/voxel-edit/history`, 2026-11-15) | Enforced: `maxDepth` 1 to 1,024 steps (default 64), `maxCells` per pushed grid, `maxBytes` over the stored copies (default none). By method: a push discards the redo branch, then drops the oldest steps while depth or bytes are over (Scott's ruling 2026-11-15, as GIMP's "Maximum undo memory" does, GIMP 3.2 User Manual, "Undoing", https://docs.gimp.org/3.2/en/gimp-concepts-undo.html); the new step always stays. | Each step is a full copy of the grid, so memory, not step count, is what runs out on large models. | One step larger than `maxBytes` is kept as the only step, so `bytes` is over `maxBytes` then and there is nothing to undo to; whole copies cost the full grid per step even for a one-cell edit. | Raise `maxBytes`, or keep sparse snapshots (`./sparse` delta snapshots) for large models. |
| Goxel and VoxEdit files (`@margoengine/voxel-edit/formats`, 2026-11-08) | Enforced: `.gox` versions 1 and 2 read, 2 written; BL16 blocks of exactly 64 x 64 pixels; at most 4,096 layers; `maxCells` (default 16,777,216) counts each layer's block bounds before cropping; names and dictionary values written up to 255 bytes. `.vxm` versions 3 to 13 read, 12 written; at most 255 materials (palette indices 1 to 255) and 255 models, all of one size; textures up to 2,048 and face lists up to 262,144 quads are skipped, larger ones refused. By method: from a clean-room specification, not from either program. | Neither format has a public specification; the one Margo reads was written from two programs' behaviour and eight sample files, and lists what it could not determine. | Skipped and lost on a round trip: `.gox` cameras, light, preview, material lists beyond one default on writing, layer matrices of plain layers (written as identity), and the fork-only PLAC, CLRH and CUST chunks; `.vxm` baked meshes, textures, surface data, palette chunks and the trailer. Unknown and so not checked: the `.gox` chunk CRC (no writer computes one; written as 0), the colour space of block colours, the meaning of alpha 1 to 254 (read as solid), clone layers under a rotating `mat` (each voxel centre goes to the cell it lands in), and the inside test at a shape's exact edge (centres on the edge count as inside); `.vxm` versions other than 4 and 12 (no sample files; version 13 in particular rests on one program's reader), the v6 to v10 texture compression, the pivot X convention of v10 and older (returned as stored), and whether VoxEdit opens a file with no baked mesh, as `writeVXM` writes. | Open a written `.vxm` in VoxEdit before relying on it; keep `.vox` (`./vox`) as the exchange file when a model must keep cameras, materials or meshes. |
| Voxel-net entities (`@margoengine/voxel-net/entities`, 2026-11-08) | Enforced: `maxEntities` (default 4,096, at most 1,048,576), `maxPerPlayer` (default 256, nearest first), kind 0 to 65,535, state 0 to 255, `leaveRadius` at least `radius` (default 64 and 10% more). By method: entities over a chunk the server has not loaded do not move; each entity is quantized once per tick and sent as a delta against the player's last message; a player away (parked) gets every entity again in full. | Sending only what is near and changed keeps a crowded world within the 20 Hz tick and each link. | A world of many entities steps every one each tick on the server's thread, with no sleeping of far ones beyond unloaded chunks; brains run on the main thread; no pathfinding (only `wander`). | Keep entities near players; write your own brain for chase or flee; raise `maxPerPlayer` with care for the link. |
| Voxel-net shards (`@margoengine/voxel-net/shards`, 2026-11-08) | Enforced: `regionSize` a multiple of 32 blocks (default 256), `margin` 0 to half the region (default 8), `secret` at least 16 characters, tickets good for `ticketLife` (default 10,000 ms) and once, a handed-off player closed with 4001 after `grace` (default 5,000 ms). Measured on loopback in one process only (two servers, real sockets); not measured between machines. | Each shard is a plain VoxelServer that owns its regions' edits; tickets carry the player across, so no shard needs another's state. | A shard sees only its own edits: the other side of a border shows as generated until the player crosses. A handoff keeps position, not velocity, and lands on the ground; the next shard sends the chunks around the player again. | Put busy areas inside one region; make regions larger than the view distance so borders are crossed rarely. |
| Voxel-net WebTransport (`@margoengine/voxel-net/webtransport`, 2026-11-08) | Enforced: `inputCopies` 0 to 8 (default 3), the copies of one message at most 120 steps; a gap of more than 240 lost steps closes the client with 1002. Measured over an in-memory stand-in link only (a third of datagrams lost each way, every 5th survivor late): no step lost with 3 copies, client and server within 0.05 blocks. | Inputs are small, so copies cost little and make a lost datagram free; whole snapshots cost more bytes than deltas but need no acknowledgement. | A dropped session is not resumed. The slow-client check does not see a WebTransport stream backing up. Players snapshots go whole, so they are larger than over a WebSocket. | Connect again on close; keep `playerDistance` small for crowded worlds; use a WebSocket where WebTransport is missing. |
| Voxel-net chat and inventory (`@margoengine/voxel-net/chat`, 2026-11-09) | Enforced: client app messages at most 16,384 bytes and `appRate` 20 per second (burst 20) per player, the rest dropped; a chat line at most 256 UTF-8 bytes after cleaning, `rate` 1 per second (burst 5); inventories 1 to 1,024 slots (default 36), `stackLimit` default 64. Measured over real sockets on one machine only. | The server owns lines and items, so a client can only say a line or ask to move its own items. | Lines over the rate and moves that are not possible are dropped or answered with the slots as they are. Inventories live in server memory; no chat history for players who join later, no channels or mute lists. | Raise `appRate`, `rate` or `burst`; drop lines with `filter`; save inventories with `slots` and restore them with `load`. |
| Voxel-net lag compensation (`@margoengine/voxel-net/rewind`, 2026-11-09) | Enforced: `maxRewind` above 0 and at most 4,000 ticks (default 0.5 s); a view tick older is checked `maxRewind` back, a future one now; `maxDistance` default 64 blocks. Measured over real sockets on one machine only, a walker at 2.5 blocks per second. | A client draws others about `interpolationDelay` behind, so without rewinding its aim is behind the target. | A client can claim any view tick up to `maxRewind` back. Blocks are not rewound: one placed since the view tick stops the shot. Shapes blend in a line between ticks, as the client draws them. | Lower `maxRewind` to give a cheat less; pass `hitbox` for heads or capsules; call `shoot` yourself for shots of your own. |
| Voxel-net database store (`@margoengine/voxel-net/sql-store`, 2026-11-09) | Enforced: `table` letters, digits and `_`, at most 63 characters, optionally after one `schema.` (default `margo_chunks`); chunk coordinates -2^26 to 2^26-1. Tested on `node:sqlite` only; the Postgres SQL runs through SQLite, never against a Postgres server. | A folder with a file per chunk grows past what file systems list and back up well for large worlds. | On SQLite each query runs on the server's thread, so a slow disk stalls ticks. The store cannot list its chunks. | Use a Postgres `Pool` to keep queries off the thread; turn on SQLite WAL (`PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL`); one `table` per world. |
| Voxel-net built-in TLS (`@margoengine/voxel-net/server` option `tls`, 2026-11-09) | Enforced: `tls` needs PEM `key` and `cert` that build a secure context, checked when the server is made and on `setTls`; a TLS handshake must finish within `helloTimeout` (default 3,000 ms). Tested over loopback with a self-signed certificate only. | Small hosts want `wss://` without running a reverse proxy. | `maxPending` and `maxPerAddress` count from the WebSocket upgrade on, so bare TLS handshakes are not capped by them. One certificate per server (no SNI choice between names); no HTTP/2. | A firewall or reverse proxy in front for floods, many names or HTTP/2; `setTls` for renewals; `tls: { ca }` on Node clients for a certificate of your own. |

## CAD import and the B-rep kernel (2026-11-13)

`@margoengine/cad` reads STL and OBJ on the page and STEP, IGES, ACIS SAT, Parasolid XT and JT through
`@margoengine/brep` in a worker. Each cap fails with a `RangeError` that names it and the way past it (regression tests
in `packages/cad/test/cad-limits.test.js`).

| Limit | Starts at | Why | What you see | Escape hatch |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| CAD file size | Enforced: 64 MiB per file ([cad-parser.ts](../packages/cad/src/cad-parser.ts)) | Bounds the worker's memory for untrusted files | `RangeError: CAD exceeds 64 MiB (...); tessellate it offline with @margoengine/brep, export it as GLB with @margoengine/exporters and load it with @margoengine/gltf/pbr` (STL and OBJ: `export it as GLB`) | A GLB through `@margoengine/gltf/pbr`, which has no CAD cap |
| Vertices per geometry, distinct triangle indices | Enforced: 1,000,000 vertices, 3,000,000 indices | One geometry's buffers stay within what every backend draws in one call | The same `RangeError` form, naming the cap | As above |
| Meshes per file | Enforced: `maxParts`, default 100,000 ([limits.js](../packages/shared/limits.js)) | Every mesh becomes a core entity | `Too many CAD parts (...; raise the maxParts option)` | `maxParts`, up to core's 8,388,608 entities |
| Worker time | Enforced: `timeoutMs`, default 120,000 ms | A file the kernel cannot finish does not hold a worker for ever | `RangeError: CAD import did not finish within 120000 ms (raise the timeoutMs option)`; the worker is terminated | `timeoutMs` |
| Placed bodies per assembly | Enforced: `maxInstances`, default 1,000,000 ([structure.ts](../packages/brep/src/step/structure.ts)) | Bounds memory for an assembly that places one body many times | A `RangeError` that names `maxInstances` | `maxInstances` on `parseSTEP` |
| Vertices per tessellated face | Enforced: `maxFaceVertices`, default 50,000 (at least 64; [tessellate.ts](../packages/brep/src/mesh/tessellate.ts)) | Refinement of one face stops before it runs away | The face stops refining at the cap | `maxFaceVertices` on `tessellateSTEP` |
| Tessellation bytes across CPUs (2026-11-15) | By method: analytic surfaces (cylinders, cones, spheres, tori, revolutions) are evaluated with `Math.sin`, `Math.cos`, `Math.atan2` and `Math.acos`, which ECMA-262 leaves implementation-approximated | The JavaScript engine supplies them; a portable sine and cosine in the kernel would slow every surface evaluation | The same STEP file can mesh to vertex positions and normals that differ in the last bit between an x64 and an arm64 machine (14 of 24 test meshes did on an arm64 Mac), and such a bit can tip a refinement decision | Hash meshes only on one machine, or compare them within float32 rounding; `packages/brep/tests/step-tessellate.test.js` pins its digests with `tests/support/exact-math.js` in place of the engine's trigonometry |
| Reader warnings | Enforced: at most 100 in `model.warnings` | A broken file does not flood the caller | Later warnings are dropped | None |
| B-rep modelling: sweep and loft (`model.sweep`, `model.loft`) | Enforced: a sweep takes a closed planar profile across the start tangent of a tangent-continuous path of lines and arcs, with analytic faces only (no helix or spline path); a loft is ruled between closed planar sections with the same number of segments (no loft to a point, no spline sections) | The solid stays exact: its volume and area are the closed forms the tests hold it to, and it passes `checkBody` | A `RangeError` that names the cause: a corner, an arc tighter than the profile reach, path pieces within twice the reach, a twist between sections | Split the path at its corners and `boolean` the pieces, or revolve or extrude the profile |
| B-rep body check (`model.checkBody`): touch margin | Enforced: an edge touches a face it does not bound when it comes within ten times its own tolerance (at least 1 um) along its length, or ten times a vertex's tolerance inside that reach of the vertex; a crossing inside a vertex's reach is the edge meeting its neighbours and is not reported. A loop's sense counts each curve's end where it lies apart from the next curve's start by more than a millionth of the face's size | Tolerant topology: a vertex's tolerance is a ball round its point and an edge's a tube round its curve (Jackson 1995, docs/clean-room.md BR12); the factor of ten is the margin the check keeps over the distances it samples | An edge nearer a face than that margin but not within the stated tolerances can be taken as lying in it; a face narrower than a millionth of its size whose curve ends are apart by less than that can be read with the wrong sense | Give edges and vertices the tolerances the geometry has (an import measures them) |
| B-rep modelling: offset, shell and draft (`model.offsetFaces`, `model.shell`, `model.draft`) | Enforced: faces on planes, cylinders, cones, spheres and tori; a line or circle edge stays one where its faces still meet in one, and any other edge (or one whose faces move apart into another curve, as a plane moved off a torus's axis) is the faces' new intersection traced between its new ends; an offset that changes the topology (a face moved past a neighbour, walls thicker than the part) is refused, and so are B-spline faces | A re-solved body is checked on both faces of every new edge; a topology change needs a different construction | A `RangeError` that says why; nothing is returned half done | Build the thicker or thinner shape with `extrude`, `revolve` and `boolean` |
| B-rep sewing (`model.sew`) | Enforced: a closed edge matches another only when their vertices join; the nearest-open-edge search grows with the square of the open edges | Bounds the search a loose-face set can cost | The `SewReport` lists open edges with their gap distances; a very large loose set is slow | Sew the faces in groups, or raise the tolerance to the gap the report shows |
| Mesh-only JT parts, `.brep` files | Not read: a JT part with only triangle LODs is listed in `warnings`; the native format of the earlier importer's kernel is not a supported input | No exact B-rep to mesh, a format outside the published standards the kernel is written from | The model warns; a `.brep` URL makes `loadCAD` throw a `TypeError` that lists the formats it reads | Export the part as STEP |
| Load time and memory | Not measured on the engine's machines yet | | | |

## Rendering

| Limit | Starts at | Why | What you see | Escape hatch |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Black hole ray budget (`@margoengine/shader/black-hole`) | Enforced by design: each ray gets at most `steps` (default 260) fourth-order Runge-Kutta steps through Kerr spacetime. The null condition stays under 1e-5 on escaping rays (packages/shader/test/black-hole.test.js) and drifts more on retrograde captured rays inside 4 M. | A fixed budget keeps the full-screen pass bounded. | Rays that graze the photon orbit and neither escape nor fall in within the budget end dark, a hair inside the photon ring. | Raise `hole.steps` for stills. |
| Negated scaled components in a division on the Radeon 680M (D3D12) | Measured 2026-11-14 with packages/shader/test/negated-division-check.mjs (driver 32.0.21030.2001, Edge 157): `(-(v * 2.0).z) / (v * 2.0).x` and the same inside atan2 lose their sign; the RTX A6000 and every WebGL2 path are exact. | Below Margo: the driver's D3D12 shader compiler (docs/known-bugs.md). | Margo's own shaders avoid the pattern; a user shader that divides a negated component of a constant-scaled vector gets the wrong sign on that GPU. | Negate outside the call (`-atan2(v.z, v.x)`), negate before scaling, or divide by a length. |
| A derivative used only inside a per-pixel branch, WebGL2 layer on ANGLE Direct3D 11 (RTX A6000) | Fixed 2026-11-15 in the layer: every derivative and implicit-derivative sample of a fragment feeds the outputs through a select that never takes it, so the Direct3D 11 compile can no longer move it into the branch (docs/known-bugs.md). | One add per derivative or implicit sample on the layer; webgl2-compat/glsl +294 B gzip. | None for output: the layer returns WebGPU's differences (features.html derivativeBranch). | None needed; the black hole still keeps its derivatives in uniform control flow, which is right on every backend. |
| Texture units and large uniform blocks in one stage, WebGL2 layer on ANGLE Direct3D 11 (RTX A6000) | Fixed 2026-11-25 in the layer (KB-BOUNCE-COMPATUNITS1): ANGLE gives a uniform block of 50 or more rows a shader resource after the textures, and past 16 the GPU process crashed at the first draw ([d3d11-srv-crash-repro.mjs](../packages/webgl2-compat/test/d3d11-srv-crash-repro.mjs)). A stage whose texture units and uniform blocks pass its texture unit limit declares its blocks inside a struct of the same layout, kept as a constant buffer. | Stages within the limit are unchanged; a stage past it reads its blocks as constant buffers on Direct3D 11 (on Vulkan and GL they already are). | None: the scene of [compat-units-gpu-check.js](../scripts/compat-units-gpu-check.js) draws on ANGLE Direct3D 11, Vulkan and native WebGPU. | Texture units themselves still stop at the GL limit (16 here). Since 2026-11-26 the layer counts them per stage before linking (`device.textureUnits(descriptor)`) and refuses a pipeline past a limit with code `unsupported` (errors#texture-units, naming the stage and each binding); gltf materials past it pack their five base maps first, four units fewer. |
| Exact repeat of 4x captures, WebGL2 layer on ANGLE Direct3D 11 with NVIDIA (RTX A6000) | Measured, open (docs/known-bugs.md, "ANGLE D3D11 returns two versions of the same MSAA-resolved HDR texture"): identical WebGL2 command streams resolve to two images one float16 step (or one 8-bit level) apart in a few channels. Exact on the same GPU under ANGLE Vulkan, and on an Intel Arc 140V under ANGLE Direct3D 11 (rechecked 2026-11-25). | Below Margo: the NVIDIA Direct3D driver path; the layer's resolve is one `blitFramebuffer` with no vendor branch. | Two captures of an unchanged 4x scene can differ by one step in a few channels on that machine; 1x is exact. | Exact captures on that machine: launch the browser with `--use-angle=vulkan`, or render at 1x. |
| One directional light in core | Enforced by design: core's lighting is one direction and one radiance, plus a colourless scalar ambient. Its BRDF is glTF 2.0 Appendix B's: GGX, height-correlated Smith G2 (Heitz 2014; since 2026-11-11, before that separable), Schlick, Lambert, single scattering only (rough metals lose the energy of multiple bounces between microfacets). Clustered lights, the materials package and the other PBR shaders use the same G2 since KB6016; environment's image-based split-sum table still integrates the separable G (KB6016b, docs/known-bugs.md). | Every light model beyond one sun is an optional package, so apps that need one sun pay for one sun. | No API for a second sun in core; core's own ambient does not light metals. | `@margoengine/clustered`: up to 1,024 point and spot lights (`RangeError: Expected at most 1,024 lights` past that). `@margoengine/clustered/shadows`: shadows for up to 16 of them ([local-shadows-gpu.json](../examples/package-benchmarks/results/local-shadows-gpu.json)). `@margoengine/clustered/area` (8,946 B gzip): up to 64 rectangle area lights (`RangeError: Expected at most 64 area lights`), unshadowed, no texture bindings ([area-lights-gpu.json](../examples/package-benchmarks/results/area-lights-gpu.json)). More directional lights: `@margoengine/clustered/directional` (1,563 B gzip), up to 16 (`RangeError: Expected an array of at most 16 directional lights`), unshadowed. IES profiles: `@margoengine/clustered/ies` (3,697 B gzip), at most 16 distinct profiles, type C files only. Projector spots: `@margoengine/clustered/projector` (2,618 B gzip), at most 16 images of up to 4,096 texels a side. Physical units: `@margoengine/clustered/units` (833 B gzip). All three light entries use storage buffers, no texture bindings ([light-features-gpu.json](../examples/package-benchmarks/results/light-features-gpu.json)). Configurable ambient: `@margoengine/environment` `HemisphereLight` and `AmbientLight`, one per engine. Image-based lighting: `@margoengine/environment`. |
| 16 sampled textures and 16 samplers per shader stage | Enforced by WebGPU's guaranteed minimum; Margo's device asks for no more. gltf/pbr's physical material with directional shadows, IBL and local shadows uses exactly 16 (asserted in [instancing.test.js](../packages/gltf/test/pbr-instancing.test.js)). | Every adapter, phones included, supports 16. Requiring more would make the same app fail on some devices. | A `RangeError` naming the combination, e.g. `gltf/pbr: physical material + shadows + environment:lighting + clustered + clustered:shadows + shader patch needs 17 sampled textures per shader stage; this device allows 16`. | Drop one lighting feature for that material, or use the standard material (8 of 16 with everything attached). `VolumetricFog`, SSAO, clustered lights, area lights and light probes (`@margoengine/environment/probes`: one storage buffer; with an environment fallback they take EnvironmentLighting's place and its bindings) add no textures. Texture arrays are planned after 1.0. |
| Raster coverage far from the origin, colour against pick | Measured with [far-origin.browser.mjs](../packages/selection/test/far-origin.browser.mjs) (RTX A6000, 2026-11-10): a rotated unit box 1e5 m from the origin on a 64 x 64 canvas without MSAA. The forward-pass ID target agrees with colour on every pixel; the separate 3 x 3 pick pass (`Picking.attach(engine, {capture: false})`, overlays, custom pipelines, sections) disagrees on 7 edge pixels on native WebGPU and 6 on the WebGL2 layer. Near the origin, and at 1e5 with `FloatingOrigin`, 0 pixels disagree on both. | Core composes `model * position` and then `camera * world` in float32 world space, and no shader marks its clip position `@invariant`, so the colour shader and the pick shader may round a vertex on an edge one pixel differently once the translations are large. | A click on the outermost pixel of an edge can miss a mesh that is drawn there, or hit one that is not; the 3 x 3 neighbour fallback hides most of it. These counts compare the picked set with the colour coverage grown by one pixel; agreement of the centre pixel alone, without the fallback, is not measured, as `pick` has no exact mode (Rust engine port R23). | `FloatingOrigin` in `@margoengine/cameras/origin` keeps the camera and placed roots near local zero: 0 disagreeing pixels at 1e5 on both backends. The default `Picking.attach(engine)` reads the ID target written with the colour pass. |
| float32 coordinates | Measured on the GPU ([large-coordinates-gpu.json](../examples/package-benchmarks/results/large-coordinates-gpu.json), 10 mm part, camera 50 mm away): core alone jitters 0.38 px at 1 km and 42 px at 100 km; at 6,000 km the part is not drawn. Per-stage CPU breakdown in [large-coordinates.md](large-coordinates.md). | Core and its kernel store positions and matrices in float32: half the memory and bandwidth of float64, and the format GPUs consume. | No error. Parts shake while the camera moves, small features collapse, specular shifts (2.8° at 100 km), and far enough out geometry disappears. | `FloatingOrigin` in `@margoengine/cameras/origin` (1,258 B gzip, 0 core bytes): 0.019 px jitter at every distance up to 6,000 km, and `engine.pick` hits the part at every distance ([large-coordinates.md](large-coordinates.md#the-plugin)). Vertices or child offsets that are already kilometres from their root inside one asset must be re-centred at export. |
| Transparency | Default: transparent materials and gltf/pbr `BLEND` primitives are sorted back to front per mesh; core meshes are opaque. Measured ([oit-gpu.json](../examples/package-benchmarks/results/oit-gpu.json), a 50 % housing over gears orbited 360 × 1°): 13 steps with more than 1 % of covered pixels popping. | Sorting is exact for separate objects and needs no extra targets. | Popping where transparent parts interpenetrate or nest, as the camera moves. | `@margoengine/oit` (2,210 B gzip): 0 popping steps on the same orbit. Weighted blended OIT is an approximation: colour error against exact blending 0.5 / 4.6 / 8.7 (0-255) for 1 / 2 / 4 layers; on the batch 168 five-pane scene MAE 1.568 where `PeelOIT`, `ExactOIT` and the per-mesh sort measure 0.048, the same as Babylon.js dual depth peeling (accepted difference KB3148a: the weighted average is the method; use `PeelOIT` or `ExactOIT` for the exact over operator, `packages/oit/test/gpu/reference-check.mjs`). Transmission and custom blending keep the sorted path unless `blending` is set; limits in its [README](../packages/oit/README.md#limits-the-wboit-approximation). |
| Screen-space reflections | Enforced by method: only what is on screen reflects. Core meshes and models passed to `ssr.add(model)` (gltf/pbr, materials, terrain, water) show reflections; other custom shaders are reflected but do not reflect. Cost measured on a worst-case glossy floor ([ssr-gpu.json](../examples/package-benchmarks/results/ssr-gpu.json), quiet-gated): 2.2-2.3 ms at 1280×720, 5.8-5.9 ms at 1920×1080. | Reusing depth and colour that are already rendered avoids a second scene pass. Each custom pipeline needs its own capture into SSR's targets. | Reflections fade at screen edges and miss off-screen objects (reflection probes fill in where attached); water and terrain not added keep their own sky reflection. | `@margoengine/post/ssr` (9,068 B gzip) is itself the opt-in. Off-screen reflections: reflection probes in `@margoengine/environment/probes`; SSR removes the probes' own specular only where its ray hits on screen and keeps the probe's reflection elsewhere ([probes-gpu.json](../examples/package-benchmarks/results/probes-gpu.json): off screen the floor equals the frame without SSR, 95th percentile 0/255). Limits in the [post README](../packages/post/README.md). |
| Ray-traced reflections (`RTReflections` in `@margoengine/post/rt-reflections`, FG-17 piece 6b, 2026-11-25) | Enforced: `scene` a `GPUSceneBVH`, `shadows` a boolean, `bias` finite and at least 0, plus every SSR option. By method: where SSR's march leaves a share of the ray, one ray per pixel through the scene BVH; traced hits are lit by core's BRDF, the engine sun with a shadow ray, core's flat ambient and the instance's emissive, with one material record per instance and the triangle's flat normal; a disposed scene or one from a lost device runs as SSR. Checked on real frames ([rt-reflections-browser.mjs](../packages/post/test/rt-reflections-browser.mjs), WebGPU and the WebGL2 layer). GPU cost not measured (build phase). | Tracing only the share the screen misses keeps the march's cost and look wherever the screen has the answer; one material record per instance keeps the trace to one storage read per hit. | Off-screen things, things behind the camera and things hidden behind the depth buffer reflect; traced hits show no textures, IBL, probes, clustered lights or shadow maps, and curved meshes reflect faceted. | Put every reflected mesh in the scene with a material record close to its look; keep reflection probes for environment light at traced hits. |
| Ray-traced bounce light (`RTGI` in `@margoengine/post/rt-gi`, FG-17 piece 6c, 2026-11-25) | Enforced: `scene` a `GPUSceneBVH`, `shadows` a boolean, `bias` finite and at least 0, plus every SSGI option. By method: each SSGI ray with no screen hit traces the scene BVH from the same start, faded by distance like screen hits; traced hits are lit like `RTReflections` hits; a disposed scene or one from a lost device runs as SSGI. Checked on real frames ([rt-gi-browser.mjs](../packages/post/test/rt-gi-browser.mjs), WebGPU and the WebGL2 layer). GPU cost not measured (build phase). | Tracing only the rays the screen misses keeps SSGI's cost and look wherever the screen has the answer. | Light from off-screen and hidden surfaces bounces; no ReSTIR GI reuse or SVGF denoise (noise is SSGI's rays and blur); traced hits carry direct light only, not the multi-bounce history. | Put the bright off-screen surfaces in the scene with a material record close to their look; raise `rays` for less noise. |
| Rough reflections with contact hardening (`contactHardening` on environment's Reflector, Refractor, PBRReflector and water's WaterReflection; SSR's blur, 2026-11-25) | By method: the blur is the capture's 2x2 box mip chain read trilinearly, at most 8 levels on planar captures (footprints over 128 capture texels stop growing) and 5 half-resolution levels in SSR (over 64 pixels). Isotropic: no stretching of the reflection along the view as a GGX lobe has at grazing angles. The cone of roughness r is capped at 1.4 rad, reached near r = 0.76. | Volumetric fog | Enforced by design: one froxel grid (default 160 × 90 × 64) whatever the screen size, so shadow edges in the fog are about one froxel wide (8 × 8 px at 1280 × 720). Effects measured in [volumetric-gpu.json](../examples/package-benchmarks/results/volumetric-gpu.json). | A froxel volume makes light shafts follow real shadows at a fixed cost per frame. On the WebGL2 compatibility layer each froxel integrates its own column (steps 0 to its slice, one store) so the layer runs it on the GPU: (slices + 1) / 2 times the native steps (2,080 instead of 64 per column at the default grid), no CPU work (KB5663a, 2026-11-11). Clustered lights are integrated over each slice's depth, not sampled at points (KB-FOG-BEAM1, 2026-11-15), so a thin spot beam is one shaft; a beam much thinner than a froxel row still ripples across the screen on one frame (each column 0.762 to 1.186 of its true light for a beam 0.2 m across in froxels 0.4 m wide and 1.3 m tall, `npm run test:fog-beam-continuity:browser`), which the temporal jitter averages out. | Particles, VFX, splats and transparent surfaces are fogged only when added with `fog.add` (additive, multiply and transmission surfaces never); past `range` the fog is the smooth medium in closed form (the height fog integral along each opaque pixel's ray, lit by the horizon sky with a Sky), without shafts, noise, local lights or `volumes`, and an added transparent past `range` takes the same far air (KB-FOG-FAR-TRANSPARENT, fixed 2026-11-17); with no `depth` option the composite reads the depth a `Water` drew this frame (its surface is not in the capture's depth, KB-FOG-WATERDEPTH1), and with several `Water` surfaces in one view it reads the last one drawn, so the sea of an earlier one ends its rays at the sea bed or the sky; the default is clear air, 23 km visibility with a 1.2 km scale height (`density: 0.02` gives the fog before 2026-11-16); local fog volumes only from `/fog-volumes`; multiple scattering (`multipleScattering`) is a per-froxel estimate: it follows the froxel's own sun shadow, clustered lights add none, and f is capped at 0.95. The froxel pass keeps every binding of the lights' hooks it does not read (bounce, IES, projector, shapes, layers) statically used, so its automatic layout matches the lights' bind group (KB-FOG-HOOK-BINDINGS1, 2026-11-16; before, any such hook stopped the fog every frame). Errors: `RangeError: Volumetric grid exceeds device limit`; `VolumetricFog replaces environment Fog '<name>': set its enabled = false or remove it`; `VolumetricFog needs scene depth: attach a post capture (Tonemap, Bloom, PostStack, SSAO, TAA) first or pass options.depth`. Errors: `RangeError: Volumetric grid exceeds device limit`; `VolumetricFog replaces environment Fog '<name>': set its enabled = false or remove it`; `VolumetricFog needs scene depth: attach a post capture (Tonemap, Bloom, PostStack, SSAO, TAA) first or pass options.depth`. | `@margoengine/environment/volumetric` (13,323 B gzip) is itself the opt-in: a finer `grid` sharpens edges at a higher cost; `fog.texture` lets custom shaders (particles) sample the fog. | Far shadows (`@margoengine/shadows/distance`, 2026-11-07) | By method: only the height field casts, so what is not in it casts nothing past the reach, and overhangs do not exist. | Deforming mesh motion blur (`@margoengine/voxel-pathtracer/mesh` `previousPositions`, FG-17 piece 4b, 2026-11-25) | Each vertex moves on a straight line from `previousPositions` to `positions`, so a curved vertex path within one frame is a chord. | Volumetric clouds (`@margoengine/sky/volumetric-clouds`, 2026-11-07) | Every pixel marches up to `steps` samples (64), and each cloudy sample takes `lightSteps` (6) more toward the sun. | By method: one layer between two heights; a full-resolution march of up to `steps` samples (64) with `lightSteps` (6) toward the sun at each cloudy one, steps of at most `stepCap` (150 m) near the camera growing by a power law with distance (2026-11-17), no temporal reuse and no half-resolution pass (TAA averages a moving start under `temporal: 'auto'` when the scene has it), one layer of one blended cloud type (fair cumulus, stratus or storm from the `weather`), and the sun and moon under the deck dimmed by one two-stream share for the whole scene (`Sky.deck`), with no shadow shapes unless cloud shadows are wired, so cost follows pixels times steps (a 256 x 192 view took about 15 ms on a Radeon 680M, diagnostic). With multisampled depth the march stops at each pixel's first sample. `maxDistance` bounds the stretch of each view ray marched inside the layer, from where the ray enters it, not the distance from the camera (as Unreal's tracing max distance): a camera under the layer sees cloud at the horizon from about 138 km, faded by the haze (half at 28 km of sea-level air; the air a ray crosses is its length times the mean of exp(-height / 8 km) between the camera and the cloud since 2026-11-17, so a camera in an aircraft sees far cloud below it through the thin air it crosses). The sky light is the sky's 64 x 32 reflection map, which includes the sky's own procedural layer if that is on. Proved on one GPU, a Radeon 680M, by behaviour (coverage, depth, motion), not against a reference renderer. The light inside the cloud (2026-11-17, KB-CLOUD-DECKLIGHT1) is a plane-parallel two-stream per sample: a full deck passes and returns the light the two-stream of its own columns gives within 25 percent (RTX A6000), but light does not leak out of the sides of a finite cloud, so cumulus bases are brighter than a 3D transport would leave them; each cloudy sample takes three more base-shape samples down the column to the base (one more at night with no light to march toward). The light rays read the base shape and the view the eroded one, so the light sees about 1.5 times the optical depth the eye does (Schneider 2015's cost split); and `cloudDeckTransmittance` is the plane bound of the nominal depth, while the noise leaves columns from near 0 to about twice it, so a full deck at nominal tau 80 passes about 0.19 to 0.22 where the bound says 0.14 (the independent column approximation, Cahalan et al. 1994). | Fixed noise volumes (64³ and 32³) repeat every `scale` metres; static per-pixel jitter leaves a fine grain instead of bands. | Lower `steps` (and `lightSteps`) on slow GPUs, or shorten `maxDistance`; all are live on `clouds.options`. |

| Snow drift (`@margoengine/weather/snow-drift`, `Snow` `field`, 2026-11-17) | Enforced: `width` and `depth` 2 to 2,048 samples, at most 4,194,304; `cellSize` 0.05 to 100 m; `step` 0.5 to 600 s; every other option in its documented range (`validateSnowDrift`). | Drawn lightning bolt and the light along it (`@margoengine/sky/lightning-bolt`, 2026-11-17) | Enforced by `lightningChannel`, `channelLightPoints`, `LightningBolt` and `Weather`: detail 8 to 400, spread 5 to 85 degrees, branching 0 to 0.5, orders 0 to 3, candidates 2 to 32, eta 0 to 8, `maxSegments` 8 to 2,048 (default 768), a start above its end, finite ends; `lightning.bolt` width 0.01 to 100 m, glow 0 to 2,000 m, fade 0.001 to 1 s, scale 0 to 1,000, top 1 to 20,000 m; `lightning.light.segments` a whole number 1 to 8 and `line` a boolean; a bad value throws `TypeError` or `RangeError`. At most 4 bolts draw at once (the 4 newest live strikes). The core and glow are screen-facing ribbons from one storage buffer with maximum blending and a read-only depth test, so a hill hides the bolt but fog, rain and cloud between the camera and the channel do not dim it (the cloud deck's own flash, the whole-frame overlay and the fog's lightning light carry the scattering, and the glow is a fixed width in metres, held to 5 percent of the frame height near the camera, not a scattering model: Dobashi et al. 2001 is not built). | Ash and sea spray (`@margoengine/weather`, 2026-11-17) | Enforced by `assertState`, `coarseExtinction`, `ashForExtinction`, `seaSalt` and `validateDrive`: `ash` and `spray` 0 to 1 (100,000 ash^2 micrograms of ash and 5,000 spray^2 micrograms of dry sea salt per cubic metre); a negative or non-finite concentration, wind or extinction, a radius or density not above 0, or a negative distance throws `RangeError`; `WeatherDrive` options `ashLight` and `sprayLight` (0 to 100), `ashFromEruption` and `sprayFromSea` (boolean), `eruptions` (each with `visibility(x, z)`) and `surf` (finite [x, z] points) throw on a bad value. Lovett's (1978) sea-salt fit scatters by up to 10 times; an eruption's ash at the camera is its ground-level falling ash, not the umbrella cloud overhead; a `water:N` plugin counts as sea, a lake too; the light on the haze (`hazeLight`) treats the light the layers scatter as entering at their top (a lower bound) and leaves dust out, as `sunTransmittance` does. | Volcano, coast and storm films: ash that greys the air and takes the sun, spray that whitens the sea air and thickens at the breakers, both from the eruption and the wind without wiring. | One size per load; | Sky layers on the WebGL2 layer (`MilkyWay`, `Aurora`, accepted difference, 2026-11-15) | Measured (packages/sky/test/compat-gpu.mjs, RTX A6000, Edge, ANGLE Direct3D 11 for the layer): the frames without the layers are identical; with them 25 and 38 of the star field's 196,608 capture values and 153 of the aurora's differ, each by at most two half-float steps. Inside the shaders the solid angle stays within 5.7e-7 of float64, the aurora's shell distances within 2.2e-7 and its height within 6.6e-5 km, on both devices. | The two devices compile the same WGSL with different compilers (Tint and DXC for native WebGPU, the layer's GLSL and ANGLE's HLSL through FXC for the layer), which fuse and order multiply-adds differently, so the ray through a pixel differs by one rounding of the matrix product's terms. Both specs allow it: WGSL lets an implementation reassociate and fuse operations (W3C, "WebGPU Shading Language", 2026, section 15.7.5, https://www.w3.org/TR/WGSL/#reassociation-and-fusion), and GLSL ES 3.00 lets a * b + c be one rounded operation or two and leaves the trigonometric functions' precision undefined (Khronos, "The OpenGL ES Shading Language 3.00", 2016, section 4.5.1, https://registry.khronos.org/OpenGL/specs/es/3.0/GLSL_ES_Specification_3.00.pdf). The layer's asin and atan2 are its own helpers on this GPU, the native ones the driver's. | Any difference at all between two outputs can show as two half-float steps: Direct3D converts a shader output to a smaller float format toward zero (Microsoft, "Direct3D 11.3 Functional Specification", 2015, section 3.2.2, https://microsoft.github.io/DirectX-Specs/d3d/archive/D3D11_3_FunctionalSpec.htm), so two outputs one float32 ULP apart on either side of a half float are one half step apart before the blend, and a tie in the sum rounds them apart to two (the test's blend pair: 0.0356445275 and 0.03564453125 onto 0.0179901123 give 0.0535888672 and 0.0536499023). A tighter bound needs bit-identical float32 maths from two compilers, which neither spec promises. | Compare captures within two half-float steps, or compare float32 results within a few ULPs. |
| Light shafts (`@margoengine/sky/shafts`, 2026-11-07) | No counted threshold; the limits come from the method. | The shafts are computed in screen space, so only what is on screen takes part. | By method: screen space (Mitchell 2007), so only what is on screen occludes: a mountain or cloud off screen casts no shaft, a sun off screen still casts them from its place beyond the edge, and they fade out as the sun passes 75 degrees off the view axis; none from behind the camera or with an orthographic camera; the moon casts none. The mask is half size and reads the first sample of multisampled depth; the clouds in it are marched `cloudSamples` (12) times per texel with the clouds' own field, no haze, and from above the layer the clouds occlude nothing. Each pixel takes `samples` (48) filtered reads, so cost follows pixels (about 12 ms per frame at 256 x 192 with Bloom on a Radeon 680M, diagnostic). On a display target the light is blended after the display transform, an approximation. Proved on one GPU, a Radeon 680M, by behaviour (angle, hole, linearity, clouds). | Use it with Bloom, tonemapping or another HDR scene capture, where the blend is exact; lower `samples` (48, 8 to 128) or `cloudSamples` (12, 2 to 64) to cut cost. |

| Astronomical sky (`@margoengine/sky/astro`, 2026-11-07) | No counted threshold; the planet elements are valid 1800 to 2050. | Each part uses a published method with a stated accuracy. | By method: the sun by Meeus' low-accuracy method (about 0.01 degree), the moon by his chapter 47 series (about 10 arcseconds) with its parallax, the planets by Standish's Keplerian elements (valid 1800 to 2050; tens of arcseconds, several arcminutes for Saturn), nutation by the short series (0.5 arcsecond); aberration (up to 20.5 arcseconds) is not applied, and the planets are points, not discs; planet magnitudes are Meeus' chapter 41 except Saturn's, which includes its rings (Mallama and Hilton 2018, Eq. 10; to their printed -0.55 and +1.17 within 0.006), and Mars' is that paper's Eq. 6 with its rotation and season tables (within 0.003 of JPL Horizons on 18,786 dates from 1985 to 2045; see Mars magnitude tables below). Delta T is Espenak and Meeus' polynomials from the year -500 to 2150 (to their fits: 0.6 s apart where they meet from 1700 on, up to 4 s at -500, 500 and 1600, where Delta T itself is uncertain by minutes or more), their parabola outside. Refraction is Saemundsson's down to the apparent horizon (a true altitude of -0.574 degree, lifted 34.4 arcminutes); below it, where nothing is seen, the lift fades linearly to none at -6 degrees, so places are continuous and the geometric twilight altitudes hold. Stars are points of a 1 px Gaussian with no twinkle; on a float target the sky behind a star is dimmed by 1/64 of the star's alpha (an 8-bit target replaces it by the alpha), and stars are drawn over the moon's disc. The catalogue is the user's to serve (`fetchBrightStarCatalog`; the test copy is not shipped). Proved on one GPU, a Radeon 680M. | Set `planets: false` for dates outside 1800 to 2050, and give your own `deltaT` (seconds) where the polynomial fit is poor. |

| TAAUpscale temporal stability at silhouettes (`@margoengine/taa/upscale`, 2026-11-15) | Measured and enforced by [stability-browser.mjs](../packages/taa/test/stability-browser.mjs): a 0.1 m bright post 4 m from a camera that orbits it at 0.01 rad a frame, in front of a flat wall at 44 m, scale 0.67, 640 x 480; edge alternation (per pixel and frame, max(0, \|x[t] - 2x[t-1] + x[t-2]\| - \|x[t] - x[t-2]\|) in sRGB luma levels, over 24 frames round the post) at most 0.25, and the orbiting camera at most twice the 0.001 rad a frame one. A fragment's `vertexIndex` and `instanceIndex` are the triangle's first vertex's. `modelMatrix` leaves out an instance's matrix. A depth pass reads the main camera's values (`positionView`, `linearDepth`, the matrices and camera planes), not the light's, and a `positionNode` that reads `tangentLocal`, `tangentWorld` or `bitangentWorld` casts the mesh unmoved. | A per-pixel frame from screen derivatives would line up with the UVs, but derivatives need uniform control flow and do not exist in a vertex stage; the fixed frame works in both stages and inside any branch. | `tangentWorld` on a mesh without tangents does not follow its UVs, and in a depth pass a `positionNode` that reads `tangentLocal`, `tangentWorld` or `bitangentWorld` casts the mesh unmoved; the camera values there are the main camera's, not the light's. | Workaround: `computeTangents` from `@margoengine/geometry`, or `varying()` for a per-vertex value. |
| Skinning and morph nodes (`@margoengine/shader/deform`, 2026-11-06) | By method: four bones per vertex, linear blending, so a bone with non-uniform scale skews `skin.normal()` and strong twists lose volume. `skinningFromModel(model, primitive)` reads a loaded glTF skin, refuses `JOINTS_1`, leaves morph targets to `morphing()`, keeps bind pose bounds, and `update()` reads the last transform update, so from `onFrame` the skin runs a frame behind the joints. | The graph runs where the pass runs, which is what lets an effect sit on top without a second vertex buffer. | Every pass that draws the mesh repeats the deformation: a pose costs 16 storage reads per vertex per pass, against one compute pass for `@margoengine/animation`. TAA velocity, CPU raycasts and BVH picking do not follow it, as for any `positionNode`: they see the bind pose. | Workaround: `@margoengine/animation` for a character with no effect in the vertex stage, or one reading `positionLocal` on top of its output. |
| Scene passes (`@margoengine/shader/pass`, 2026-11-06) | By method: opaque and masked gltf/pbr surfaces only; blended surfaces, core meshes, the sky and other plugins are not in the pass, and `sceneColor` reads all of those but blended surfaces from the frame's own snapshot, for a surface that is `transparent: true`. Each model draws a second time, and `color` shades it twice. Targets are single-sampled, so edges in them are not antialiased. `velocity()` covers camera motion unless a mesh passes its previous position, and follows one camera: in a multi-view frame it holds the last view's matrix. Multi-view frames draw each view into its rectangle of the targets, but only a full-canvas view has a check, and `screenUV` is relative to the whole target. Formats must be filterable colour formats; `ScenePass` refuses `rgba32float` and integer formats. | The pass runs before the colour pass so a surface can read it in the same frame with no one-frame lag, which is what costs the second draw. `sceneColor` needs the opaque phase finished, so it costs a full-frame copy and sees no other blended surface. | Each model draws a second time and `color` shades it twice; edges in the targets are not antialiased. | Workaround: add the models that matter, and leave out what a surface need not see. |
| Utility nodes (`@margoengine/shader/utils`, 2026-11-06) | `normalMap` and `bumpNormal` work in fragment nodes only. | `parallaxUV` moves the texture lookup only, and blend modes follow the W3C formulas for colours from 0 to 1. | By method: `parallaxUV` moves the texture lookup only, so the outline stays flat and no shadow follows it; a `Texture` height is read at level 0, and views past about 84 degrees are held there. Blend modes are the W3C formulas for colours from 0 to 1, so HDR light above 1 clips. `triplanar` costs three reads per sample and blends colour only: it has no normal-map form. | Give `parallaxUV` a height function that samples with an explicit level (`texture(map, q, level).r`) in place of a `Texture` read at level 0; `PbrMaterial` with `triplanar: true` projects normal maps too. |
| Cellular noise on the GPU (`@margoengine/shader/noise`, 2026-11-06) | Distances are Euclidean only; there is no Manhattan or Chebyshev form. | By method: `voronoi2` and `voronoi3` search two cells each side, which is exact: 25 and 125 cells, three hashes each in 3D, so `voronoi3` and `worley3` cost far more per pixel than simplex. Not timed. | `voronoi3` and `worley3` cost far more per pixel than simplex. | Run it once in a compute pass, or at low resolution, and sample the result; on the CPU `new Noise(seed).worley(x, y, z)` gives the same field. |

| Points and lines of a loaded model (`@margoengine/exporters`, 2026-11-15) | By method: `exportModel` writes a model's `pointsAndLines` as glTF mode 0 (POINTS) and 1 (LINES) primitives in their mesh, in source order, with their attributes and materials. LINE_LOOP and LINE_STRIP are written as LINES, and TRIANGLE_STRIP and TRIANGLE_FAN as indexed TRIANGLES: the lists gltf/pbr decodes them to, so the vertices and indices read back the same (glTF 2.0 section 3.7.2.1, mesh.primitive.mode in section 5.24.4). | glTF 2.0 keeps points and lines; the engine exporters' scene model is triangles. STL (3D Systems 1989) and core 3MF (3MF Consortium Core Specification 1.3, mesh of triangles) have no point or line form. OBJ, PLY, COLLADA and USD have one and write it (2026-11-15): OBJ `p` and `l` elements (Wavefront Technologies, "Appendix B1. Object Files (.obj)", Advanced Visualizer manual, about 1992, https://paulbourke.net/dataformats/obj/), PLY vertices and an `edge` element of `vertex1`, `vertex2` (Greg Turk, "The PLY Polygon File Format", 1994, https://paulbourke.net/dataformats/ply/), COLLADA `<lines>` (Khronos, COLLADA 1.4.1 Specification, M. Barnes and E. L. Finch, 2008, https://www.khronos.org/collada/), USD `UsdGeomPoints` and linear `UsdGeomBasisCurves` (Pixar, OpenUSD UsdGeom schema docs, https://openusd.org/release/api/usd_geom_page_front.html). COLLADA has no point primitive. Each round-trips through this repo's readers (`packages/exporters/tests/points-lines.test.js`), which now read them: `parseOBJ` `pointIndices`/`lineIndices`, `parsePLY` `lineIndices`, `parseDAE` `geometry.lines`, `@margoengine/usdz` `curves()`. | STL, 3MF and `exportRobloxGLB` leave points and lines out, and COLLADA its points; each calls `onWarning` once per mesh or data node with code `unsupported` (default `console.warn`). Since 2026-11-15 `exportGLTF` and `exportGLB` write them as mode 0 and 1 primitives after the mesh's triangles (flattened too), without NORMAL when they have none, as glTF then draws them unlit (glTF 2.0 section 3.7.2.1; Khronos glTF 2.0 Specification, https://registry.khronos.org/glTF/specs/2.0/glTF-2.0.html), checked with the Khronos glTF validator and read back by gltf/pbr; the animated USDZ writes them as `UsdGeomPoints` and `UsdGeomBasisCurves` under their animated node, unskinned (UsdSkel binds meshes); a data primitive's `mode` (glTF names or 0 to 6) reaches every writer, and `sceneOfGLB` keeps a GLB's modes. Bundles: the Godot bundle keeps the GLB's points and lines as written (Godot's `Mesh.PrimitiveType` has POINTS, LINES and LINE_STRIP, https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/classes/class_mesh.html). Godot 4.7.2 (official build, its own `GLTFDocument` import run headless on 2026-11-15) keeps them: a GLB from `exportGLB` with a triangle, an attached line, a free line loop and a point cloud came back as one MeshInstance3D surface each, `surface_get_primitive_type` 3 (triangles), 1 (LINES) and 0 (POINTS), the line in the triangle's mesh as surface 1, every vertex kept, `KHR_materials_unlit` read as an unshaded StandardMaterial3D, and `point_size` left at 1, as Godot reads no width from glTF. The Unity profile refuses them with code `unsupported`, as it takes one atlas-bound triangle mesh; Roblox meshes are triangles (Roblox Creator Hub, mesh specifications, https://create.roblox.com/docs/art/modeling/specifications), so `exportRobloxGLB` warns, now through the caller's `onWarning`; the Unreal script imports the GLB the caller passes. What Unreal's Interchange glTF import does with POINTS and LINES primitives has no published source: Epic's pages "Importing glTF Files into Unreal Engine" (https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/en-us/unreal-engine/importing-gltf-files-into-unreal-engine) and "glTF File Format Support in Unreal Engine" (https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/unreal-engine/gltf-file-format-support-in-unreal-engine), both for Unreal Engine 5.9 and read on 2026-11-15, do not mention primitive modes, and Unreal is not run here, so nothing is claimed for it. glTF has no line width (glTF 2.0 section 3.9.7); the widths of `@margoengine/lines` and the sizes of `@margoengine/points` go in primitive extras (see the plugin row below). A strip's original mode is not kept, only its segments (OBJ and USD join them back into polylines). glTF gives a point or line no size, so USD writes a constant width, `lineWidth` (default 0.01 scene units). AR Quick Look is not known to draw Points or BasisCurves; not tried on a device. The other rivals' exporters were not compared for points and lines. | `exportModel` (`@margoengine/exporters/model`) keeps them as glTF. |
| Skin from melanin and blood (`@margoengine/materials/skin` `skinColor`, `skinProfileOf`, `skin({ melanin })`, sheet row 15, 2026-11-18) | Measured (packages/materials/test/skin-measured.test.js): the diffusion code gives Jensen et al. 2001's measured skin Rd within 0.012; the fitted Gaussians hold the Donner and Jensen 2006 two-layer profile within 0.025 of the light at radii 0.05 to 3 mm for melanin 0.002 to 0.3; the best colours inside the published ranges are 8.6 (light skin) and 6.1 (dark skin) CIELAB units from the ColorChecker skin patches; the model's median reach is 1.2 to 2.3 times Christensen and Burley 2015's Monte Carlo fit for the same dermis. | Plugin lines and point clouds (`@margoengine/exporters`, 2026-11-15) | By method: every scene writer reads the lines of a `@margoengine/lines` `Lines` plugin (`lines`) and the clouds of a `@margoengine/points` `PointsPlugin` (`pointClouds`) through `engine.plugins`, by their public fields, so exporters imports neither package. | Neural networks (`@margoengine/compute/nn`, 2026-11-05) | Enforced by method: f32 only. | Graph algorithms (`@margoengine/compute/graph`, 2026-11-05) | Enforced by method: vertices below 2^30; distances in `shortestPaths` are f32 sums, exact up to 2^24 for whole weights. `bfs` and `shortestPaths` take up to one round per edge of the longest shortest path (`shortestPaths` at most the vertex count, plus one to tell a negative cycle apart), and `connectedComponents` takes about log(vertices) rounds on the graphs tested (2,000-vertex shuffled path: under 64). Speed is not measured. | Each round runs over every edge at once with an atomic minimum, so a graph needs no frontier queue, the code is the same on the GPU and the CPU backend, and negative weights work. | A round visits every edge whether or not its source changed, so a long thin graph costs edges x its depth: a frontier-based search would do less work there. Not included: strongly connected components, minimum spanning trees, centrality. | Use whole or dyadic weights for exact sums; raise `checkEvery` on deep graphs to read back less often. |
| Workgroup autotuning (`@margoengine/compute/autotune`, 2026-11-05) | Default: 6 candidate sizes, 2 warm-up and 7 timed runs each, so 54 runs of your kernel on the first call and none on later ones. Results last for the context, or across sessions with `store`. | Measuring beats a fixed rule because the best size depends on the GPU and the kernel; timed runs take turns so drift is shared, and the median drops spikes. | The first call pays for those runs and for compiling every candidate.
