| Degree-3 splat cloud vs the storage binding (`Splats.attach`, 2026-11-08, rerun 2026-11-11) | Enforced: `setup` refuses a buffer past `maxBufferSize` or `maxStorageBufferBindingSize`. Core asks for the adapter's figures (d9be88943f), so natively the binding is the adapter's (2 GiB and more on the RTX A6000); on a default device it is 134,217,728 bytes, and on the WebGL2 layer 1 GiB at maxTextureDimension2D 8,192 since KB2604d. Degree-3 SH is 16 coefficients per channel, float32, 192 bytes a splat, so at 128 MiB 699,050 splats fit and 699,051 do not (`packages/splats/test/storage-fit.test.js`). The published truck at iteration 7,000 has 1,692,538 splats (325 MB of SH): it attaches and draws natively and on the WebGL2 layer (refused there until KB2604d, 2026-11-11). | The SH buffer is one storage binding. | On a device with the default binding size, a degree-3 cloud longer than 699,050 splats throws `RangeError: Splat attributes exceed device storage limits; use fewer splats.` A shorter degree, or no SH, fits more. | Use an adapter that offers a larger binding (core asks for it), or drop `sphericalHarmonics`. All three sizes run on a real GPU (`node packages/splats/test/gpu/scale-check.mjs`, natively and with MARGO_COMPAT=1, 2026-11-11, busy machine, diagnostic): 3,000,000 splats without SH at 13.6 ms a frame natively and 597.9 ms on the WebGL2 layer, 699,050 of degree 3 at 4.9 and 120.5 ms, the truck's 1,692,538 of degree 3 at 9.0 ms natively and 259.7 ms on the WebGL2 layer (KB2604d run; the WebGL2 figures are a speed bug in the speed-phase inventory). |
| Splat projection near the view's edge (`Splats`, 2026-11-11, KB2604f) | By method: the EWA Jacobian is linearised at the splat's view direction clamped to 1.3 times the half-view tangent, as 3DGS training does, so a splat whose centre lies far outside the view draws a narrower ellipse than its exact projection would. The Truck capture at iteration 7,000 scores 20.882 dB PSNR against its `000001` photograph (full cloud, RTX A6000, `packages/splats/scripts/truck-photo.mjs`); not the paper's dataset average. | Trained captures expect this clamp; without it splats beside the camera stretch across the frame. | A large splat just outside the view may show a slightly smaller edge than an exact ray-traced Gaussian. | None needed for trained captures; for exact Gaussians at the edge, widen the field of view. |
| Core meshes culled on the GPU (`CulledMeshes`, 2026-11-10) | Enforced: up to `maxStorageBufferBindingSize / 96` instances of one geometry, 1,398,101 at the default 128 MiB binding, else a `RangeError` naming the figure. Before this, past 1,048,574 instances of one geometry core's instance buffer doubles to 2,097,150 slots (201 MB) and CulledMeshes bound all of it and sized its own lists to the next power of two: every frame failed with `gpu-lost`. | Compressed splat input (`parseSpz`, `parseSog`, 2026-11-10) | Enforced: an SPZ version 2 or 3 gzip stream is cut off with a `RangeError` once it expands past 195,000,016 bytes (a 16-byte header and 3,000,000 splats of degree 3 at 65 bytes each, the largest body the reader accepts); a deflated SOG ZIP entry once it passes the size its directory declares. | Markup and style sheets (`@margoengine/ui/markup`, 2026-11-08) | Enforced: well-formed markup (every tag closed, attribute values quoted, no repeated attribute or id); known elements, properties and actions; numbers, true or false, and 1, 2 or 4 numbers where an option takes them. Not done: DOCTYPE, CDATA, namespaces and named references beyond the five of XML; pseudo-classes, attribute selectors, `+`, `~`, `@` rules and `!important`; restyling a built screen. Unmeasured: build time of large screens (LIM-528). | A small subset keeps the parser and the cascade a few hundred lines, and the selectors are the ones designers use for widget trees. | A sheet written for the web may use selectors the parser rejects, with the line named. | Give the element a class or an id; set options in code after `buildScreen` for anything dynamic. |
| Label decluttering (`@margoengine/labels/declutter`, 2026-11-08) | Enforced: `padding` 0 or more, `cell` 1 or more, `positions` pairs of finite numbers, `priority` a number (infinity allowed). By method: boxes are the elements' `offsetWidth` by `offsetHeight` times their distance scale, measured once; the greedy order is priority, then shown last time, then distance, so a lower label can lose a place a later one would have left free. Unmeasured: cost per frame with thousands of labels (LIM-532). | Greedy placement by rank is the standard fast method for point labels and keeps the important ones; a full search for the most labels is far slower. | A label whose text grows keeps its old box until `remeasure()`; a rotated or round element is treated as its bounding box. | Call `label.remeasure()` after changing its text; give labels that must stay a higher `priority`. |
| Depth with CSS 3D objects (`CSS3DObject` in `@margoengine/labels`, 2026-11-08) | By method: an element is cut at the near plane by its layout rectangle (`offsetWidth` by `offsetHeight`, measured once until `remeasure()`), so content painted outside its box is cut with it; an element not laid out yet measures 0 and is shown or hidden by its origin. Not done: no per-pixel depth test against the canvas; the `occlude` hook hides a whole object. While cut, `clip-path` flattens the element's own 3D children (LIM-540). | HTML over the canvas cannot read the depth buffer, and CSS perspective does not clip at the near plane, so the renderer clips by geometry. | A panel half inside a wall shows whole in front of it; a shadow painted outside the box is cut with the box. | Hide panels behind geometry with the `occlude` hook and a raycast; call `remeasure()` after content changes size. |
| Leader lines and callouts (`@margoengine/labels/callouts`, 2026-11-08) | Enforced: `width`, `dot` and `minLength` finite and 0 or more; `screenOffset` two finite numbers. By method: one straight line per label from its projected point to the nearest point of its box (the measured element size times its distance scale), drawn under every label; a label whose box covers its point, or lies within `minLength` of it, gets none. Not done: lines are not kept from crossing labels or each other, and `Declutter` places boxes without looking at lines. Unmeasured: cost per frame with many callouts (LIM-542). | A leader line is a pointer, so the nearest point keeps it short; routing lines around labels is a layout problem of its own. | Two callouts whose offsets cross draw crossing lines; a line can run under another label. | Choose offsets that fan out from the model (left labels to the left), or let a wrapped `Declutter` move overlapping boxes. |
| Scaled ancestors (`LabelRenderer` in `@margoengine/labels`, 2026-11-08) | By method: the overlay follows CSS scales on the canvas's ancestors, read from drawn widths each update; in another `parent` the canvas's scale is its drawn width over `offsetWidth`, a whole number of pixels, so a canvas of fractional CSS width is matched to about half a pixel across. Not done: rotations and skews on the ancestors, and any transform on the canvas element itself (LIM-546). | `getBoundingClientRect` reports drawn sizes and `offsetWidth` layout sizes, so their ratio is the scale; a rotation needs the full matrix, which the DOM does not give. | Labels drift off their points inside a rotated element or on a canvas with its own transform. | Put the transform on an ancestor of the canvas, not the canvas; keep rotated frames for static pages. |
| Smooth partial occlusion (`fade` in `@margoengine/html`, 2026-11-08) | Enforced: `radius` 0 to 256 CSS pixels, `samples` a whole number 2 to 8, `duration` 0 to 10 s. By method: the opacity is the clear share of a `samples` x `samples` grid of depth tests over a square around the anchor, so it moves in steps of 1 / samples squared and a gap in the geometry narrower than the grid spacing can be missed; samples off the canvas count as clear. Both backends (WebGL2 by occlusion queries, LIM-552); results arrive a frame or two late (LIM-550). Unmeasured: cost per frame at full capacity (up to 64 depth reads an anchor). | One compute dispatch reads every anchor's grid from the shared depth target, so the fade needs no extra render pass; the grid is what bounds its work. | An anchor at a thin pole or a fence fades by the share of the grid the pole covers, not by the share of the element's box. | Raise `samples` for finer steps, or `radius` to the element's half size to fade by its whole box. |
| Failed allocations on the WebGL2 layer (`@margoengine/webgl2-compat`, 2026-11-11) | By method: after each `bufferData`, `texStorage2D`/`texStorage3D` and `renderbufferStorage` the layer reads `gl.getError()` once; `GL_OUT_OF_MEMORY` becomes a `GPUOutOfMemoryError` (`CompatOutOfMemoryError`) on the `out-of-memory` error scope or `uncapturederror`, any other GL error an `internal` one ([device.test.js](../packages/webgl2-compat/test/device.test.js), "an allocation the driver refuses is an out-of-memory error"). A queue write, or a submit, that uses a destroyed buffer, texture or query set is a validation error and makes no GL call, as WebGPU refuses it (a failed submit runs none of its command buffers); before, the deleted objects raised GL errors that the next allocation reported as its own ([destroyed-use.test.js](../packages/webgl2-compat/test/destroyed-use.test.js), KB-C34c). Uncaptured errors are dispatched in a task of their own, and `onSubmittedWorkDone` resolves in a later task, also on a destroyed device, as on WebGPU. | WebGL2 reports a failed allocation only through `getError`, and the object then draws as if empty. | One `getError` per allocation (none per draw or submit); each command encoder keeps one list of the resources its commands use (one entry per pass attachment, bind group, vertex, index or indirect buffer, copy and bundle), walked once at submit; on browsers that defer allocation the error may come at first use instead, which the layer does not see. | Watch `out-of-memory` scopes or `uncapturederror` around large allocations, as on WebGPU. |
| New textures and sRGB twins of compressed textures on the WebGL2 layer (`@margoengine/webgl2-compat`, 2026-11-11) | By method: every new texture level and layer is written with zeros at creation (a clear per level and layer for renderable formats; a whole-level upload from a zero-filled pixel unpack buffer for the rest, the buffer kept up to 4 MiB; compressed formats left to the browser), work the browser did lazily before. A block-compressed texture whose `viewFormats` name its sRGB twin keeps its written blocks in memory (up to the texture's own size) until a twin view is made, then holds a second GPU copy of that size instead. | Firefox warns at every lazy initialisation; GL cannot render into or reinterpret a compressed texture, so the twin needs the blocks. | Correct pictures; creation does the zeroing the browser did at first use. | Leave the twin out of `viewFormats` when no twin view is made. |
| Compressed views of another dimension on the WebGL2 layer (`@margoengine/webgl2-compat`, 2026-11-16, KB-COMPAT-DECODERS1) | By method: a `2d-array`, `cube` or one-layer `2d` view of a compressed texture whose GL storage has another target reads a decoded copy, made at its first use: `rgba32float` (16 bytes a texel, every level; `rgba16float`, 8 bytes, where 32-bit floats cannot be filtered), one per view target, format and first layer, redrawn from the blocks when they change. A context that renders no float format refuses such a view with code `unsupported`. Equal to native WebGPU bit for bit in the features check (BC1, RTX A6000, ANGLE D3D11). | GL fixes a texture's target and cannot copy or render compressed blocks; the GPU's decoder is the only exact source. | Such views work; each costs GPU memory several times the compressed size. | View compressed cube textures as `cube` and others as `2d`, or pass `textureBindingViewDimension` at creation, so the view matches the storage and no copy is made. |
| Compressed copies on the WebGL2 layer (`@margoengine/webgl2-compat`, 2026-11-16, KB-COMPAT-DECODERS1) | By method: a compressed texture made with `COPY_SRC` keeps the bytes of all its blocks in page memory (its own compressed size), updated by every block write; `copyTextureToTexture` and `copyTextureToBuffer` out of it read them, equal to native WebGPU bit for bit in the features check. A copy out of a compressed texture made without `COPY_SRC` is a TypeError, as WebGPU makes it a validation error. | WebGL2 can neither read compressed texels back nor copy them between texture objects. | Copies work; each such texture costs its compressed size again in page memory. | Leave out `COPY_SRC` on compressed textures that are never copied from. |
| Storage bindings on the WebGL2 layer (`@margoengine/webgl2-compat`, 2026-11-10, group total and binding size raised 2026-11-11) | Enforced: the adapter's `maxStorageBufferBindingSize` is 16 x maxTextureDimension2D squared bytes, 1 GiB at 8,192 and 64 MiB on a 2048 context, and its `maxBufferSize` is that or WebGPU's 256 MiB, whichever is larger; as in WebGPU a device keeps the default 128 / 256 MiB (less on a smaller context) unless `requiredLimits` asks for more, which core does (KB2604d, [device.test.js](../packages/webgl2-compat/test/device.test.js) "limits come from the context");  a bind group with a storage binding over it, or whose storage bindings together pass one RGBA32UI data texture of maxTextureDimension2D x maxTextureDimension2D texels (1 GiB at 8,192, 64 MiB at 2,048), reports a WebGPU validation error naming the figure and binds nothing ([device.test.js](../packages/webgl2-compat/test/device.test.js)). `createBuffer` past the device's `maxBufferSize` reports a validation error and allocates nothing (a RangeError when mapped at creation), as in WebGPU (KBnew-compat-maxbuffer, device.test.js "createBuffer refuses a size past the device maxBufferSize"). The texture is 2,048 texels wide and grows wider only for a group that would otherwise pass maxTextureDimension2D in height. | WebGL2 has no storage buffers: the layer reads them through one data texture per bind group. A storage buffer a compute shader writes is drawn into R32UI word textures of 4,096 x 8,192 words (128 MiB) each, as many as the buffer needs, one draw per texture the binding reaches ([compute-browser.mjs](../packages/webgl2-compat/test/compute-browser.mjs), a 160 MiB scatter target, and a 40 MiB one over three 2,048 x 2,048 word textures on a 2,048 context). Steady-frame work for buffers up to 128 MiB is unchanged: one word texture, one draw. | Before 2026-11-10 an over-size binding reached GL unchecked and failed there; from then to 2026-11-11 a group past 256 MiB in total was refused, so a 3,000,000-splat cloud (360 MB in its projection group) did not attach; until KB2604d a binding stopped at 128 MiB, so the 1,692,538-splat truck's 325 MB of SH did not attach. A storage buffer also keeps a CPU copy on the layer, so a 1 GiB buffer costs 1 GiB of page memory besides the GPU's. | Keep each storage binding within the device's `maxStorageBufferBindingSize`. |
| Occlusion on WebGL2 (`HTML` in `@margoengine/html`, 2026-11-08) | By method: on the `@margoengine/webgl2-compat/preview` preview backend each depth test is an `ANY_SAMPLES_PASSED` occlusion query of a one-pixel point drawn after the scene at the anchor's depth less `depthBias`, through the renderer's own camera matrix; one round is in flight per anchor, read when the browser makes it available (a frame or more later); samples off the view count as clear; `fade` runs here too, so the fade row's "WebGPU only" no longer holds (LIM-552). Not done: geometry other passes draw after the html pass is not seen. Unmeasured: cost per frame with many anchors (one draw call and query per test). | The preview draws straight to the canvas, whose depth WebGL2 cannot sample or read back; a query against it is the only test of that depth. | Many anchors with `fade` on WebGL2 cost samples x samples draws each per round. | Keep `samples` small on WebGL2, or use WebGPU, where one dispatch tests every anchor. |
| DOM drawn into the scene (`HTMLTexture` in `@margoengine/html/texture`, 2026-11-08) | Enforced: `pixelRatio` 0.25 to 4, a size above 0 (the element's CSS size or `width` and `height`), a matrix of 16 finite numbers, WebGPU (the WebGL2 fallback throws). By method: the element is drawn as a texture, so the quad shows a picture of it, drawn again on a mutation, input, focus, hover or HTML-in-canvas paint event, a frame or more after the change; with `'foreign-object'` the element's fonts and images must be data URLs the SVG image embeds (it loads nothing), and changes no event shows (a loaded font, a style sheet) need `invalidate()`; the pointer is routed by the nearest quad under it, so scene geometry in front of a quad does not stop the pointer reaching the element (LIM-556). Unmeasured: raster cost per redraw, cost with many surfaces. | The browser's own hit test, focus and events reach the element only where it is laid out, so the invisible holder is moved under the pointer; HTML-in-canvas snapshots only elements inside the viewport, so the holder rests at its top left. | A panel half behind a wall still takes clicks through the wall. | Turn `interactive` off on a surface while geometry covers it, or keep interactive quads unblocked. |
| Anchor capacity (`HTML` in `@margoengine/html`, 2026-11-08) | Enforced: `capacity` a whole number 1 to 1,048,576 (default 1,024), so at most 16 MiB of anchor points and 16,384 workgroups of 64. By method: slots and buffers grow by doubling to the capacity and never shrink; per-frame work runs to the highest slot ever used, so removing the newest anchors does not shorten it; buffers grow at the next depth test, so a new anchor past the old size waits one test (LIM-559). Unmeasured: cost per frame with many anchors (each still has its own DOM element; on WebGL2 one query a test). | Growing to the anchors in use keeps a large `capacity` free until it is used; one dispatch still tests every anchor. | A page that adds 100,000 anchors and removes most keeps their slots and the work to the highest. | Reuse anchors, or make a new `HTML` overlay after removing most of them. |
| Terrain on the WebGL2 compatibility layer (`@margoengine/terrain` with `@margoengine/webgl2-compat`, 2026-11-08) | Measured: native and layer pictures differ by at most 1 of 255 per pixel (rules, painted weights and a hole, the runtime virtual texture); a frame of six clipmap levels is 6 GL draws and 48 GL calls on the layer (50 with the virtual texture); Radeon 680M, ANGLE on Direct3D 11. Unmeasured: frame time on the layer, other GPUs and ANGLE back ends (LIM-503). | The terrain's passes are draws only, which the layer translates as they are, so terrain has no WebGL2 route and no WebGL2 code. | Only the root entry and `rvt` are checked on the layer; `layers-pbr`, `stream`, `sculpt`, `deform`, `displace` and `blend` have not run there (the compute passes of `sculpt`, `deform` and `displace` would run on the layer's own tiers). | Call `install()` from `margoengine/webgl2-compat` before `Engine.create`; keep to the root entry and `rvt` on WebGL2 until the others are checked. |
| Planet terrain (`@margoengine/terrain/planet`, 2026-11-08) | Enforced: `radius` above 0, `resolution` an even 4 to 64, `maxLevel` 0 to 24, `screenError` above 0, `budget` 0 or more, `maxPatches` 6 to 16,384, `height` finite. Measured (diagnostic, Node on the busy AMD mini PC): about 1.3 ms of main-thread time to build a patch at resolution 32 with the default ground; a view 100 m above the ground at 1280 x 720 needs 1,682 patches (2.2 s with no budget). Unmeasured: frame cost, other GPUs (LIM-507). | Heights are sampled on the CPU in float64, so any height function works and patches draw relative to the eye with no float32 world coordinates; the price is main-thread building, spread over frames by `budget`. A split builds all four children (culled ones too), so the view never shows a hole while it refines. | By method: no shadows, SSR, lighting effects or layer textures; colours by height and slope only; one view a frame; the drawn surface is the height sampled at the patch's vertices, so `altitude` reads the exact ground, not the drawn one; past `maxPatches` the farther ground stays coarser; the GPU holds about 24 KB a patch (50 MB at the default 2,048). | Raise `budget` for faster refinement, lower `screenError` or `resolution` for fewer patches, and keep a camera above `altitude` 0. |
| Orthographic tile selection (`TilesRenderer`, 2026-11-07) | Proved in Node on generated view-projection matrices (LIM-370), not on a GPU. By method: a camera counts as orthographic when its matrix's clip w row is (0, 0, 0, w) to 1e-9 of w; the view height is 2 w over the length of the clip y row, in world units, divided by the frame's scale. | Core keeps one view-projection matrix for every camera, so the renderer reads it rather than a camera type. | Before the first frame core's matrix is all zeros and selection is perspective; a projection that is neither (a clip w that changes only slightly with depth) is read as perspective. | Call `tiles.update()` after the first frame, or give `Tileset.update` your own `orthographicHeight`. |
| Hosted tileset sign-in and credits (`@margoengine/tiles/ion`, 2026-11-07) | Proved in Node against stand-in servers that answer as the ion endpoint and a keyed service are documented to (LIM-374); no live service was asked (no token on this machine). Credits read from real Khronos GLBs. By method: one renewal per expiry, after a 401 from the asset host; only `asset.copyright` of drawn glTF, b3dm and i3dm tiles is counted. | Tokens are short-lived and the services document a 401 on expiry; the copyright of what is drawn is what the services ask to show. | An ion asset of an external type (Bing, Google 2D maps) is refused with code `unsupported`; nothing draws a logo for you. | Stream external imagery with its own provider; show `credits.html()` where a service needs its logo. |

## Entities

| Limit | Starts at | Why | What you see | Escape hatch |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Bulk transform writes (`TransformWriter`, `@margoengine/scene/bulk`, 2026-11-05) | The mesh list is fixed when the writer is made. Measured diagnostic, 10,000 meshes, Node, CPU only, other jobs running: positions 0.12 ms against 0.59 with setters, positions and quaternions 0.84 against 1.60, positions and Euler 0.80 against 1.69. | One pass checks every value first, so a bad row changes nothing; rotations still cost a quaternion or Euler conversion per mesh, the same maths as the setters. | A mesh disposed since the writer was made throws `disposed`, even when another mesh took its slot. | Make a new writer when the list changes; `{ from, count }` writes part of a list. |
| Scene graph helpers (`@margoengine/scene`, 2026-11-05) | Each `getWorldPosition`, `getWorldQuaternion` and `worldMatrix` call walks up the parents, at most 64 levels. | They read the local values, so a result is right before any frame; `mesh.matrix` is the last frame's. | Joint limits apply at the next frame, so a value outside its limit counts as written until then. Under a rotated, unevenly scaled parent `getWorldQuaternion` and `getWorldScale` give the nearest values. | Read `mesh.matrix` in a per-frame loop over many meshes; `worldMatrix` stays exact under shear. |
| Scheduler (`@margoengine/ecs/schedule`) | Enforced: one fixed step size per `Schedule`, at most `maxSteps` (default 8) steps an update; time past that is dropped. Systems are synchronous and single threaded; the fixed phase always runs before the frame phase. | A cap stops a long stall from costing more steps than the next frame can pay for, which would snowball. | `update` returns the steps run and `schedule.dropped` holds the seconds lost. A frame system ordered before a fixed one throws MargoError `'state'`. | Raise `maxSteps`, or run a second `Schedule` for a second rate. |
| Change detection (`@margoengine/ecs/changes`) | Enforced by method: only `component.add`, `remove`, `touch` and `world.destroy` are seen. A write straight into `fields` is invisible until `touch` reports it, and a row counts as changed even when the value written is the same. 24 bytes per world slot per tracker. | `fields` are plain typed arrays, so loops over them stay at full speed; intercepting each write would cost that speed. | The entity is missing from `changed`. | Call `component.touch(entity)` after direct writes. |
| Query filters and tags (`@margoengine/ecs/query`, `world.tag`) | Enforced: `with` needs at least one term, and a `Query` cannot run inside its own `forEach`. Entities that start matching during `forEach` wait for the next call. A tag stores no fields but keeps the 8 bytes per world slot of its entity index. | The smallest `with` store is the list to walk, so there must be one. The match list is one buffer per query. | MargoError `'state'` or `TypeError`. | Use a second `Query` to nest. |
| Engine bridge (`@margoengine/ecs/engine`) | Enforced: one way, component to mesh, and one mesh per entity. Each group is whole or absent. Values pass through `TransformWriter` from `@margoengine/scene/bulk`, an optional peer, one write per changed group for each run of changed rows, so scattered changes cost a write each; `sync` costs one pass over the links even when nothing moved, as the setter loop did, and one pass to rebuild the writer after a link changes. Parents are not copied. | The setters' checks and the Euler view of `mesh.rotation` must hold, so the bridge cannot write the store columns blindly. | `TypeError`, `RangeError` or MargoError `'disposed'` from `link`, `sync` or the constructor. | Read a mesh back by hand when something else moves it. |
| Relationships (`@margoengine/ecs/relations`) | Enforced by method: pairs carry no data of their own and live in Maps and Sets, not typed arrays. `acyclic` pays a walk up from the target on every `add`. | Pairs change rarely next to component rows, and Sets keep both directions direct to read. | A loop on an `acyclic` relation throws `TypeError`. | Keep per-pair numbers in a component on the source. |
| Growable worlds (`@margoengine/ecs/growable`, accepted difference in speed, 2026-11-05) | Enforced: at most `limit` slots, 1,000,000 at most, and a slot retires after about 4,294,967,295 / `limit` reuses. Measured ([ecs-growable.mjs](../examples/package-benchmarks/ecs-growable.mjs), Node 26, three runs on a busy machine, diagnostic): a loop over 100,000 rows takes about twice as long as on a fixed `World`, ratio 2.02 to 2.09. | Ids are 32 bits and spaced by `limit`, so they survive growth. Resizable buffers keep every array reference valid while growing; plain arrays would be replaced, and a cached `fields.x` would silently write to the old copy. A fixed `World` pays nothing. | `create` throws `RangeError` at the limit. | Use a fixed `World` when a bound is known; lower `limit` for more reuses per slot. |
| Roll in `FlyControls` and `TrackballControls` (`enableRoll`, 2026-11-05) | Proved on stand-in input, synthetic events on a fake element. By method: off by default, so the horizon stays level. With it on, the control owns `camera.up`. Orbit, map, first-person, pointer-lock and walk controls do not roll. Not checked: an engine `CameraProjection` answers `camera.up` with its own `up` for an exactly vertical view, so a roll is not kept at that one orientation. | The level controls read their frame from world +Y; a roll would fight it. | Turning `enableRoll` off leaves the camera rolled, and `camera.up = [0, 1, 0]` throws at an exact vertical view. | Level the horizon with the view off the vertical, or use `ArcballControls`. |
| Gizmo occlusion (`occlude` on `TransformControls`, 2026-11-05) | By method: only the drawing is hidden, through the scene's depth buffer. Picking is on the CPU and has no scene depth, so a hidden handle can still be grabbed. | Reading depth back to the CPU would stall the frame on every pointer move. | The part of each arrow inside the object is hidden as well, and a handle behind a wall still takes the pointer. | Leave `occlude` off (the default), or filter grabs in the app. |
| Third-person camera (`ThirdPersonControls` in `@margoengine/controls/third-person`, 2026-11-05) | Proved on stand-in input, synthetic events on a fake element. By method: the arm is swept with nine rays a frame, not a true sphere, so an object thinner than the gaps between the rays can slip through the sweep. Skinned models collide in their bind pose, as for the bvh Raycaster. Not checked: the camera has no collider of its own, so it does not stop for something that moves into it from the side beyond the rim rays. | Nine rays against cached trees is cheap on the CPU and needs no physics package. | A pole near the camera may graze the view for a frame. | Raise `probeRadius`, or drive the camera from `@margoengine/physics` shape casts. |
| `DragControls` rotate mode, groups and children (2026-11-05) | Proved on stand-in input, synthetic events on a fake element. By method: a turn goes about the grabbed object's origin, not the grab point or the group's centre. `recursive` and `transformGroup` follow core mesh children; a model is always dragged whole. | A model's nodes are not meshes the control can list. | A group with a far-off grabbed member swings wide. | Grab a member near the middle, or use `TransformControls`. |
| Orbit target radius and `orthoZoom` (2026-11-05) | Proved on stand-in input, synthetic events on a fake element. By method: `minTargetRadius` and `maxTargetRadius` act on the target and move the camera by the same step, after `targetBounds`, so the sphere wins when the two disagree. A target exactly on `cursor` leaves along +X. `orthoZoom` needs a `CameraProjection` or a `projection` with a numeric `zoom`. | The shell has no way to slide past its centre, and a plain camera has no zoom. | With `minTargetRadius` above 0, the target cannot pass through `cursor`. | Set `minTargetRadius` to 0, or keep the shell thick. |
| Several objects on `TransformControls` (`attachMany`, `pivot`, 2026-11-05) | Proved on stand-in input, synthetic events on a fake element. By method: an object's size has only its own axes, so a non-uniform stretch along another frame gives each axis its share instead of a shear, exact when the axes line up or the factors match. A mesh with an attached ancestor follows that ancestor. | Meshes store position, rotation and scale, with no shear. | A turned object scaled unevenly in `world` space keeps its shape family, not the sheared shape a matrix would give. | Scale evenly, or scale in the object's own axes with `individual` and `local`. |
| Interactions (`@margoengine/input/interactions`, 2026-11-05) | Proved on stand-in input, dispatched events on a fake clock; no real gamepad has run it. By method: time is read once per update, so a rule is exact to one tick, and a 500 ms frame can turn a tap into a canceled tap. Rules do not arbitrate: a tap and a double press on one action both run. A gamepad press shorter than one update is unseen (gamepads are polled); keys, mouse and touch buttons keep it for one update. | Rules run on the sampled action, so they work on every device and on replayed input. Waiting for one rule to fail before another fires would add `gap` of delay to every press. | A single tap beside a double press fires on the first press too. | Use the double press's `canceled` as the single press. Run input on a fixed tick. |
| Local players (`@margoengine/input/players`, 2026-11-05) | Proved on stand-in input, dispatched events on a fake clock; no real gamepad has run it. By method: one mouse and one keyboard per browser, because the browser merges every keyboard and every mouse into one, so `'keyboard'` cannot tell two physical keyboards apart. A gamepad is known by its index: a pad that comes back on another index is a new device. Each player's `Input` holds its own listeners, 8 on the target per player. | The browser gives keyboard and mouse events no device id. The Gamepad API's `id` names a model, so two identical pads share it. | Two players on keyboards share one with `schemes`. A pad plugged back after another took its index goes to that index's owner. | Listen for `lost`, pause and use `assign` to pair the pad again. |
| Gyro aiming (`@margoengine/input/motion`, 2026-11-05) | Not measured on a real device: the sign and axis maps come from the Device Orientation specification and are tested with synthetic events. One event integrates 100 ms at most. Drift is not corrected after `calibrate`. Aim is in the screen's frame, so a device held at an angle turns the view about the screen's up, not the world's. Needs a secure page, and on iOS a tap. | No phone is in the test setup. A gap in sensor events must not jump the aim. | `available` stays false on a desktop. Browsers that break the specification's axis order would turn the wrong way. | Offer an invert option in your settings: `scale: -1` on the binding. |
| Input recording (`@margoengine/input/replay`, 2026-11-05) | Proved on stand-in input, dispatched events on a fake clock; no real gamepad has run it. By method: records what bindings gave, one value per tick, so a replay matches only if the game also steps the same way: same ticks, same `dt`, same random seed. Events between ticks are not stored, and raw positions from `Gestures` or `Pen` samples are not part of a clip. A recorder grows until you drop it: about 3 numbers per change and 1 per tick. | Input is recorded at the level the game reads, which is what makes a replay independent of devices. | A game that reads `performance.now` itself drifts from its recording. | Step the game on a fixed tick and take time from `replay.time`. |
| Pen input (`@margoengine/input/pen`, 2026-11-05) | Not measured with real hardware: tested with synthetic pointer events. Values are what the browser reports: a pen or driver without pressure gives 0.5 while touching, and without tilt gives 0 (upright). One pen at a time: two pens on one element share its readings. | The Pointer Events specification sets those fallback values, and a page cannot tell them from real readings. | A mouse-like stylus paints at an even half pressure. | Offer a fixed-size brush option. | Navmesh routes (`@margoengine/navmesh`, 2026-11-10, search over portals 2026-11-11) | By method: A* runs over portals (each way into a polygon is a node, KB2604b), crosses each portal where the walk from the entry to the goal through it is shortest, keeps for each portal the entry with the lowest cost so far plus straight line on, and breaks ties by position, so a mesh loaded from a file routes the same way; the funnel then pulls the corridor taut, so a route is near the shortest, not proved shortest (Polyanya-style exact search is not built); an off-mesh link cheaper than the straight line between its ends scales the straight-line estimate down to the cheapest link's cost per metre (0 for a free teleporter, which makes the search plain Dijkstra and expands more polygons). | The estimate must stay a lower bound of the cost for A* to return the cheapest corridor (Hart, Nilsson and Raphael 1968); one entry point per polygon is what a polygon search can hold. | Routes through cheap links are the cheapest, checked against a Floyd-Warshall oracle; with area costs, a later and dearer entry into a portal can be cheaper onward and is not kept, so a route can cost a little more than the true optimum. Measured: every straight walk over an open voxel floor (363 rows) stays straight across tile lines; on a generated 40 m city the tiled routes are within 0.503 of one whole mesh's on 90 seeded pairs. Accepted difference: on the gapped floor of perf history entry 94 Margo's path is 23.823 against Detour's 23.778 (0.19 percent). Cause: the eroded walkable edge follows whole cells, so the hole's corner is the square cell corner (1.25, 8.25), 0.354 from the true corner, where a disc agent of radius 0.25 could cut closer (bound about 23.69). Margo keeps the radius from every drop exactly; the trade-off is up to one cell at convex corners. | Give a link a cost of at least its length when it need not be a shortcut, so the estimate stays whole; split a big costly polygon so entries sit closer together. |

By method: density is a 1 m Gaussian over the agent and those ahead in a 3 m grid, rebuilt every update; Weidmann's fit is in metres. | Weidmann's relation is the fit to the measured studies, and only the people ahead slow a walker. | Unidirectional density only: counterflow and crossing streams slow by ORCA alone, not by a measured counterflow diagram; no pushing or crowd pressure (crowd crush) and no group walking. | Crowd walls, corners and arrival (`@margoengine/navmesh` `Crowd`, 2026-11-25) | Measured (packages/navmesh/test/crowd-walls.test.js, crowd-corners.test.js, crowd-arrival.test.js): no frame where a wall stops an agent through a Z bend at 3.5 m/s or in a diagonal corridor; no agent turning back to a missed corner; agents sent to seats 0.5 m apart, or nine to one point, all arrive within 30 s and end at least their radii apart (within 1 mm). By method: the walls are the border edges in front of the agent within `maxSpeed * maxSpeed / maxAcceleration`, gathered through portals every update; the border bounds the agent's centre (radius 0), as a mesh built with `walkableRadius` means; a corner is passed once the next one can be walked to straight. | Jump links (`@margoengine/navmesh/links`, 2026-11-07) | Enforced: radius, height, `maxFall`, `spacing`, each jump's height and distance finite and above 0; `climb` and `jumpCost` finite and 0 or more; `directions` 1 to 64. ## Copies of a model

| Limit | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Textures of `cloneModel` copies | Shared: one GPU texture per device, image and format, freed with its last holder (`p-morph`: 7 textures for 100 copies, not 700). A second model loaded from the same file holds its own images, so it uploads its own textures. |
| Geometry of `cloneModel` copies (2026-11-06) | Shared: vertex and index buffers per device, asset and array, and in the deformation arena one copy of the bind-pose vertices, morph deltas and skin influences per page. Each animated copy still adds 80 B per vertex of deformed output, 64 B per bone and its morph weights, because those are what differ between copies. A second model loaded from the same file packs and uploads its own. |
| GPU morph weights (`@margoengine/animation/morph-gpu`, 2026-11-06) | Not measured for speed yet: the 16 B a frame and one dispatch per page are counted, the frame time is not. `Animation.upload` still loops over each copy to check its weights and bones, so CPU work is smaller per copy, not zero. Time is float32 in the shader: steps of about 0.24 ms after an hour of play. Copies must share one asset. Driven weights ignore `setMorph`, and `primitive.weights` on the CPU does not follow them. Why: The tracks are shared, and reading weights back would stall the frame. What you see: A long-running crowd loses fine timing slowly. CPU code that reads `primitive.weights` sees old values. Escape hatch: Set `player.time` back by whole loops of the clip (exact for copies at `speed` 1; a copy at another speed samples `time * speed`, so it jumps unless the step is whole loops at its speed too). Use `Animation` for a character whose weights you read or set by hand. |
| Animation LOD (`@margoengine/animation/lod`, 2026-11-06) | CPU only, and not measured for speed yet: how many copies update is counted, the frame time is not. Every copy still goes through the GPU deform dispatch each frame, and each still draws. Visibility is a sphere at the model root against the view, with no occlusion. `depth` counts node levels from the scene roots, so its meaning depends on the rig. A tier with a depth does not play `KHR_animation_pointer` channels. Deeper bones hold, so a far character can show a slightly wrong pose until it comes closer. Why: A skipped pose must still draw, and the deformed output is what draws. What you see: A crowd limited by the GPU gains little. A copy far larger than its `radius` can stop updating while part of it shows. Escape hatch: Set `radius` to cover the character. Use `VATCrowd` when the GPU is the limit. |
| Clip editing (`@margoengine/animation/clip-utils`, 2026-11-06) | By method: an eased or cubic segment that a cut passes through becomes straight keys at `fps` (default 60), so it follows the curve only to that step; segments kept whole stay exact. Works on `KeyframeClip`s, not glTF clips. `makeAdditive` leaves property tracks out, and `applyAdditiveClip` poses a `Skeleton` only, without morph weights. Why: An eased curve is defined over its whole segment, so one key cannot carry part of it. What you see: Very fine motion inside a cut curve can flatten between samples. Escape hatch: Pass a higher `fps`. For a glTF clip use an `@margoengine/animator` additive layer. |
| Engine ticks per `cloneModel` copy (2026-11-06) | None when the copy can take its source's static batches, skinned models included, so a crowd no longer costs a tick of every mesh per copy. One when the source moved since baking, has a parent, or had its geometry rewritten: the copy bakes for itself. A copy's world matrices publish with the next tick; a direct `node.matrix` read before it sees the old value. The time saved is not measured yet. |
| Work per `cloneModel` copy (2026-11-10, accepted difference) | A copy builds what it needs to draw at once: a core node per glTF node plus its root (75 for RobotExpressive), a uniform slot and bind groups per primitive; `destroy` disposes them. three's `SkeletonUtils.clone` makes JavaScript objects only and builds GPU state at its first render, so `p-skeleton-clone` times less work on three's side. The node copy itself makes one array a copy and the constructor groups primitives in one pass. The like-for-like row "clone + first draw" is pending the quiet rerun. |
| Work at load of an animated glTF (2026-11-10, accepted difference) | `parseGLTFAsync` packs vertices, bakes static batches and uploads GPU buffers, and `Animation.attach` places the deformation resources, so the model draws on its first frame with no further setup. three's loader defers buffer uploads to its first render, so `p-gltf-animated` times less work on three's side. The like-for-like row "parse + first frame" is pending the quiet rerun. |
| Dual quaternion skinning (`@margoengine/animation/dqs`, 2026-11-06) | Per `Animation`, fixed when it is created. `Skin` on raw data, `bakeVAT` and bone-texture crowds stay linear. Stretch blends linearly about the mesh origin, so between bones of different scale the result differs from a linear blend. Each bone costs a polar decomposition on the CPU every frame. Frame time is not measured yet. |
| Bone-texture crowds (`@margoengine/animation/instanced-skin`, 2026-11-06) | One material, opaque, no CPU culling, like `VATCrowd`. Morph targets are frozen at bake time, and bones blend linearly. Two clips a member: more needs another bake. Texture rows cap at 8,192 of 2,048 texels, about 5.5 million bone frames. Each vertex reads up to 96 texels when two clips blend across eight influences (24 for one clip and four). Frame time against `VATCrowd` and `Animation` is not measured yet. |
| Geometry caches (`@margoengine/animation/geometry-cache`, `/point-cache`, 2026-11-06) | PC2 and MDD are read, proved on files Blender's published add-ons wrote; the triangles come from the caller, as neither format holds them. Alembic is not read: the format has no published specification, and Margo is built from specs and papers. Mesh sequences (FG-11, 2026-11-24): `encodeMeshSequence`/`streamMeshSequence` and `margo-convert sequence` (per-frame OBJ, PLY or STL) write any per-frame mesh bake, the topology free to change each frame, so baked fluids from Blender come in through a per-frame mesh export instead of Alembic; every topology change is a new chunk, so a fluid that changes every frame stores its triangles every frame (no compression across frames). 3 to 1,000,000 vertices a chunk, one mesh, one material. The CPU interpolates and writes the whole mesh to the GPU every changed frame, so upload bandwidth is the ceiling: 80 bytes a vertex. Vertices are uncompressed. A seek back on a URL rereads from the start of the file, and a loop rereads it every lap unless it is one chunk: no range requests and no index of chunks. A stream source keeps every chunk it read. No mix across a change of mesh: the last frame holds. Motion vectors, frame time and upload cost are not measured yet. |
| Animator crossfades and graph exit times (`@margoengine/animator`, `/graph`, 2026-11-14) | By method: the state a crossfade leaves keeps playing at the current state's clip rate until its weight reaches 0; a transition taken during a crossfade fades from the blended pose it cut in on, held still, because no one state is left to play. By design: `exitTime` is the normalized time from which a transition may be taken, so on a looping state `exitTime: 0.5` with a condition fires as soon as the condition holds anywhere past the first half cycle, not only at the half mark of each later loop as in the controller of some desktop engines. Escape hatch: a base Animator transition whose `when` predicate reads `animator.normalizedTime % 1`. |
| Inertialization (`@margoengine/animator/inertialize`, 2026-11-06) | By method: an offset fades along one line per bone, so speed sideways to the offset is dropped at the switch; the new pose shows from the second frame after the switch. Not a published speed: diagnostic, shared machine, 58 bones, 14.5 to 17.1 us a frame during a fade against 16.5 to 21.5 for a crossfade, and about the same once idle. |
| Sync groups (`@margoengine/animator/sync`, 2026-11-06) | By design: clips are looping cycles, every clip of a marker group has the same markers in the same order, and a state is in one group. A crossfade keeps the old state in phase at the new state's rate. Not measured for speed. |
| Warping (`@margoengine/animator/warping`, 2026-11-06) | By method: travel past `maxTurn` (default 90 degrees) needs a clip for that direction, and a clip cannot play backward, so feet slide on the part of a turn past the limit. Stride scales about the hips on flat ground; it does not follow slopes, for which `addFootPlacement` runs after it. The clip rate changes one frame after the speed does. A pelvis drop past `maxPelvisDrop` leaves the foot short. On real CMU walks a planted foot slides 24 to 50 mm at 0.7 to 3 m/s against 21 mm in the take itself: the take's own slide scales with the stride and the hips' surge is not scaled away. The surge stays on its recorded axis when the hips turn, so a walk 90 degrees off the facing slides 51 mm. A take that curves is warped along the requested straight line, 62 mm on subject 2 at 1.6 m/s. Clip speed and a distance warp's travel are measured along the world ground through the travel joint's ancestors' current rotations and scales (a centimetre rig under a 0.01 scale or a scaled model reads in world units). Not measured for speed. |
| Full-body IK (`@margoengine/animator/fbik`, 2026-11-06) | By method: the torso is solved from the animated pose every frame in up to 12 steps, with no memory of the last frame, so a set of targets that needs more steps stops short and says so in `result`. Limbs are three-joint chains; hands, feet and head are the only targets, and a spine joint turns at most `maxBend` from the animated pose. Balance is static (centre of mass over the support hull, about world +Y, from fixed segment shares and centres (Winter's table: arm 0.530 from the shoulder, leg 0.447 from the hip, on the straight line from the limb's root to its end, so a bent elbow or knee is weighed as if straight) taken over the segments the rig lists, so a rig with no head or arms weighs only its trunk and legs): it knows nothing of momentum or of the model's real masses. A pinned foot on a limb with no target holds its animated place, so a walking clip keeps its steps. Speed not yet measured. |
| Motion matching (`@margoengine/animator/motion-matching`, 2026-11-06) | By method: the character does what its clips show, so a request with no matching clip plays the nearest row; the weights are defaults made for loops with no start or stop clips, so a real set may want its own. The root is the hips' smoothed ground path about +Y, with a yaw-only character; ground slope is left to foot placement. Scale tracks on the hips' ancestors are read at build but not in the running pose step. Proved on stand-in clips, on Fox.glb's real clips with hand-labelled speeds, and on eight CMU takes (769 rows). A row whose path runs past the end of its take cannot be landed on, so a take has to outlast `trajectory` by a good margin: a 1.1 s run jumps 19 times in 4 s, a 3.5 s walk 4. Foot slide at a jog and a run is not measured. Speed not yet measured on a large table. |
| Runtime mirroring (`@margoengine/animator/mirror`, 2026-11-06) | By method: partners need the same place in the tree on both sides, or `addMirror` refuses them. A rig whose rest pose is not symmetric keeps its own proportions, so the mirrored pose lands that far from an exact reflection. Scale tracks trade between partners as they are. Switching `enabled` is a hard cut. Speed not yet measured. |
| Spline IK (`@margoengine/animator/spline-ik`, 2026-11-06) | By method: bones are chords, so a bend tighter than a bone is cut across, and a chain longer than the curve carries on straight past its end. The curve's frames are rebuilt every frame, and a curve of points is rebuilt too, so a very long chain costs more than one on a fixed `Spline`. `space` needs a uniform scale. Speed not yet measured. |
| Spring bones (`@margoengine/rigging/springs`, 2026-11-06) | Enforced: 256 joints a chain, a joint in one chain only, 8 steps a frame (longer frames slow the swing), jiggle up to 15 Hz. By method: a tail can pass through a collider it crosses within one step, as in the specification; after the push the length hold can leave up to 1 mm of overlap; colliders hold their pose for the frame during a long frame's steps; spheres and capsules only, no planes or inside shapes; a chain has no twist, each bone turns by the shortest arc; strips do not pull on their neighbours, so a skirt of chains can part. 144 Hz differs from 60 Hz by up to 2% of the chain's length. Speed not yet measured. |
| VRM avatars (`@margoengine/rigging/vrm`, 2026-11-06) | Enforced: VRM 1.0 only; VRM 0.x files are refused with a coded error. By method: MToon draws as its glTF fallback, and a colour bind only MToon has is listed in `unsupported` and not shown; `VRMC_node_constraint` is kept on write and does not run; `firstPerson` runs through `@margoengine/rigging/vrm-first-person` (next row); colour binds are checked by value, not in a picture. Not proven: no outside VRM tool has read a file `writeVRM` made (stand-in: read back by Margo only). Not measured: speed. |
| VRM first person (`@margoengine/rigging/vrm-first-person`, `xr.layers`, 2026-11-15) | Enforced: VRM 1.0 only (convert VRM 0.x with `convertVRM0Bytes`); `loadVRM` downloads at most 64 MiB; layers 0 to 31 and the two must differ; an `auto` mesh left in a loaded model is refused with a coded `state` error naming `loadVRM`. By method: the `auto` split is the specification's (any head weight above `threshold`, default 0, makes a triangle head), so stray head weights put collar triangles in the head part; an unskinned `auto` node is third person only under the head bone, else `both` (the specification is silent); a split primitive's old bytes stay in the BIN chunk; a view, mirror or probe with no mask draws every layer, `firstPersonOnly` meshes included; shadows are not filtered by a view's layers, so the whole avatar casts in every view; a set mask replaces the caller's own layer on that node until `dispose()`. Proven: CPU split exactness on the Twist sample, Seed-san and built files; on the GPU, native and WebGL2, the masked first-person view equals the render with the head hidden pixel for pixel, the mirror shows the head, and both XR routes filter both eyes ([evidence](rigging-vrm-first-person.md)). Not measured: speed. |
| Uneven bone scales in IK (`@margoengine/rigging/ik`, `@margoengine/animator`, 2026-11-06) | Enforced: flat and mirrored bones are refused. By method: any positive scale is taken, and an uneven scale stretches the bones under it as they turn, so a chain lands as close as that stretch allows (within 0.14% of its length at 0.9995, 1, 0.9986). A `CCDSolver` keeps one scale per joint, so `addCCDChain` uses the mean of the three, and `setParentMatrix` still takes uniform scales only. |
| Hands (`@margoengine/rigging/hands`, `@margoengine/humans`, 2026-11-17) | Enforced: grip diameter 5 to 120 mm, flexion -30 to 130 degrees, spread -40 to 40, key weight 0 to 1, threshold 0 to 90. By method: poses are joint angles, not contact: `grip(d)` closes on a bar the size you give from each finger's measured lengths, but nothing finds the bar in the scene, so a hand that misses the rail closes on air (contact grip is not built yet). A rig with no fingertip bones has its last phalanx guessed at 3/4 of the middle one. The relaxed pose leaves the thumb to the clip, since bind poses splay it. Clips that key their own fingers are left alone, so a clip baked with a poor grip keeps it. Proven: a 30 mm grip puts every fingertip within 2 mm of the bar and none more than 1 mm in, on Mixamo, VRM and MPFB names; seeks equal playing. Not measured: speed. |
| Repeated bone names (`@margoengine/rigging`, 2026-11-15) | Enforced: `checkRig`, `rigJoints` and every entry that takes `RigJoint`s refuse two joints with one name, with a TypeError that names it. glTF 2.0 (3.4) does not require node names to be unique, but rig joints, IK chains, retarget maps and the VRM tools find bones by name, so a repeat would bind the wrong bone. Rename repeated nodes before rigging (for example add the node index). |
| Voxel weights (`@margoengine/rigging/voxel-weights`, 2026-11-06) | Enforced: resolution 8 to 512, closing 0 to 8. By method: parts closer than about one voxel join, so a finer grid is what keeps fingers apart, and memory grows with the cube of `resolution` (about 20 bytes a voxel). An open mesh is filled only from a bone inside it, through voxels with surface on four of six directions. A part no bone reaches takes straight-line distances, counted in `unreached`. Authored weights are the yardstick by strongest bone, not by value: the mean row gap to the authored weights is 0.30 to 0.54, as bone heat's is 0.32 to 0.43. Not measured: speed in a quiet run (Seed-san's hair mesh took about 3 s at resolution 64 and 33 s at 128 while other lanes ran). |
| Automatic rig (`@margoengine/rigging/autorig`, 2026-11-06) | Enforced: resolution 32 to 384, closing 0 to 8. By method: one humanoid standing in a T or A pose, arms clear of the body, two separate feet at the lowest point of the mesh, so a figure on a plinth, with its feet joined, or in another pose fails with code `failed` or gets a wrong skeleton. Fingers are not placed; the hand is one bone. Joints go by body proportion along the solid's paths, so a joint sits 2 to 4 percent of the height from where people put it (LIM-282), and more on a body far from adult proportions. A skirt or coat that joins the legs on a figure of over 4.5 heads puts the hips by proportion, not by what the mesh shows. Facing comes from the feet; on feet with no clear front +z is assumed and `facingFound` is false. A figure turned more than two degrees against the grid is voxelized again square on, which costs a second pass; a turned figure's joints still move by up to 0.03 of the height, a voxel or two. Bone rotations are all zero: the pose carries offsets only. Stand-in: the refused box and the README's figure of boxes are written by hand. Run only by hand and not committed, as their licences do not allow it: two more unrigged figures, which gave plausible skeletons with nothing to mark them against. Not run: a rigged mesh drawn on a GPU or opened in another tool. Not measured: speed in a quiet run (0.5 to 3 s a figure without weights while other lanes ran). |
| Corrective shapes (`@margoengine/rigging/correctives`, 2026-11-06) | Enforced: 1 to 64 samples a pose space. By method: `pose` and the joint's rotation are read as rotation vectors from `rest`, so a shape reads up to half a turn from rest and the reading jumps sign past it; a clip's track on a driven target is overwritten. Not proven: no real file with correctives was found, so the proof is a real rig and clip with a stand-in morph target. Not measured: speed. |
| Weight transfer (`@margoengine/rigging/transfer`, 2026-11-06) | By method: the two meshes must be in one pose and space. Either facing passes the angle test, so a layer with its surface parallel to the wrong limb's and inside `maxDistance` takes that limb. The fill is a weighted average, so it blends and never sharpens. A target with nothing of the source around it gets the nearest weights, which can be far from an author's: 41% to 69% agreement on parts of the Twist sample with no surface around them. Not measured: speed in a quiet run. |
| Face tracking (`@margoengine/rigging/face`, 2026-11-06) | By method: morph targets and VRM expressions only, so a jaw or eye moved by a bone is not driven; the VRM presets are a fixed reading of the 52, and no value stands for `relaxed`. A clip's track on a driven target is overwritten. Not proven: no real model named with these shapes was found and no live tracker has been run; the name matching is proven on stand-in targets, the avatar path on a real VRM avatar with frames the test wrote. Not measured: speed. |
| Powered ragdolls (`@margoengine/ragdoll/powered`, 2026-11-06) | By method: joint motors keep a pose and cannot lift a character, so standing needs the `root` spring, which is an outside force. Motors add mass and inertia to small bodies (up to an eighth of the heaviest neighbour, a tenth of the heaviest limb), so a powered ragdoll is a little heavier than a limp one. A joint's torque cap and gains come from the limb's real centre of mass and inertia in the pose motors were added in, so a limb whose mass sits close to its joint gets a soft motor: with the hips pinned, Seed-san's head sags 0.080 rad and stays there, where a rod per body read 0.030, and Knight's holds at 0.000 where a rod per body fell 0.82 rad. A higher `frequency` stiffens it. The default cone clips most clips. Measured on the Rig_Medium walk at 6 Hz: mean 0.1 rad behind the clip, the worst bones (hands, feet) 0.5 rad at peak. Not proven: Rapier 0.21 is the only version run; no timing yet. |
| Partial ragdolls (`Ragdoll.activate(limb)`, 2026-11-06) | By method: a limb is a bone and everything under it, so a hand without its fingers takes a list of parts of `ragdoll.bones` instead. A limb hangs from bodies that reach each frame's pose at that frame's physics step, so it is drawn up to one step behind a fast parent. A bone of the limb under a limp parent that is handed back alone follows its parent's drawn pose a frame late. |
| Getting up (`@margoengine/ragdoll/getup`, 2026-11-06) | By method: two clips, chosen at the root bone only, so a body on its side takes whichever is nearer. `root` is a top-level node. The character turns about the up axis only and the blend covers the rest; a limb far from the clip's pose crosses the body during the blend, with no collision. Not proven on an authored get-up clip: none is in the repository, so the proof plays the rig's Death_A and Death_B backward (stand-in clips, real rig, real physics). |
| Body shapes from the skin (`@margoengine/ragdoll/hulls`, 2026-11-06) | By method: one skin is read, the first that holds the root bone, since skins have separate bind spaces. A bone the skin has no bind pose for keeps its capsule. Vertices shared evenly by bones count for none at the default `minWeight`, so a hull can stop short of a joint. A hull is convex: a bone that carries a concave part overshoots into the hollow. The box lies along the bone, the smallest over 18 turns 5 degrees apart. Measured on Knight.glb, ray silhouette overlap with the mesh over a front and a side view: capsules 0.13, boxes 0.65, hulls 0.93; on Fox.glb, capsules 0.43, hulls 0.78. Thicker shapes reach the floor sooner: with limits the body cannot meet lying down, such as the default quarter-turn cone on a T-posed arm, a limit and a contact fight and the limb keeps moving (hand at about 0.8 m/s after 16 s on Knight.glb, limits held to under 1 rad over). Skipping the limit correction on touching limbs settled it, but let a spine fold 2.3 rad past its limit, so it is not done; give a fitted body limits it can reach (`swing` 2.5 settles under 0.05 m/s). |
| Saved profiles (`@margoengine/ragdoll/profile`, 2026-11-06) | By method: bones bind by node name, so a renamed rig needs its profile edited. Limits are measured from the pose the ragdoll is built in, so a profile fits only that pose; the humanoid preset reads a T or A pose and its hinges and ranges are wrong for any other. One cone per joint is narrower than a real shoulder or hip in some directions and wider in others. Mass shares are one published adult male table, de Leva 1996. A hinge is a knee or an elbow only: spines, shoulders and ankles are cones. Proved on Knight.glb, with Mixamo names only as stand-in names on the same rig. |
| Balance (`@margoengine/ragdoll/balance`, 2026-11-06) | By method: it stands on joint torques alone by default, every one a pair inside the body with the ankle held to what the sole answers; `carry` is an outside force, off unless set. It adds inertia to feet and shins (0.012 of the whole mass times the leg's length squared) brings the character's island to 8 solver passes at the least, and gives a hull foot a flat sole of four corners while it balances. Its torques are forces through the whole step, so a world set above 8 only helps: over 24 roundings at 8, 10 and 16 passes no figure steps late or falls, and no hips drift 0.0020 m. A stance knee takes its torque from the balance with a spring beside it that has no damper and grows with how far the knee is off its bend, full at 0.15 rad, so `motors.setStrength` does not reach it. It stands and steps at the heading it was added at: no turning or walking. Flat ground only, at the height of the feet; no stairs or slopes. `motors.hit` weakens a limb's motor, not the balance torques, which follow the global `strength` only. Measured over 24 hull roundings each at 8 passes: all seven figures settle with no step after the first second, at 0.0006 m/s at most. Worst drift of the hips over five seconds: Knight.glb 0.0009 m, Barbarian 0.0004, Ranger 0.0006, Rogue 0.0010, Mage 0.0003, Seed-san 0.0019, RiggedFigure 0.0005; no foot slides more than 0.0012 m. On 96 other roundings at 8 passes one Seed-san foot slid 0.0020 m and 8 of the 672 figure runs shook a bone over 0.005 m/s; at 10, 16 and 20 passes none did (known-bugs.md, "A standing figure can shake"). Pushes of 1.5 m/s in four directions over 32 roundings on Knight.glb: 125 of 128 pass the push test's reading and none fall; the old assist passed 122 and fell in none, holding about half the weight from outside. The other three are still stepping six seconds after the push and stand still by fourteen. Those 128 pushes at 8 / 10 / 16 passes, failing the reading / falling within four seconds: Knight 3/0, 1/0, 7/0; Rogue 1/0, 4/0, 2/0; Ranger 7/0, 8/0, 8/0; Mage 21/0, 25/0, 13/0; Barbarian 29/9, 36/14, 43/30; RiggedFigure 96/95, 92/88, 96/96; Seed-san 113/108, 121/120, 128/128. Falls in 128 pushes at 8 passes at 0.5 / 1 / 1.5 m/s: Knight, Ranger, Rogue and Mage 0 / 0 / 0, Barbarian 0 / 8 / 9, RiggedFigure 60 / 63 / 95, Seed-san 69 / 93 / 108, so only the first four stay up at 1.5 m/s and RiggedFigure and Seed-san do not reliably take 0.5 (known-bugs.md, "A push throws"). Not measured: speed, including the cost of the added passes. |
| Uneven bone scales in ragdolls (`@margoengine/ragdoll`, 2026-11-06) | Enforced: zero and mirrored bones are refused. By method: any positive scale is taken. Bodies are rigid and sized in world units when the ragdoll is built, so a scale animated afterwards does not resize them. A bone's own uneven scale costs nothing: a fall with a stretched spine matches the same rig built unstretched to under 1 mm. A bone turned under an uneven scale above it is skewed, so the bones drawn below it stretch as it turns, as in IK, while the bodies keep their joint distance; the pose holds exactly where the bone went limp and drifts from its body as it turns away. A hull fitted to a skewed bone takes the scales of the bone's axes and not the skew. Proved on Seed-san's own scales (`hair_E`, 0.9995, 1, 0.9986); scales as large as 0.1, 3, 40 only on a stand-in rig. |
| Swept collision (`@margoengine/kinematics-constraints/swept`, 2026-11-06) | By method: colliders hold still during a check, so a moving obstacle needs its own stepping. The path checked is the shortest arc per bone for a chain, and the shortest arc about the hull's origin for a hull; if your animation plays another path, this one is certified, not yours. A contact is any gap at or below `minClearance` plus `tolerance` (1e-4), and a motion that starts there stops at time 0, so keep `minClearance` below the gap the pose was solved with. A gap of `d` and a speed bound of `s` give a step of `d / s`, so a motion that grazes a surface for a long way takes many steps: past the budget of 4,096 poses it ends `exhausted`, which is not clear; raise `maxSteps` or `tolerance`. |
| Robot swept collision (`@margoengine/robot-planning`, `sweepRobot`, 2026-11-06) | By method: as the swept collision row above, on the straight line in joint space between the two poses; if your animation plays another path, this one is certified, not yours. Self collision is checked only with `selfCollision: true`, on the pairs `Robot.selfCollisionPairs` lists. |
| Joint-limit solver (`@margoengine/robot-planning/limits`, 2026-11-06) | By method: a local solver, so a start behind an obstacle can stall with a way round it; that is reported as `blocked`, and the planner is the way out. Convergence is proved from starts near an answer, not from anywhere. Ranges are per scalar joint: a ball joint is three of them, so a cone limit is a box of angles. Obstacle gradients are finite differences, so each nearby pair costs one pose per joint per iteration, and at most 48 pairs count per iteration, the closest. |
| Motion planner (`@margoengine/robot-planning/plan`, 2026-11-06) | By method: sampling planners are probabilistically complete, so `no-path` means the budget ran out, not that no path exists, and a narrow passage can need far more samples. Paths are feasible, not optimal: shortcutting only shortens them. A continuous joint plans on the line of its value, not on a circle, and samples stay one turn each way of the start. Colliders hold still during a plan. `planToPose` picks the first clear pose at the target; if that pose cannot be reached it reports `no-path` without trying another. Nearest neighbours are a plain scan, so a tree's cost grows with the square of its nodes. `Roadmap.grow` and `query` run on the calling thread. |
| URDF import (`@margoengine/robot-planning/urdf`, 2026-11-06) | By method: a mesh collision shape becomes its convex hull, so a concave link reads fatter than it is. A cylinder is a prism drawn round it, 16 sides by default. Only collision meshes are fetched; visuals are data, for your own loader. `<transmission>`, `<gazebo>`, `<material>` and sensors are not read, and `xacro` is not expanded: pass the generated URDF. A floating joint is six plain joints, three of them rotations in a fixed order, so it has the gimbal lock of Euler angles. A package path not listed in `packages` is a guess at the folder above the document. Mesh units are as the file gives them; only `scale` applies. `/urdf` loads `@margoengine/loaders/xml` at once and the rest of the loaders and `@margoengine/geometry` only when a mesh is met. |
| Batched GPU clearance (`@margoengine/robot-planning/gpu`, 2026-11-06) | By method: f32, about 1e-6 of a scene of size 1, so it sorts poses and proves nothing; `Roadmap.addPoses` proves each survivor on the CPU. An overlap reads zero or less with no depth. Poses only, not the motion between them: edges still take the CPU swept check. The base, the shapes and the colliders are read once. A `MeshVolume` and a field that is a plain function are refused. One invocation walks every pair of a pose in turn, with no broad phase, so a pose with many shapes and hulls of many points costs in proportion. A field query keeps 48 or 64 cells on its stack and past that answers with the safe lower bound, as `maxCells` does. Run on the RTX A6000 only. |
| Concave obstacles (`@margoengine/kinematics-constraints/sdf`, 2026-11-06) | By method: `SDFVolume` is only as fine as its grid. A wall thinner than a cell may not be in the field at all, and the default margin of one cell's diagonal reads every obstacle that much fatter; a grid must hold the whole obstacle, because past its edge a reading is the distance to the grid. Both volumes take a rotation, one uniform scale and a move, no shear. A crossing segment reads minus its radius and an overlapping hull reads zero or less on a mesh, which ranks poses and is not a depth. Mesh queries prune with a box round the query, so a long diagonal link visits more of the tree than it needs. `/sdf` is the one entry that loads `@margoengine/bvh/inside`, for the sign of a solid mesh. |
| `p-morph` build plus first frame (accepted only for now, open in [known-bugs.md](known-bugs.md#build-plus-first-frame-of-100-morphed-copies-is-still-slower-than-threes-webgl-backend)) | 154 ms, or 125 to 143 with `PBRModel.compile()` (first frame 17), against three's WebGPU 217 and WebGL 54, busy-machine diagnostic. |
| `PBRModel.compile()` | Compiles for the canvas pass under the lights and effects set when it is called. A later change to either, a batched textureless mesh, and any pass other than beauty compile on the draw as before. |

## Browser matrix (batch 273, 2026-11-15)

Measured with `packages/webgl2-compat/scripts/browser-matrix.mjs` (the copy-paste command is in the
[webgl2-compat README](../packages/webgl2-compat/README.md#how-it-is-tested)) in the browsers that most often lack
WebGPU. Every case runs natively on WebGPU and through the WebGL2 compatibility layer in the same browser. A pass meets
the case's own bar (the compatibility check's 0.1% of pixels and 0.25 mean for the basic scene, float64 within 1e-5 for
inverse trig, the materials check's unlit colours within 3, the voxel traversal check's bar); a refusal throws a coded
`MargoError` with its help link; a difference is a measured gap that is not a bug; unmeasured is a row the browser
itself cannot give (no WebGPU adapter for a native row, or a screenshot that shows no WebGL2 canvas for a picture
row). Results only: no timings.

| Browser | OS | GPU (as the browser reports it) | Rows | Bugs |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Firefox 157.0 | Windows 11 | NVIDIA RTX A6000; WebGL2 reports "ANGLE (NVIDIA, NVIDIA GeForce 8800 GTX Direct3D11 ...), or similar", WebGPU adapter info empty | 91 | 0 |
| Safari 27.2 | macOS 27.2.1 | Apple M6; WebGL2 reports "Apple GPU", WebGPU adapter vendor and architecture "apple" | 25 measured | 0 (4 rows not measured, below) |
| Chrome 124.0.6367.219 | Android 15 (Pixel_8 emulator, user build) | SwiftShader through ANGLE on Vulkan ("Android Emulator OpenGL ES Translator"); `navigator.gpu` present, no WebGPU adapter | 84 (native 8 refusals, 31 unmeasured; layer 33 pass, 12 unmeasured) | 0 |
| Safari, iOS Simulator | iOS 27.2 (iPhone 18 Pro) | the Mac's GPU (a simulator, not a device result) | pending | Remote Automation is still off in the simulator's Safari settings (no simulator holds the setting, checked 2026-11-15), so `safaridriver` finds no session host; the Mac's screen was also locked |

In Firefox and Safari every row not listed below passes, natively and on the layer: the basic scene (4x MSAA, exact
pixel, two views), the compatibility feature level (native only: the layer has no adapter to ask), 32 of the 33
feature probes, the eight materials scenarios, the gltf/pbr quad and the voxel path tracer traversal.

| Row | Browser | Native WebGPU | WebGL2 layer |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| features: msaaAspects | Firefox 157 | pass | refusal `compatibility-layer`: sampling a stencil aspect needs `WEBGL_stencil_texturing`, which this WebGL2 lacks |
| features: bitmapCopies | Firefox 157 | pass | difference, 1,521 values: a straight-alpha copy of a pixel with alpha 0 keeps its colour on the layer ([11, 200, 7, 0]) where Firefox's native copy zeroes it ([0, 0, 0, 0]); the layer keeps both copy rules the probe checks, native breaks one |
| post: GTAO creases | Firefox 157 | pass | difference: 16 x 16 occlusion values, mean 0.938, largest gap 0.0225 and mean gap 0.00056 against native |
| features from canvasRead on (27 probes), materials, gltf/pbr, post | Safari 27.2 | not measured | not measured: the Mac's screen locked during the run, Safari then fired no animation frames, the canvasRead probe waited for one and the WebDriver session stopped answering ("fetch failed", then timeouts). A run earlier that day, before the lock, passed them all except bitmapCopies (a difference of 1,196 values, the same alpha 0 copy rule as Firefox) and the GTAO gap; its report was overwritten, so these rows are rerun with the screen unlocked. The matrix now refuses at the start when the browser fires no frames; a rerun later on 2026-11-15 was refused that way, the screen locked again |
| basic scene (3), gltf/pbr, post, voxel traversal, materials, compatibility feature level | Android Chrome 124 | refusal: `webgpu` for the basic scene ("WebGPU adapter unavailable"), `unsupported` for the others | basic scene, gltf/pbr and materials (12 rows) unmeasured: the emulator shows no WebGL canvas at all, a plain one cleared to red included (in [known-bugs.md](known-bugs.md)); GTAO and the voxel traversal, read back, pass |
| features (31 probes) | Android Chrome 124 | unmeasured: no WebGPU adapter | pass, judged alone (inverseTrig within 1e-5 of float64, bitmapCopies keeps both copy rules, the rest without an error or GL error); no native result to compare |

Found and fixed by the matrix: every pick in Firefox answered the first mesh, because Firefox clears an integer
target through float32 (KB-FX273 in [known-bugs.md](known-bugs.md)). Safari's WebDriver element screenshot of a
WebGPU canvas comes back black in Safari 27.2, so the matrix crops the canvas out of the page screenshot instead; that
is a WebDriver behaviour of Safari and not a Margo defect. The same run found that `DynamicInstances.pick` on the
layer could answer null right after the first frame, while the layer's CPU culling route was still loading (fixed, in
[known-bugs.md](known-bugs.md)). On Android the matrix found that it could not drive Chrome on a user-build image
(Playwright's command line is ignored there) and that its cases assumed a native adapter; both are fixed in the script,
which now drives Chrome through its own DevTools socket and runs the layer's probes alone (in
[known-bugs.md](known-bugs.md)).

## Platform

| Limit | Starts at | Why | What you see | Escape hatch |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Physics kernel download (`@margoengine/physics`, `Physics.load()`, 2026-11-24) | By size: the kernel is a deflated Wasm blueprint inside the entry's JavaScript, inflated and compiled by the first `Physics.load()`, once per app; no Wasm file, bundler plugin or peer install. Before 2026-11-24 the solver was Rapier, a 3,082,103 byte Wasm (1,176,707 gzip) with a 270,338 byte lazy chunk. | One file less for every app, and a solver that is Margo's own. | `Physics.load()` rejects with a `MargoError` (`failed`) when the blueprint cannot be compiled (a Content Security Policy without `'wasm-unsafe-eval'` among them); the next call tries again. | Allow `'wasm-unsafe-eval'` as `docs/csp.md` says. |

| Precipitation (`@margoengine/weather/precipitation`, 2026-11-25, ATMO-04) | By method: raindrop fall speeds from the Loftus and Wordsworth drag balance run up to 7 percent under Gunn and Kinzer's measurements (6.6 percent at 1 mm, 3.5 percent at 2 to 4 mm, 0.3 percent at 5.8 mm); snow aggregates take the Brown and Francis mass law with maximum dimension (its authors used a mean dimension, which makes flakes heavier and up to about a third faster than measured below 2 mm); graupel's speeds follow Heymsfield and Wright's fit within 2 percent from 2 to 5 mm but fall to half of their power law at 0.5 mm; no evaporation below cloud base, no aggregation or breakup on the way down, hail and graupel do not melt, one fall speed (the strongest rain's median drop) carries the whole shaft sideways, a raindrop takes the air's temperature, and the snow share uses air temperature alone (no humidity). A sample costs about a millisecond. Enforced: rates 0 or more, sizes, heights, temperatures and gravity finite and above 0, graupel and hail fractions in [0, 1] with a sum of at most 1, hail density at most solid ice's 917 kg/m^3. | Fall speeds from each particle's physics follow the air with height, and one rate sets the sizes, counts and energy of what lands. | No below-cloud evaporation, no melting of hail, no humidity in the snow line. | Rain cells from the cloud solver (ATMO-03) when it lands; sample a grid and interpolate for many particles. |

| Sea waves (`@margoengine/physics/waves`, 2026-11-25, SEA-01) | By method: ST4 physics by default (Ardhuin et al. 2010, the WAVEWATCH III TEST471 constants with the sheltering s_u calibrated to 1 on Kahma and Calkoen's stable fetch law in friction-velocity scaling), or WAM Cycle 3 (`physics: 'wam3'`); third-order ULTIMATE QUICKEST propagation split by axis, no garden-sprinkler correction, no currents (no Doppler or frequency shift), no diffraction, reflection or triads, no spectrum above its highest frequency, the source terms integrated semi-implicitly in each cell.
