| A hull on the sea (`HullSolver`, `wettedLoads` in `@margoengine/physics/seakeeping`, SEA-08, 2026-11-25) | By method: the water's pressure integrated over the wetted part of the hull mesh, the part under the sea's surface found by cutting each triangle where the surface crosses it (the linear cut and two secant steps on the surface). The pressure is the sea's (a `SpectralSea` or any `SeaSurface` made in the hull solver's origin cell; another cell is refused, as the solver cannot convert between cells): hydrostatic plus the waves' dynamic part, the nonlinear Froude-Krylov load; still water to its local surface when the sea gives no pressure. Dunavant's degree-four rule on each wet piece is exact for the hydrostatic force and moment, and close for a wave pressure smooth over a piece (keep the hull's triangles under an eighth of the shortest wavelength). Added mass: strip theory at infinite frequency from Lewis forms of the sections under the current mean waterline (small heel and trim taken as level); heave, pitch, sway, roll and yaw (surge takes none yet); the lateral block from the sections' radiation solved at w^2 M / g = 64 and 128 and carried to infinite frequency by a straight line in 1 / (w^2 M / g); a real hull's added mass at its natural frequency is somewhat larger than at infinite frequency, so its period runs a little short. A section outside Lewis's range is held to its border (very fine or bulbous sections fit poorly). The added mass acts through M (M + A)^-1 on the forces the solver sees; contacts and joints act on the body's own mass. Radiation: heave, pitch, sway, roll and yaw and their couplings, by strip theory (Ursell-Tasai on each section's Lewis form, 16 multipoles on 64 points: the damping from the pressure and from the waves agree within 0.2 percent up to w^2 M / g = 4), roll about the centre of mass, at the hull's still-water draft (a hull far from its draft keeps the damping it had there), from 56 log-spaced frequencies up to w^2 B / (2 g) = 48 with the damping linear between them, convolved over the last 20 s at the solver's step; driven heave is within 0.6 percent of the frequency-domain answer at 60 steps a second, driven sway and roll within 1.1 percent, coupled heave and pitch within 1.2. Roll's viscous damping by Ikeda's components (ITTC 7.5-02-07-04.5): each section's bilge eddies (an empirical fit to 2-D models: on the box of Jung et al. 2006 the decay coefficient comes out 7.7 percent under the measured, and Standing 1991 found it low on flat barges) and Kato's laminar skin friction at the hull's natural roll frequency, about the centre of mass held at most 0.95 of a section's draft deep; no bilge keels, skegs or forward speed (lift and the speed corrections), so a hull with bilge keels rolls longer than it should. Potential flow gives a box less added roll inertia than measured (0.097 against 0.124 kg m^2/m on Jung's box), so its roll period runs about 3 percent short. The load is taken (s - 1) / (2 s) of the rigid step on (s its substeps), where a held load is energy-neutral. Two-dimensional sections in deep water: no three-dimensional end effects or finite depth. Forces the solver does not see are estimated from the body's last two steps for the added-mass solve. Diffraction by strip theory's relative motion principle (each section's added mass and radiation memory on the water's motion), at the long-wave depths that stand for a section's motion (its mean draft in heave, the depth of its mean wave pressure for long waves; its centroid's depth in sway and roll), so a section in waves short next to its draft takes them a little off; zero speed only, and only from a sea that gives the water's motion. Measured: head-sea heave within 1 percent of strip theory, beam-sea held loads within 1.5. Wave drift: the far-field mean drift of each section in beam waves (two-dimensional scattering with the hull's heave, sway and roll; no pitch or yaw in it), applied across the hull for a wave's share across it times its size (s abs(s), so none from ahead: the added resistance and the drift along the hull in head seas are not modelled), over the waves by Newman's approximation (difference frequencies from the diagonal coefficients), for a free-floating hull (a mooring stiff at wave frequencies changes the motions it assumes) in deep water; measured within 3 percent of the wall's force against the far field, with a long-wave residual of 4 percent of it. Green water: shallow water on a deck grid (first order; the deck's grid sets how fine its flow is), in the deck's frame by the body's linear acceleration (no centripetal, rotational or Coriolis terms), its load the water's weight rho G h straight down the deck (no push along it); edges at the deck's own height (no bulwarks, hatches or deck structures: a deck that is a closed top surface of the mesh); the sea beyond an edge its local surface height and the water's orbital motion there. Measured: Ritter's dam break within 1.1 percent at 400 cells, the edge's inflow Ritter's critical flux, the quasi-static deck the whole box's buoyancy. Not built yet: bilge keels and forward speed in the roll damping, surge added mass, bulwarks and deck structures in the green water. The load is taken at each step's middle from the pose at its start and held over the step (explicit): a light hull of small waterplane in a stiff sea wants a fast rate. | Floating bodies ride the sea's pressure through the framework. | Bilge keels do not damp a hull's roll yet. | Add a bilge keel's damping yourself (a linear damper on the body) until it is built; step the hull and rigid solvers at a higher level for a light, small hull. |

| Physics world (`PhysicsWorld` in `@margoengine/physics/world`, 2026-11-25) | By design: time is base ticks of 7,680 Hz and every solver steps at 60 * 2^level Hz for a level from 0 to 7, so a rate between those levels is not offered; frames map to ticks through the film clock (`FilmClock`, `@margoengine/math/clock`) in exact integers, frame rates of whole numbers or fractions with terms below 2^31 and tick counts up to 2^53 (about 37,000 years; a longer shot is refused with the fix); a frame before the world's time is refused (restore a snapshot to go back); a restore needs the same solvers and fields. A solver's level is chosen from its state at each 1/60 s boundary, so a stability limit that changes within 1/60 s waits for the next boundary; a solver is added where a step of its level would begin. Two solvers whose ids hash to one 32-bit random-stream number are refused with a `state` error (rename one; a hundred solvers meet about once in 900,000 worlds); the world seed is a 32-bit word. Origin cells are a power of two of metres (default 4,096), so an f32 offset inside a cell keeps about 0.25 mm. Solvers not coupled otherwise (`couple`, next row) exchange staggered, in coupling order. | One clock, no dropped time, the same physics at any frame rate, and a state that replays bit for bit. | Nothing measured yet (speed phase): a visit of a tick walks the solvers due on it. | Pick a solver's level from its stability limit; keep a shot's world near its origin cell with `shiftOrigin`. |
| Coupling schemes of the physics world (`PhysicsWorld.couple`, 2026-11-25) | Enforced: every scheme but `staggered` couples exactly one coupling group, and its members step at one level (the fastest any chooses); `strang` couples two solvers and its whole-stepped one must step below level 7; `iterated` runs a tick 2 to 64 times (default 4) and needs `iterate()` on every member and a field one member writes and another reads; `predicted` extrapolates only f32 and f64 fields; `implicitPressure` needs a member that adds to another's fields; with `bodyMass` and `addedMass` a once-a-tick scheme is refused unless the body is `margin` (default 2) times heavier than its added mass. By method: an iterated group runs Jacobi (every member on the same shared values, then all publish) and keeps the last run's result, not a converged one, so too few runs leave a residual; Anderson's history and Aitken's relaxation start again each tick. Couplings are set on a 1/60 s boundary. | Fixed counts and fixed-order sums keep a run the same bits on every machine; one level per group keeps `iterate`, which re-runs one tick, enough. | An iterated group cannot substep one member against another. | Raise `iterations` for a stiffer coupling; split a group whose members need different rates into a staggered pair. |
| Cloth as measured fabric, solved exactly (`@margoengine/physics/soft`, 2026-11-25) | By method: a woven sheet's threads are springs of the fabric's KES-F tensile stiffness (2 WT / EMT^2, linear over 0 to EMT and held rigid past it), its diagonals of its shear rigidity, both solved exactly with the links and the contacts with bodies, until every row is within its tolerance (0.1 percent strain for threads, 1e-5 m otherwise). Presets are representative, not exact: the same named fabric measured elsewhere differs by up to ten times (shirting cotton G = 0.367 gf/cm/deg in Luible 2008 against 3.50 in Seo and Tamura 2017; wool gabardine 0.588 against 2.93; silk habutae 0.11 to 0.51 across three papers), and no KES-F measurement of canvas or sailcloth was found, so those presets are the nearest measured fabrics (jute and polyester plain weaves). Rows with no compliance are damped Levenberg-Marquardt style (contacts by sqrt(f32 epsilon) of their diagonal, edges and links by their violation squared up to that), so a contact set with no answer (a particle between surfaces closer than its thickness) is met as nearly as it can be, not exactly. A light body pinched by a cloth leaves no faster than the sides close while they pinch it; afterwards it rides the cloth. The two halves of a cut body separate once by their contact thickness (the particles' radius plus the faces'), up to 4 radii in a step. Measured cost, paired A/B against the sweep it replaces (this Mac, loaded, one process, per-round minimums of 7; quiet rerun before release): a 12 by 12 cloth of 1 kg particles pinned at its corners, 1.05 to 4.26 ms a step (4.1 times); the same cloth with a 1,000 kg box on it, 1.49 to 62.2 ms a step (42 times), where a thousand-to-one mass ratio needs hundreds of Newton steps in its hardest pieces (the sweep took none, and let the box through or threw it). | The cloth stretches as the fabric does, whatever the iterations, substeps or the mass of what lies on it. | A default cloth costs more to step than the sweep did, most with a heavy body on it. | `material.tensile = null` for inextensible threads (still exact), `setAirDrag(false)`, fewer particles for a large cloth. |

| Sea surface (`SpectralSea` in `@margoengine/physics/sea`, 2026-11-25) | By method: linear (first-order) waves, one per frequency and direction bin of the spectrum, so crests and troughs are alike (no Stokes asymmetry, no breaking); between the still-water level and a crest the water moves as it does at the still level, and the pressure takes its depth factor there; one flat bottom at the spectrum's depth; the spectrum is read at one place (`at`) and taken for the whole sea until `refresh()`. | Grid-particle liquids (`FlipSolver`, `DeckWaterSolver` in `@margoengine/physics/flip`, 2026-11-26, FLUID-03) | Enforced: 1 to 1024 cells a side, 1 to 4096 substeps a step (default at most 64; a faster liquid is refused, naming the fix), eight particles a cell where it starts, capacity as given. | Water entry and exit (`EntrySolver` in `@margoengine/physics/entry`, 2026-11-26, SEA-14) | By method: the slam (Wagner's wetted radius, Korobkin's modified Logvinovich model) is for the body's equivalent body of revolution about the surface normal through its lowest point, and holds while the wetted radius is inside the widest section; the impact pressure, the slam and which faces are wet use the local surface plane under the body's centre (the sea's own pressure uses the whole sea), so a body much longer than the waves is wetted as on a plane; the cavity is Duclaux's and Aristoff's (radial walls, the contact line pinned at the widest section, no air pressure, no surface seal: a fast entry whose splash domes over before the deep seal is not modelled), 64 sections along the path; the jet's speed is 9.85 times the entry's normal speed, calibrated on one sphere (about 25 percent uncertain); no wave radiation, so a body left floating bobs with only the impact pressure's damping (float it with `HullSolver` instead); a streamlined body under water takes Hoerner's drag, a blunt one the impact pressure (C_D about 0.5 for a sphere). | Safe writes (`@margoengine/save/safe`, 2026-11-07) | Enforced: a write goes only over the copy that is not the newest good one; both copies bad rejects, never gives bad bytes; a write when the newest copy's generation is 2^64 - 1 rejects before any copy changes (another would wrap to 0 and lose the save), and `check` rejects a generation above 2^53 - 1 rather than round it. By method: two copies, so a key takes twice the room; a write is two reads, a write and a read back, each of the whole save. A failed read of the newest copy counts as damage, so the write after it can go over that copy. CRC-32 finds accidents and is no signature: the 802.3 polynomial has Hamming distance 4 up to 91,607 bits (about 11 KB), and 3 at least to 131,072 bits (Koopman, DSN 2002), so on a bigger save every 1 or 2 bit error and every burst of 32 bits is found, and other damage slips past about once in 2^32. Two processes on one key are not coordinated. A key ending in `~a` or `~b` of a plain save reads as a copy. Files (`fileStorage`): a key's file name, escaped, must fit the file system, usually 255 bytes; a read refuses a file past `maxBytes` (default 268,435,456 bytes) from its size, before reading it; the temporary file is made exclusively (`wx`) under the process id, so a name another writer holds rejects with MargoError `'failed'` and that file is left alone; one writer per folder, as two processes saving one key race and the last rename wins; a kill leaves a `.tmp` file behind, which no call clears; `keys()` lists only file names this storage writes, so another program's file in the folder is not listed; on Windows a save another program has open cannot be replaced, so the write rejects with the old save in place. Stand-in: prefixes, torn and reordered writes are built on a stand-in storage from the paper's crash model. Real: a process killed during writes of real files, 12 times each, on Windows NTFS, macOS APFS and Linux ext4, which also ran the real folder fsync (run by hand on the Mac and on Ubuntu, not in `npm test`). Not proved: power loss, which nothing here has tested, so that the fsync really orders the disk is taken from the system's promise. Not measured: no timed number. | Two copies are kept, and a write goes only over the copy that is not the newest good one. | On Windows a save another program has open cannot be replaced, so the write rejects with the old save in place. | Close the other program that holds the save open and save again. The old save stands until then. |
| Cloud saves (`@margoengine/save/remote`, 2026-11-07) | Enforced: a write needs a base, the tag of a read, or `If-None-Match: *`; a weak tag or none cannot be a base and is refused with the reason; a conflict takes at most 5 tries; a `Retry-After` over a minute fails the call. `remoteHandler` takes 64 MiB by default and stops reading a body at that limit, with or without a content-length. | A write is conditional on a tag, and tags live in memory. | By method: tags live in memory, so a new page or device reads before it writes, or the write counts as a conflict. A delete of a key never read is unconditional. A function policy merges the whole save, in memory, and may run again if the server moves on. A write is a whole save: no partial upload, no resume, no compression of its own. Each attempt's body is held in memory. `remoteHandler` reads a save to tag it on each request, and its turns hold in one process: two processes on one storage can split a precondition from its write. It has no auth of its own; `authorize` is yours. Keys: `keys()` needs a JSON array, which WebDAV servers do not serve. Apache with mod_dav sends no tag with a PUT and a weak one for about a second after a change, so a second write in that second is refused. Real: Chromium through real CORS against `node:http`, and Apache 2.4.67 with mod_dav on macOS, by hand. Stand-in: lost answers, 429 and 503 are a scripted fetch. | Adaptive render delay (`@margoengine/netcode/interpolation-delay`, 2026-11-07) | Enforced: `quantile` 0.5 to 1, `window` 16 to 65,536 arrivals, delay from `min` to `max` (default 0 to 1 s). A file that has both a Modality LUT Sequence and rescale values is a `RangeError` (PS3.3 C.11.1 allows one). A series must share one size and SeriesInstanceUID. The volume draws axis-aligned in index order; `matrix` gives the voxel to world or patient transform for other data. `RangeError` for a damaged file or a box outside the array. dicomSeries refuses a slice whose ImageOrientationPatient or PixelSpacing differs from the first slice by more than 1e-4 (relative above 1), the rounding DS text allows; the slice step is the median gap between sorted positions, and a step more than 1.5 times it (a missing slice) rejects unless allowGaps is set, which stacks the slices at the median step and lists the gaps in the result's gaps (3D Slicer warns that such images are not equally spaced and offers acquisition geometry regularization; Margo does not resample). | Decode compressed DICOM pixels with your own codec and pass the slices to `dicomSeries` as `DICOMImage` objects; recompress such Zarr chunks with gzip, zlib, zstd or Blosc LZ4. |
| Sciviz unstructured grids (`@margoengine/sciviz/grids`, 2026-11-08) | Linear tetrahedra (10), hexahedra (12), wedges (13) and pyramids (14); `parseVtk` also reads voxels (11) as hexahedra. One value per point or per cell. | Surface and slice are built on the CPU each call; a moved slice is a new `sliceGrid` call and `layer.update(set)`. Cells are taken as convex with planar faces; a twisted hexahedron face is split along its 0-2 diagonal. | `parseVtk` reads legacy files up to version 4.2 (CELLS with a count before each cell); version 5.1 files (OFFSETS and CONNECTIVITY), XML `.vtu`, binary `long` data and other DATASET kinds are refused naming what. Other cell types (vertices, lines, surface and quadratic cells) are skipped and counted in `skipped`. Wedges follow VTK's corrected order (0-1-2 counter-clockwise seen from 3-4-5); a file written in the older drawn order shows those wedges inside out. | Convert 5.1 or `.vtu` files to legacy 4.2 in ParaView (File, Save Data, legacy VTK), or pass the arrays to the grid functions directly. |
| Sciviz graph layouts (`@margoengine/sciviz/graph`, 2026-11-08) | Any node count the memory holds; edges up to the GPU's `maxStorageBufferBindingSize` / 8 per layer (16,777,216 at the 128 MiB default). | The layout runs on the main thread, one iteration per `step()`, about E + N log N work; `run()` yields between iterations. No speed is claimed. | Undirected straight edges; weights scale the pull. No frame walls (a pull toward the origin instead), no edge-crossing or label placement. Like any force layout it can settle in a local minimum; ten 24-node ring seeds at the default theta 0.9 settle with edges 3 % to 6 % uneven and no crossing. The tree opens cells by Barnes's 1994 test (d > side / theta + the centre of mass's offset), not the 1986 one, which kept one ring seed in ten (seed 3) crossed with edges 13 % uneven: on a 20,000-node graph that opens 10 % more cells on the first step in 2D (19 % in 3D) and 21 % (41 %) over the next 100 steps, counted. The layer frames the positions it was made with unless `bounds` is given. Edges are one-pixel lines. | Run the layout in a worker and send `positions` to `layer.setPositions`; pass `bounds` for a layout that will grow. |
| Sciviz 2D chart pan and zoom (`Figure.create(canvas, { mode: '2d' })`, 2026-11-15) | Zooming in stops when a window side is 2^-17 of its largest coordinate (2^-100 near zero); zooming out and panning stop where an end would pass the largest float32 (3.4028234663852886e38). `setLimits` still takes any finite window. | Plot coordinates and the data-to-scene transform reach the GPU as 32-bit floats: below 64 float32 steps across, points no longer separate, and past the largest float32 they are infinite. | Light-tier frame rate | Enforced ([index.ts](../packages/quality/src/index.ts)): `paceEngine` holds the light tier to an even rate of at least 60 FPS: 60 on 60, 120 and 240 Hz, 72 on 144 Hz, 83 on 165 Hz, 67 on 200 Hz, and every refresh of 75, 90 and 100 Hz. | Each frame spans a whole number of refreshes, so the rate cannot land on exactly 60 on every display, and an uneven 60 on 100 Hz would judder. | A 100 Hz display renders 100 FPS on the light tier, which asks twice the GPU work of the 50 FPS it used to get; a GPU that cannot keep up misses refreshes as it would on any uncapped tier. | Supersampled stills (`@margoengine/quality/ssaa`, 2026-11-06) | Enforced ([ssaa.ts](../packages/quality/src/ssaa.ts)): 1 to 1024 frames, picture size up to the device's `maxTextureDimension2D`. | Feature scaling (`@margoengine/quality/features`, 2026-11-06) | A step that saved under 3% of the frame rests 120 decisions, about a minute at 60 FPS. | A saving is the frame cost before minus after one step, over one 30-frame window: anything else that moves the cost in that window counts toward it, and a measured value is averaged with the last, so it corrects over time. | A step of shadow `resolution` or `cascades` or of the fog `grid` allocates textures, one hitch each. | Sea from the wind (`@margoengine/water/sea-state`, `WaterOptions.wind`, `Water.setWind`, 2026-11-17) | Wind 0 to 100 m/s at 10 m, fetch 1 to 1e7 m, 1 to 8 trains on fixed wavelengths (8 trains: 2 to 1,500 m, log-spaced). The threshold is the swell's own crest spread times a measured score table (Margo calibration), not a spectrum integral. The sun's glint lobe gets Cox and Munk's mean square slope 0.003 + 0.00512 U less the swell's and the ripples' (about 0.003) times 2.6 (GGX against a Gaussian lobe, measured), so its half width is within a factor 1.5 of Cox and Munk's crosswind half width at U 2 and 12; the sea's body is lit by the sky it mirrors (0 to 1 of a clear day's sky light), so a Water with no options at night is not brighter than the sky. The default sea (no `wind`, no `waves`) is the sea of 6 m/s since 2026-11-17 (Hs 0.8 m, 4.7 s, 0.17% foam; before it two hand-set trains of 0.3 and 0.15 m); passing `waves` keeps the trains you give, and the two old trains are listed in the water README. | The water root carries the sea code (26,411 to 26,832 B gzip, +421); sea-state alone is CPU only. | Floods (`@margoengine/water/flood`, 2026-11-17) | Enforced: a Water `terrain` of 2 cells a side up to the device's `maxTextureDimension2D` (8,192 on every WebGPU device; 512 until 2026-11-24, FG-02) within its storage binding limit (one word a cell, nine with the open-sea surf); at most 16 walls and 16 inflows (one uniform); a fixed step of 1 / (120 m) s with m from Courant 0.25 at `maxDepth` (default 20 m) and `maxSpeed` (15 m/s), refused when m would pass 16; at most 240 steps a frame, the rest carried over; boundaries 'wall', 'open' (zero gradient) or 'sea' (Flather open boundary, with a surge, up to 8 tsunamis, wind and rain); a tick is 1 / 120 s, 240 ticks a frame at most (`settle()` runs more); one uniform per tick in a ring of 256 pairs (a tick that changes nothing writes nothing). `inflow` 0..100 scales the discharge of every source live, `rain` 0..2,000 mm/h; `FLOOD_SETTINGS` rows are checked against these ranges before anything is written (`@margoengine/water/settings`, 2026-11-17). Two stage passes per step: a 512 x 512 map at m = 1 is 240 passes a second of film. A sea side lets a trough in down to 5/9 of its still depth and no further: there the water leaving is critical (Ritter 1892) and nothing from outside reaches the map, so a 42 m trough over 60 m of sea stands at -33.3 m at the side (FG-01, flood-sea.browser.mjs case 10); the side goes where the still depth is at least 1.8 times the trough. A flood cannot be seeked backwards (a fresh one replays); at 512 x 512 a 20 s seek is 4,800 passes at m = 1, not timed. | Bodies below the root (nested meshes and `follow`, 2026-11-07) | By method: a body has a position and a rotation, so scale from a parent that shears a part is not represented; a body is fitted at the world scale it had when added. Only a core `Mesh` can sit below a root. `follow` needs a `kinematicPosition` body on a core `Mesh`, and a mesh that jumps in one step moves its body at the speed that takes, pushing what it meets as hard. The sort that writes parents first is an insertion sort, which costs most with many nested bodies in reverse order: not measured. | Parents first is what makes a child's local pose right in the same frame. | Measured speed with thousands of nested bodies. | Put bodies on root meshes, or on no mesh (`addBody(null, options)`), where you can: only bodies on child meshes are sorted parents first. |

| Colliders from alpha (`@margoengine/physics2d/outline`, 2026-11-07) | No counted threshold; the limits come from the method. | Alpha is what the artist drew, and a convex piece is what a solver can fill. | By method: samples sit on pixel centres, so a hard corner is cut by up to about 0.7 pixel. | Own physics kernel (`@margoengine/physics`, 2026-11-07) | Enforced: 4,194,304 bodies per world, a world per Wasm instance, and 32-bit offsets inside it; `KernelWorld` throws above that or where memory cannot grow. Substeps run from 1 to 65,535. | By method: the integrator's own error against a parabola is `g h t / 2`, so it halves when substeps double; a dynamic body with no mass does not fall, and additional mass is spread as the colliders are, so it scales the inertia with the mass. Shapes today: ball, box, capsule, each with a closed-form mass, and hull. Enforced: a hull is a closed convex polyhedron with flat faces of at most 256 edges and no two neighbours that are one plane split in two, within about 0.8 degrees with every corner within half of FLAT, 1e-4 of the hull's size, of the other's plane (a mesh with such faces loses contact points, Gregorius 2015, so `addHull` refuses it); a real crease under 0.8 degrees between faces too wide to be one flat face is taken, as a hull of random points has them; its rows last for the world's life. By method: the separating axis test is linear in vertices per face and quadratic in edges, with no hill climbing or cached axis yet, so a hull of hundreds of faces costs a step more than it should until the quiet pass. By method: GJK stops after 64 descents, and the expanding polytope holds 96 vertices and 192 faces; a depth search that runs out gives no contact for that step and the next step tries again. By method: a point with a new id continues an old one within 2 cm on the first body, so a contact that jumps further starts its impulses from zero. By method: a contact's normal is found once a step and held for its substeps, and a point the body has not yet reached acts as a plane (Catto 2013's speculative point), so a fast body passing a corner can feel a ghost of that plane; not measured, batch 126 owns it. Contact defaults: 8 substeps, 2 passes, 120 Hz capped at a quarter of the substep rate, damping ratio 10, slop 0.2 mm, push speed 3 m/s. By method (2026-11-08): at one pass a substep a contact between two dynamic bodies that neither dominates is capped at an eighth of the substep rate (30 Hz at 4 substeps) while it carries under 50 times the lighter body's weight, as one pass settles no pile at a quarter; the ground, kinematic and dominant bodies and heavier loads keep the quarter. Measured at 4 substeps of one pass: the 20-row pyramid sleeps at 2.3 s, its top moved 32 mm, its bottom row 1.19 mm into the floor; 30 rows, whose bottom pairs carry about 40 times a cube's weight, sleep at 2.0 s and rest at 5.9e-4 m/s with sleeping off; the 1:100 and 1:1000 stacks keep the quarter and sag 14.4 and 137 mm. A deeper pile whose bottom pairs pass 50 times takes the quarter there; not measured past 30 rows. By method (2026-11-07): a substep relaxes as many times as it pushes, so 2 relaxing passes of joints and contacts at the defaults where there was 1: one pass left the friction anchors' push in a pile of 14 rows or more as speed, and it rocked for good. By method: a manifold's normal rows sweep until no impulse moves by more than rounding, at most 16 sweeps a pass, on the points' speeds alone; a relaxing pass settles in 3 to 8 sweeps on the 1:1000 stack. By method (2026-11-08): a manifold of four points ends each sweep with the exact step along the one pattern of its impulses that moves no body, the points' shares of one load among themselves, which the sweeps settled only by the leak (about 3 percent a sweep), so a soft pass ran all 16; it now settles in about 4 (perf-history 80). Friction keeps one sweep. By method (2026-11-08): inside the slop a biased pass closes a point rigidly to the slop's depth, (gap + slop) / h as a speculative row (Catto's Solver2D soft step), and the soft push acts only past it, so every point of a resting manifold rests at the same depth whatever its load: a cube released on a slope below tan t = mu holds under 1e-6 m from its first second (it moved up to 3.8e-5 m as its points sank at speeds that followed their loads). Measured on the harness, defaults and 4 substeps of one pass: creep 5.5e-5 and 5.9e-6 m to 0; the 1:1000 stack's top drifts 1.6e-8 and 1.4e-7 m (6.6e-7 and 3.7e-6 m before the exact step of the four points' shares); the 20-row pyramid at the defaults sleeps at 1.50 s (1.78 s before that step, 3.2 s earlier), and at 4 substeps of one pass, which fails its bars either way, moved its top 0.291 m (0.277) and its fastest box at 30 s 0.51 m/s (0.18); with the exact step of the four points' shares (2026-11-08) 0.270 m and 0.28 m/s, still awake until the eighth-rate spring of two movable bodies at one pass (above) let it sleep. By method (2026-11-08): a ball or a capsule meets the other surface at its core plus its radius along the normal, wherever it has turned to, so a rolling ball's point stays on the floor; its lever arm stays the step's contact point. A ball from rest at 30 degrees rolls within 1e-5 of 5/7 g sin t (it ran 1.0033 in its first second). By method (2026-11-08): a point struck while its gap is still open notes the speed it will meet the surface with, v^2 = v0^2 + 2 a d over the gap, gravity's gain added, so a ball from 1 m at e 0.5 peaks at 0.2487 m at the defaults and 0.2473 m at 4 substeps of one pass (was 0.2481 and 0.2432). By method: a resting contact sags by its load over its stiffness, which follows the lighter body, so a heavy box on a light one sits deeper: 3.9 mm at 1:100 and 3.5 cm at 1:1000 with metre cubes. A rolling ball slips 0.35 percent of its speed by 2.5 s, as friction is a stiff spring, and lands 0.13 percent over 5/7 g sin t. Enforced: a manifold holds four points. By method: the reduction always keeps the deepest point, so its area can fall short of the best four: 0.711 of the best at worst and 0.9915 on average over 3,000 random sets. Enforced: 536,870,912 pair rows and 32-bit offsets inside the block; a step throws when memory cannot hold the pairs. By method: pairs are found once a step over the motion expected at its start, so a body a contact turns round mid-step can leave its fat box until the next step; the margin is 0.04 m at any body size; a fixed body written by hand needs `touch`; a collider's row comes back only after a step. A single add or removal costs one pass over the lists, so adding one collider a frame to a very large world pays for the whole list. Until the narrow phase lands, two bodies touch when their fat boxes overlap, so islands run larger than they will. Writing a sleeper's columns does not wake it. A body at a steady pose with its energy under the threshold can go to sleep mid-air if nothing pushes it, as gravity is not a force the sleep test sees: a body at rest under gravity moves, so this needs zero gravity or `gravityScale` 0. A snapshot is the whole block, so its size follows capacity, not the bodies in use. By method: f32 state, as a far world needs `FloatingOrigin`. Needs Wasm SIMD, as core's kernel already does, so there is no second blueprint. `Physics`, `PhysicsBody` and `PhysicsCollider` of the entry serve free motion only: `setType`, `follow`, friction and the other contact settings, joints, queries, character controllers and `addModel` throw `unsupported` until their batch. `body.sleep()` and impulses take effect at the next step. A snapshot reads only in the kernel build that wrote it, and a `Physics`-level restore waits for `/snapshot`. Measured (LIM-366): 10,000 steps hash-equal in Node, native x86-64, Chromium 156 and Firefox 157 on one Windows PC; Safari, WebKit, ARM and any other machine are unmeasured. On that PC Windows would not start Playwright's Firefox (a side-by-side error on `mozglue`) because the run came from a packaged app whose `%LOCALAPPDATA%` is redirected, so the run used a copy of it under the worktree through `REPLAY_FIREFOX`; `scripts/lib/browser.mjs` now starts Firefox by its real path (docs/benchmarking.md, "Choosing the browser"). | The kernel is staged behind `/next` until the switch; the root entry still runs Rapier. Bit-equal results hold for one kernel build, not across kernel versions. | Use the root entry, which still runs Rapier. |
| Own physics joints (`@margoengine/physics`, 2026-11-07) | By method: locks are exact along a path of joints, so a chain of 50 hung straight holds a 1000:1 end mass to under 1e-5 of its length, at rest and swung at 3 m/s. By method: a lock's turning arm is read at the start of a substep, so a light link under a large pull turns as an explicit spring of stiffness about twice the pull times its arm; past about two radians a substep of that turn it grows. A chain of 50 laid out level with a 1000:1 end mass passes 1e-4 of its length at step 32 and 2 times by step 60 with 1 kg links of a sphere's inertia (0.001 kg m2 at 0.05 m arms); 16 substeps hold it to step 66, 32 to step 229, ten times the inertia to step 219 (`docs/known-bugs.md`). Where a branch or a ring ends a path, paths meet pass by pass: a grid under its own weight opens 0.18 mm at 8 by 8 and 0.95 mm at 30 by 30, a heavy hub with three arms 7.3 mm, and 5.3 to 8.7 mm with the hub started a micrometre to 0.3 mm aside, as the widest gap is the peak of a swing that rounding steers, but 1000 kg on the corner of an 8 by 8 grid of 1 kg links opens 69 mm and still moves at 0.2 m/s after 10 s (8 passes: 13 mm). By method: limits are one row at a time, so a long run of hinges on their stops carries its moment slowly: six links droop 48 mm, twelve droop 0.91 m and still move at 0.29 m/s in the last 5 s of 10. By method: a limit past its edge pushes back with the mass its row sees, as a contact does, so a limb a floor holds past its cone rests there: a hand of 0.36 kg comes to 0.02 rad past its cone, one of 3.6 g stays 0.49 rad past it under its 1.5 kg arm. At the edge a limit holds any load: a link of a hundredth of the mass carries a full one 0.008 rad past a cone of 0.2. By method: a rope is one row at a time, so two ropes under a 1000:1 end mass rest 35 mm long, 1.7 percent, and stay there. By method: a spring is implicit Euler, so with no damping one of 5 rad/s loses 23 percent of its amplitude in 10 s. `/articulation` (batch 128) is where branches and limits go exact. By method: one walk over every joint row a step, and rows and factors refreshed twice a substep, which the quiet pass may halve. By design: 2 passes at least for joints, so `iterations: 1` adds a settling pass for them; `generic` is not served yet. By design: a sensor reads the pose a step starts from, so an event comes up to a step after the overlap; two fixed bodies never meet, sensor or not; a disabled collider keeps its mass; dominance acts in contacts, not in joints. By method, four limits on the lock solve, each with a test that fails without it. (1) A row with under n u of its size left after the rows before it depends on them and carries nothing, n the rows of its path and u f32's epsilon (Higham 1990, stop 4.3 at his n u), read off Householder QR of M^-1/2 J^T so the doubles round each row only by its own length: a body held by ten rows on six freedoms stands still where it used to reach 18,904,462 m/s, and a path with 13 rows on 12 freedoms no longer keeps its dependent row (4e-7 of its size by elimination of J M^-1 J^T, 1e-32 now). Cost: a row within about sqrt(n u) radians of depending, 1.3e-3 rad on a path of 14 rows, is dropped too; and the kernel grew 4,449 B deflated (125,328 to 129,777 B). (2) A lock closes a gap at 3 m/s plus what the turning carries its anchors, the clamp of Buss and Kim 2005, whose D_max,i = d_i + D_max this is. A valid scene reaches it when a body is moved by hand off its joint or a hub turns at 8 rad/s at 100 m. Pairs are found once a step, so without it a joint 6 m open jumps a body past a wall in one substep. Cost: a wide gap takes more steps, and on the proof scenes it acted on 5 rows of 6,960 in the limb and moved no figure. (3) Where rows nearly depend on each other a push is a Gauss-Newton step outside its model, so a body's turn may rise by at most 0.2 rad a substep times N / M, and its centre by that much of its arm, N what the path asks and M what its bodies would each move (Buss and Kim 2005, section 4; they use 0.79 rad for inverse kinematics, here 0.79 lets a taut chain reach 39 m/s and 0.1 starts to cut the chain of fifty). A valid scene reaches it when a chain is pulled straight between two points further apart than it is long, the same pose as an arm reaching past its reach. Cost: what is cut stays open into the next substeps, and the whole path's push is cut, not only its bad direction, as a path has no singular value decomposition. It cut nothing in any scene of `kernel/tests/joints.rs`. (4) A warm start that would add more than a push's energy, half the island's mass times 3 m/s squared, is taken only as far as the minimum of the quadratic the passes descend. A valid scene reaches it when a limit catches a swing, as what the row holds is an impact and no load: once per catch on the proof scenes, keeping 0 to 7 percent. Cost: that row starts its substep cold, and no figure in `kernel/tests/joints.rs` moved. No paper does this; the line search is standard, its use here is our own. By method: a lock is exact and a contact is a capped spring, so a joint stretched through a wall drags its body through at about 1.5 m/s. By method: a turn past about 1 rad a substep leaves rows nothing to read, so a lock on a hub at 77 rad/s holds with 2 substeps, to 13 m on a radius of 10, and with 1 substep runs away and is refused after 59 steps. By design: a body past 1e15 in position or speed stops the world with `failed`, checked at the end of a step: a run away faster than that within one step would get past it, not seen in 200 random webs of 10,000 steps. Their top, 1.3e8 m/s for one step, is a kinematic turn of 77 rad/s forcing locks near a toggle, where the exact speed is one over the angle: only the pushing pass's bias is cut, after its speeds are solved in full, so a speed is answered in full. Scenes with no answer are only kept in the numbers: 60 random webs of unsatisfiable joints stay under 1e5 m/s, seed 45 spins under the 18,400 rad/s its kinematic turns can carry (2,559 rad/s; a cut of the whole solve once gave 162,278), and which seed is fastest changes with any constant; seeds 1 and 35 spin under 18,400 rad/s and hold every joint under the 56.85 m the scene's cube allows (956 rad/s and 38.0 m to step 400, 1,354 rad/s and 40.9 m to step 600), but near a toggle a row that does not yet depend is answered in full, so seed 49 reaches 10,991 m/s and a joint 165.8 m open and the 60 webs have no gap bar yet (`docs/known-bugs.md`). By method: each joint of the chain of 50 hung straight opens under 2e-5 m at rest and swung, under the same 1e-4 of its length as its stretch; laid out level and let fall, a joint opens 7.0 mm at 1:1, 9.7 mm at 10:1, 23 mm at 100:1 and 0.38 to 0.45 m at 1000:1 within 20 s, from rows that turn within a substep (`docs/known-bugs.md`) | A joint in a branch, a loop or on its limits settles over passes, so its gap under a far heavier load is the price; a chain is exact. | A grid or ring of joints under a far heavier load opens a gap (0.95 mm at 30 by 30; 69 mm for 1000 kg on the corner of an 8 by 8 grid), and a long run of hinges on their stops droops. | Use a chain, which is exact. Set `iterations` to 8, which narrows the 69 mm gap to 13 mm. An `/articulation` entry (batch 128) is planned and does not exist yet. |
| Own physics convex hulls (`@margoengine/physics`, 2026-11-07) | By method: Quickhull with fat planes, a point within 2^-20 of the cloud's size of the hull counting as on it, then triangles within a quarter of FLAT, 2.5e-5 of the size, of a face's supporting plane merge into one face. | Own physics triangle meshes (`@margoengine/physics`, 2026-11-07) (LIM-518) | By design: a triangle mesh gives a body no mass unless it is closed and wound outwards and asks for one with `mass` or `density` (Rapier gives a mesh none): the mass, centre and inertia are those of the enclosed volume, and an open, inside-out or non-manifold mesh is refused with what to fix; without a request it has no volume; both sides of a triangle collide, so a shape pushed past a triangle's plane is pushed on through it. Not served yet: a mesh against a mesh gives no contacts (Rapier meets composite against composite; batch 139.3). By method: one manifold of up to four points for each triangle a shape touches, each a pair row of its own, so a box across a crease holds both normals and a large box on a fine mesh solves a manifold per triangle under it. By method: `fixInternalEdges` (default false, as in Rapier) sorts an edge as convex, concave or flat from the triangle across it, joined by corner position so texture seams still join, an edge of three triangles staying open; a fold under 1e-3 (about 0.06 degrees) is flat. Measured with it on the physics-refs harness inputs (Node, workstation, 8 substeps, 2 passes): a ball and a box slide 8 s over a flat 127 m grid with velocity variance 4.3e-11 and 1.0e-12 (bar 1e-4; without it 0.34 and 0.35, the box spinning at 3.8 rad/s); 1,000 boxes on the 130,050-triangle St Helens mesh: none below the surface, no NaN; the 11 broken Thingi10K meshes all load and stay finite. Loss to fix (batch 129): on that mesh the build takes 65 ms without the edge rule (105 ms with it) where Rapier 0.21 takes 43 ms, and a step of the 1,000 boxes 1.52 ms median, 7.5 ms p95 where Rapier takes 1.14 and 4.8, both measured on a loaded machine; the tree's leaves hold two triangles and every node bins 16 ways. By design: mesh rows last for the world's life. | A manifold a triangle costs solver rows where a merged manifold would cost fewer, and keeps every face's normal | On the 130,050-triangle St Helens mesh the build takes longer than Rapier 0.21, as the row measures. | Turn on `fixInternalEdges` for sliding over a flat mesh. |

| Own physics soft solids (`@margoengine/physics/soft`, 2026-11-24) | Enforced: `youngsModulus` above 0, `poissonRatio` 0 to under 0.5, `density` above 0, `yieldStrain`, `creep` and `tearStrain` 0 or more, a cell has four distinct particles that are not in one plane, a cluster four or more particles and a positive frequency; a bad value throws a `RangeError`. By method: a linear tetrahedron locks when the mesh is coarse, so a cantilever of 8 by 2 cells sags to 55 percent of the Euler-Bernoulli deflection, 12 by 3 to 88 and 16 by 4 to about 99; the cells' damping is one number for the world (`soft.cellDamping`, default 10 per second); a body that a tear parts becomes pieces by rebuilding them, the particles along the crack duplicated (each side's share of the mass is its cells' share of the particle's rest volume) and the torn cells kept as pieces of their own, so no volume is lost; a body of edges with triangles (cloth) splits with its triangles, self contacts and a surface collider per piece, a body of cells splits with its surface (each piece's own boundary faces, the crack among them, and a surface collider of its own); shape matching, the volume constraint of a closed surface and a skin carry over to pieces of cells (a piece of cloth or a rope does not get a volume constraint: its surface is cut open), and clusters are dropped from them; the cells' bending accuracy (linear tetrahedra lock): a cantilever of 1 m by 0.25 m square at E = 3 MPa reads 55 percent of the Euler-Bernoulli deflection on 8 by 2 by 2 cubes, 88 percent on 12 by 3 by 3 and 99 percent on 16 by 4 by 4, so a bending body needs about four cubes across its thinnest section for under 5 percent error (coarser meshes read stiff; quadratic tetrahedra and a mixed formulation, the usual remedies, are not built); a cut parts whole faces between cells on the two sides of the blade, so it is jagged along cell faces; a stiff body needs many small steps (the cantilever test uses 20 substeps of 20 iterations at E = 3 MPa) or it reads soft, unless it uses the `'fem'` solver, one linear solve a substep whose stiffness does not depend on them (conjugate gradient to a relative residual of 1e-5 in at most 20 passes, or as many passes as unknowns for a body of 600 or fewer; the Neo-Hookean model there takes the co-rotated stiffness, a quasi-Newton step, and the answer is the same state; no direct factorisation exists, so a body over the dense limit may stop short of the solution on a hard step). The kernel's blueprint grew from 49,948 to 69,374 raw bytes (about 18,170 to 25,140 deflated) with the cells and their Wasm-side polar decomposition. Not timed. | Cells are constraints on the deformation gradient solved in small steps, so stiffness is the material's and not the solver's. | A body made of many cells costs the cells times substeps times iterations a step. | Refine the mesh or raise the substeps for a stiffer, steadier body; use `'corotated'` for a stiffer small-strain response. |

| Own physics collision completeness (`@margoengine/physics`, 2026-11-24) | Measured: a shape cast of a capsule sliding 5 mm clear over a box floor 800 m across reports a false hit from 1 of 25 start points (Rapier 0.21: 5 of 25), a limit of 32-bit numbers at that size; at 20 mm and above, and on floors up to 200 m, none (`packages/physics/scripts/compare-rapier-floors.mjs`). A deformable trimesh (`deformable: true`, `collider.setVertices`) moves as a kinematic body does: each vertex goes in a straight line over the step at its velocity, a triangle's speed is the mean of its three vertices', and a surface that turns or folds within one step is not swept through the turn (set it every step to follow a curve). By design: the shapes, queries, events, filters and hooks of Rapier 3D's public user guide, row by row in [physics-collision-parity.md](physics-collision-parity.md), each with a test. Enforced: a mesh, height field or voxel grid meets no other mesh (a voxel grid meets another grid), and a half space meets no mesh or half space; a compound's mesh, height field or voxel part meets convex colliders and the convex parts of other compounds, and no mesh or half space; a compound holds no compound; every convex shape, mesh, height field, voxel grid, compound and half space is a query shape; `setShape` cannot make or change a compound. Measured: rest heights, ray and cast distances and projections of the shapes added here against Rapier 0.21 as a black box (`tests/next-segments.test.js`, `next-round.test.js`, `next-halfspace.test.js`, `next-query-shapes.test.js`, `next-skin.test.js`) and against closed forms (`kernel/tests/halfspace.rs`, `round_polyhedra.rs`, `collision_types.rs`); Rapier's projection onto a round hull is iterative and differs from the closed form by up to 0.008 m, where Margo's is exact. | By method: a half space meets a convex collider through a box laid under that collider for the pair (its top face the plane), so its contacts cost a box's, and its broad-phase box is a slab or the world (1e6 m); `contactPair` against a mesh gives each triangle's own normal, without the seam smoothing of `fixInternalEdges`; an `oriented` mesh decides a point by the parity of the surface crossings of a ray from it, so a surface that is not closed gives parity's answer, and it changes point queries and solid rays, not contacts; a `contactSkin` or a `softCcdPrediction` widens a collider's box in the broad phase by that much, so a large one makes more pairs; the contact modifier is a Wasm import called for each touching pair that has a collider with `modifyContacts`, and changes only that step's friction, restitution, normal, contacts and surface velocity. A shape cast reads a start as touching when the shapes are within 1e-6 of the largest of their sizes (a few millimetres on a floor a kilometre wide, where f32 has no more to give), and not by the contact margin: a shape 5 mm above a 40 m floor slides without a hit (`kernel/tests/cast_parallel.rs`, and against Rapier in `tests/next-query-shapes.test.js`). Not measured: speed of any of it (build phase), or a contact modifier on thousands of pairs. | A skin of 0.3 m on a large floor, or a modifier on every pair of a big pile, makes a step slower than the same world without them; the numbers are not measured yet. | Keep skins to a few centimetres, set `modifyContacts` only on the colliders that need it, and filter pair queries by the colliders asked about. |
| Own physics framework memory (`@margoengine/physics/world`, 2026-11-25) | By method: the rigid kernel and the soft kernel are each their own Wasm instance with their own memory, so their state regions name that memory (`Region.memory`, transitional) instead of lying in the world's one shared memory (docs/physics-framework.md, section 3), and soft-rigid contact still copies through TypeScript. | The shared-memory module layout is being built (lane D); until it lands, the regions say where their bytes are. | Copies between the two kernels every step; nothing in a snapshot or a hash depends on it (`packages/physics/tests/world-snapshot.test.js`). | None needed: the field goes when the kernels move onto the shared memory. |
| Own physics continuous collision (`@margoengine/physics`, 2026-11-08) (LIM-506) | By design: Rapier's `ccd_enabled` as `ccd` on `addBody` and `body.ccd`, and `is_ccd_active` as `body.ccdActive`. After each step a dynamic body with `ccd` that moved further than its thinnest piece is thick is swept from the pose the step began at to the pose it ended at, against every collider whose fat box meets its path's box, and put back to its first touch with its velocity kept; the next step's contacts then stop it. Stopped on a body that moves and runs no sweep of its own (a kinematic body, or a dynamic one without `ccd`), it rides with that body for the rest of the step, and a moving body that comes at it after it stopped carries it the same way. A surface the body already touches at the start of a step holds it no deeper than half its thickness. A slow body, or one with `ccd` off, moves exactly as before (the same bits), and so does a fast one sliding on a floor. Rapier's `min_ccd_dt`, `max_ccd_substeps`, `soft_ccd_prediction` and CCD sensor events are not served yet (batch 140.5). Measured (`tests/next-ccd.test.js`): 1,000 bullets at 300 m/s turning at up to 50 rad/s, as 2 cm balls, boxes and capsules, at a 2 cm box wall, a two-triangle mesh and a height field stood on end: with `ccd` no bullet's centre reaches the wall's middle plane; without it boxes pass; 200 spinning bullets at a 2 cm kinematic wall coming at 20 m/s, and at a free dynamic plate, never end a step past its middle. Rapier 0.21 with `ccd` on, as a black box through the root entry, on the same 1,000 shots: 974 balls, 189 boxes and 2 capsules end a step with their centre past the far face of the 2 cm box wall (they stop at the touch, then the next step carries them into the wall and its contacts push them out on the far side); 4 boxes pass the two-triangle mesh; none pass the height field. By method: conservative advancement (Mirtich 1996, as Catto sets it out in 2013) on a lower bound of the gap from GJK's closest points and support planes. | The sweep tests every collider's fat box against the path's box, with no tree over colliders, so a CCD body costs time in proportion to the colliders in the world; a body is put back to its first touch, so it loses the rest of that step's motion. Two CCD bodies that meet each stop at the touch, and neither carries the other within the step. | Many fast CCD bodies in a big world are slower than on Rapier until the tree over colliders lands (batch 129). | Turn `ccd` on only for bodies that move further than they are thick in a step |
| Own physics cylinders and cones (`@margoengine/physics`, 2026-11-08) (LIM-512) | By design: Rapier's `cylinder`, `cone`, `roundCylinder` and `roundCone` as `cylinder` and `cone` with `radius`, `halfHeight` (along local Y, a cone's apex at +`halfHeight`) and `borderRadius` (default 0), as colliders and as compound parts, with rays, shape casts and point queries on them. Enforced: `radius` and `halfHeight` above 0 and finite, `borderRadius` 0 or more and finite. Measured against Rapier 0.21 as a black box (`tests/next-revolved.test.js`): the mass, centre and principal moments of sharp shapes within 1e-5 of Rapier's; 1,600 random rays hit the same body as Rapier, within 2e-5 m of an exact f64 surface and 1e-4 of its normal, never further off than Rapier; casts within 1e-5 m of the exact first touch, where Rapier's are up to 9.4e-4 m off; a cylinder on its cap and on its side and a cone on its base rest within 0.01 m of where Rapier rests them. A ray from 20 to 400 m away meets a sharp cone within 4 float32 rounding units of its length (`kernel/tests/revolve.rs`). By method: contacts by GJK and the expanding polytope on the core with the border as a margin, plus the cap, side line or apex that faces the other shape; a cap's contact points lie on a 16-sided polygon whose corners are on the rim, inside it by at most 1.9 percent of the radius between corners; mass and inertia are integrals over the rounded profile turned about the axis, so a round shape weighs its border too. | The border is a margin on GJK, so a round shape needs no mesh and no extra rows; faces held as faces let a cylinder stand on its cap with a full manifold. | A round shape weighs more than on Rapier, which weighs only the core (an accepted difference, more correct); rays and casts on a round shape run GJK's ray cast, slower than the closed forms of a sharp one; between a cap polygon's corners a contact sits up to 1.9 percent of the radius inside the true rim. | Give `mass` instead of `density` to match a Rapier scene's weights. |
| Own physics convex decomposition (`@margoengine/physics/decomposition`, 2026-11-08) (LIM-517) | By design: `convexDecomposition(mesh, options)` returns `{shape: 'convexDecomposition', parts, concavity}`, a collider on `/next` and on the root entry; `/next` refuses the raw mesh with an `unsupported` MargoError naming the entry, so the search is never on its path. The method of Wei, Liu, Ling and Su 2022 (CoACD): concavity max(Hb, 0.3 Rv) on the mesh scaled to a largest side of 1, 3,000 samples per unit area, Monte Carlo tree search over 20 axis planes per axis, 500 iterations, 4 cuts ahead, ternary refinement, merging. Enforced: a closed mesh (each directed edge with its reverse, after welding equal positions when needed), whole triangles, indices in range, finite vertices, a volume; `concavity` above 0; whole `maxConvexHulls`, `planes`, `iterations`, `depth` of at least 1; `timeLimit` above 0. By design: the same mesh, options and seed give the same parts bit for bit in every engine (only + - * / and own roots); `timeLimit` (default 60,000 ms) throws `timeout`, never a part-done answer; `maxConvexHulls` (default 64) stops cutting with the least convex parts cut. By method: neighbours merge only over a whole shared cut face, not over part of one; the candidate planes are the three axes, no PCA (the paper's option). Measured against Rapier 0.21's V-HACD at defaults (`scripts/decomposition-vs-rapier.mjs`, one busy run): tube 4 parts to 7, Eq. 10 0.050 to 0.138; cup of five slabs 12 to 12, 0.032 to 0.035; closed cup 12 to 12, 0.025 to 0.052; torus 6 to 11, 0.036 to 0.030 with 8.8 percent hull volume over the mesh to 3.7; knight 15 to 19, 0.044 to 0.052; 1.1 to 17.3 s where Rapier takes 0.1 to 0.3 s. | A cut mesh keeps fine detail a voxel grid loses, and the tree search finds the cuts a greedy one misses (the paper's Fig. 9), so a body gets fewer, closer parts. | 5 to 120 times Rapier's build time on these meshes (a loss, perf history entry 81); the torus has fewer, looser parts than Rapier's at the same threshold; a mesh with holes is refused where V-HACD voxelizes it. | Decompose once at build time and store the parts; lower `iterations` or `planes` for speed; close a mesh's holes first, or give a fixed body a `trimesh`. |
| Own physics body kinds and mass (`@margoengine/physics`, 2026-11-07) | By method: a body that stops being fixed finds the fixed colliders its boxes overlap by one walk over the sorted ends, so `setType` costs the world's collider count once; a body made fixed drops its pairs with fixed bodies. Enforced on both entries: `additionalPgsIterations` takes any whole number from 0 to 4294967295, Rapier's 32 bits, and throws a `RangeError` past it, where the root entry used to wrap 2^32 + 3 to 3 passes without a word; the kernel adds the counts without wrapping. | One body, one walk, no index kept for a rare call. | Measured on the root entry and matched: `setType(type, false)` keeps a sleeper asleep until the next step, which wakes it and what it touches whatever `wakeUp` said, and a body made fixed is not woken before that step; a still kinematic body reads asleep after the sleep window, `sleep()` stops it and a target wakes it (`next-bodies.test.js`). Accepted difference: the own solver wakes a whole sleeping island at the call (`setType(type, true)`, a velocity, an impulse), so between the call and the next step the bodies it touches read awake, where Rapier reads them asleep until its step wakes them; every pose and velocity of every step is the same. | Own 2D physics solver (`packages/physics2d/kernel`, native only until `@margoengine/physics2d/next`, 2026-11-08) (LIM-527) | Enforced: polygons of up to 8 corners; by default 4 substeps a step, each one biased and one relaxing pass. | Contacts are soft constraints with substeps (Catto, Solver2D, 2024): springs that push an overlap out at no more than 3 m/s, so stacks do not hop, held to a quarter of the substep rate (60 Hz), or an eighth (30 Hz) for an unloaded pair of dynamic bodies at one pass, which lets a deep pile settle and sleep. | By method: a pile sits lower than its boxes add up to, by its load over the springs: a two-point contact carrying load L sinks L g k / (2 omega^2), k the point's inverse effective mass. The 20-row pyramid's top drops 28.26 mm, 28.35 mm when built top down (Box2D v3 29.11, Rapier 2D 29.56 on the same scene), and a heavy box on three light ones at 1:100 drops 52.29 mm, 0.6 percent from the closed form; nothing moves once resting. The contacts are solved colour by colour, coloured from the top of the scene down along gravity, so a pile rests the same whatever order its bodies were made in. The 100-row pyramid's top drops 684 mm by 10 s (Box2D v3 726, Rapier 2D 735) and its row 30 spreads 48 mm (70, 64): a pair keeps last step's reference face while the two faces' separations lie within one slop (5 mm), and a clipped point keeps the id of the end it replaces, so resting points keep their warm start. Positions move in doubles and contacts are worked out relative to a pair's first body, so a pile 10 km out rests as the same pile at the origin. | More substeps or passes stiffen the springs: 8 substeps of 2 passes at `contact_hertz` 120 drop the pyramid's top 2.09 mm. |

| Own 2D physics joints (`packages/physics2d/kernel`, native only until `@margoengine/physics2d/next`, 2026-11-08) (LIM-534) | Enforced: revolute, prismatic, fixed, rope and spring joints between two bodies; a revolute limit reads the relative angle from -pi to pi, so its limits lie within that range. | Joints are soft constraints on the substeps as contacts are, at `joint_hertz` 60 (held to a quarter of the substep rate) and damping ratio 2, pulling error out at no more than 3 m/s. | Volume scatter in glTF (`KHR_materials_volume_scatter` in `@margoengine/gltf/extended-materials` and `install` of `@margoengine/materials`, 2026-11-06) | By method: follows the draft of Khronos pull request 2453 as of 2026-11-06, so the extension can still change, and pull request 2579 proposes another in its place. | A rasterizer has no path through the medium; the lobe is what a dense medium converges to by the spec's own comparison.
