### General water impulse sources still need SEA-06 (PA-25)

ICE-02 releases ice at its water-facing cells. ICE-03 turns those volumes into moving bodies and
exports conservative local wave sources. The general impulse propagation and inundation model,
the avalanche and lava sources, and the lahar feedback remain open under PA-25.

### Ground animal terrain and rig adapters (LIFE-02)

The engine fixture covers the real TerrainBed-to-contact path. A ground animal placed on an overhang cannot
reach the underside through a heightfield; its feet see the Bed surface. Supporting a climbing rig needs an
arbitrary-surface collider field and articulated foot binding. The queue lists the shared contact and terrain
geometry contract needed for independent impulse and animation consumers.

## Open: weather and sea do not yet publish complete material-ageing exposure (BIO-04)

A material-ageing world needs local deposition and annual climate values for atmospheric loss,
and needs corrosion current and larval supply for site-specific wreck decay. Existing weather
and sea fields leave out those quantities. A fixed `AgeingExposure` or a publisher writing
`ageing.exposureField` supplies them explicitly. Run the changing-exposure and wreck cases in
`packages/physics/tests/coupling/ageing.test.js` for a replayable producer example.
See [Framework requests](physics-work-queue.md#framework-requests) for the shared layout.

### Ice impacts and long-wave inundation (PA-15 and PA-25)

A cuboid released with ICE-03 rolls, ablates and generates a local dispersive wake. The new solver
does not yet exchange contacts with ships or grounded terrain. ICE-04 supplies floating pack-ice collisions, vessel resistance and rafting separately. General run-up and terrain, avalanche and lava sources still need SEA-06.

## Open: canonical fire and alpine canopy links (BIO-03)

BIO-03 reads a replayable exposure port for burn severity and fuel moisture until a producer in FIRE-01 and the
weather packages publishes the shared cell layout. The exposure fixture in `packages/biomes/tests/coupling/forest.test.js`
reproduces the effects on snags and live fuel. Forest growth provides the permanent axis required by TREE-3, and that
fixture checks the crown-tip direction. Existing treeline footage and its distant impostors still need a growth-axis
consumer in the shot. The remaining shared fields are listed in [Framework requests](physics-work-queue.md#framework-requests).

### Legged rig, rider and flow hand-off (LIFE-01)

The world solver can walk and run on live terrain and load a rigid platform. The recorded HORSE and COURIER
footage predates these fixtures. To exercise the scene-level hand-off, connect the solved feet and COM to the
rig and compare the posed feet to the published stance points after advancing the world. A complete articulated
handoff and reacquisition strategy, rider leaning and immersed-body displacement require the linked DYN-07,
LIFE-06 and SEA-12 couplings. The current fields provide the contact pose and wrench for those consumers.

### Pack ice grounded and continuous-sheet contacts

ICE-04 handles floating pack ice against other floes and waterline capsules. An unbroken sheet
cannot fragment into individually transported blocks under a bow in the current model. For a
repro, replace the two independent disks in the pack-ice contact case with one equivalent larger
disk. The fracture work reduces its footprint and thickens its subgrid pile while its row stays
single. Explicit bonds, fracture-created rows and contact with grounded bathymetry are needed to
move those blocks independently.

### Below-deck ingress after civilian crush (BREAK-03 / SEA-10)

A floating hull can give up normal kinetic energy, recoil from a contact, and publish lost seal integrity through `CrushSolver`. Run the floating service craft test in `packages/physics/tests/coupling/crush.test.js` to reproduce a fully failed seal. The below-deck water mass still needs a SEA-10 compartment and opening geometry to connect a damaged station to hydrostatic head, displaced water and the hull's centre of mass. EF-11 also needs its original scene and the later failure sequence. PA-52 remains open for its other paths.

### Rain-sheet breakup and shared rain suppression of ocean waves (PA-23)

A sloped film can flow off the grid and report its discharge. A nonzero discharge in the
thin-film gravity-drain test leaves the patch without spawning airborne ligaments or
atomizing into smaller drops. A wet impact emits a pressure pulse into WakeSolver. The
general sea keeps its existing wind-wave damping because heterogeneous rain suppression
and airborne secondary-drop transport are separate atmosphere and surface-wave work.

## Open: environmental airborne sources, feedback and filmed bindings (ATMO-06)

The live path receives aeolian mineral dust and whitecaps through registry fields. Existing footage and the
legacy water spray and debris renderers still use their earlier particles. Footstep dust can use the emission port;
the coupling fixture supplies its measured rate without an EARTH-05 source writer. The mass ledger tracks vapour
and deposited mass. Temperature, humidity and bed composition feedback need coastal or ground output layouts with
positions. Embers, ash, high-speed debris and snow are outside the environmental water/mineral scope here. See
[Framework requests](physics-work-queue.md#framework-requests).

### Woody plant growth geometry and moving obstacles (BIO-02)

`PlantGrowth` supplies an updated branch graph that `@margoengine/procedural/lsystem` can mesh; run the geometry case in `packages/biomes/tests/coupling/growth.test.js`. New branches avoid the supplied solid voxel grid. The solver still needs a shared moving-obstacle geometry input and an explicit seasonal transfer contract for live scatter and wind-driven branch physics. Branch growth currently changes the shared graph on a season boundary, and users rebuild the mesh from the new graph when needed.

## Open: acoustic room mesh and concert-hall cutaway consumers (SOUND-02)

The room solver accepts an explicit air-mask lattice, and the early path trace accepts finite convex faces.
To connect dynamic EARTH-02 tunnel or canyon geometry, the solver needs a canonical material and occupancy
field. The opening fixture proves shadow diffraction with explicit geometry. The concert-hall fixture verifies
early arrival cutaway points and the README plays the actual convolved response. The filmed scene still needs
to read those paths and room material inputs. See [Framework requests](physics-work-queue.md#framework-requests).

### Viscoplastic deposits and established mud scenes (PA-60)

The optional 3D solver accepts a time-varying inlet, collides with a live bed and replays its
mass ledger after restore. The existing mud scene still uses its constant source and
depth-averaged effect. Its large-scale breach and soil uptake need the hydraulic source and
entrainment fields before that scene consumes replayable discharge.
Run `packages/physics/tests/coupling/viscoplastic.test.js` for the varying-inlet regression.

### Open gas-shell topology and gas-field coupling (SOFT-06)

A closed pressurized shell deforms and transfers impulses through the real rigid contact ports. Tearing an edge
currently leaves the triangles connected, so the gas stays in its chamber. A pressure vessel that opens dynamically
will need membrane topology changes and an opening/flow contract. Solver output exposes live recorded pressure and
volume. A changing atmospheric field requires an application update until the shared pressure ports are available.

=== Using Margo with AI tools (docs/ai-tools.md) ===

# Using Margo with AI tools

AI coding tools write good Margo code when they read the right pages and check what they wrote. Margo gives them
three ways in, from least to most setup.

Before 1.0.0: margoengine.com does not serve the files below yet, and the packages are not on npm. Use the copies in
the repository ([site/llms.txt](../site/llms.txt) and [site/llms-full.txt](../site/llms-full.txt)), and run the MCP
server from a clone after `npm run build:packages`: `node packages/mcp/bin/margoengine-mcp.js --root <your project>`.

## 1. Point the tool at llms.txt

[`llms.txt`](https://margoengine.com/llms.txt) follows the [llms.txt convention](https://llmstxt.org): a title, a
summary, and sections of links with one-line descriptions (guides, one README and one API page per package,
examples). [`llms-full.txt`](https://margoengine.com/llms-full.txt) is the same material as one text file: the
guides in full and each package README (long ones cut, with a link to the rest).

- **Cursor:** Settings, Indexing and Docs, Add Doc, paste `https://margoengine.com/llms-full.txt`. Then write
  `@Docs Margo` in a chat.
- **Claude Code and Claude Desktop:** ask the tool to read `https://margoengine.com/llms.txt` first, or paste the link
  into the chat. Add a line to your project's `CLAUDE.md`: `Margo Engine docs for AI: https://margoengine.com/llms.txt`.
- **Copilot and other chat tools:** attach `llms-full.txt` as a file, or paste the link.

Both files are generated by `node scripts/build-llms.mjs` from the package READMEs, the `api/` reports and `docs/`.
The test `tests/llms.test.js` fails when either is stale. Run the generator after relevant documentation or API
changes; it only updates the files and never commits them.

## 2. Run the MCP server

[`@margoengine/mcp`](../packages/mcp/README.md) is a Model Context Protocol server that runs locally over stdio. It
answers from the docs of the version you installed, and it type-checks code against your project's real Margo types.

| Tool | Use it to |
| --- | --- |
| `search_docs` | Find the API or README section for a task or an exact name. |
| `list_packages` | See which optional package provides a feature (core is frozen; features are packages). |
| `get_package` | Read one package's README or API report. |
| `list_examples` | Find a runnable example before writing one. |
| `check_snippet` | Type-check a snippet strictly against the installed packages. |
| `port_to_margo` | Map a class or task (`OrbitControls`, `InstancedMesh`, "shadow map") to the Margo package and calls, with status, limits and code, from the [parity matrix](threejs-parity.md). |
| `explain_error` | Explain a pasted Margo error (the message, its `errors#<id>` link, the id or the `MargoError` code) with its cause and fix from the [error help page](https://margoengine.com/errors). |
| `render_snippet` | Only with `--render`: run a snippet on the GPU in Node and see the PNG it draws. Needs `@margoengine/headless`, `@margoengine/stage` and `webgpu` in the project; runs code with your rights. |

The server also offers every package README and API report and every docs page as resources
(`margo://packages/<id>/readme`, `margo://packages/<id>/api`, `margo://docs/<path>`, `margo://readme`), which a
client can attach to a conversation without a tool call, and four starter prompts: `start_scene`, `port_code`,
`fix_error` and `add_feature` (in Claude Code, `/mcp__margoengine__start_scene` and so on). Each prompt names the
tools to use, in the order below.

Setup (full steps in the [package README](../packages/mcp/README.md)):

```sh
npm i -D @margoengine/mcp typescript margoengine
claude mcp add margoengine -- npx -y @margoengine/mcp        # Claude Code
```

Claude Desktop and Cursor take the same command in a JSON config file: `command` `npx`, `args`
`["-y", "@margoengine/mcp"]` (Claude Desktop also needs `"--root", "/path/to/project"`).

A good loop for an assistant, and the one the server's own instructions suggest: `search_docs` or `list_packages`,
then `get_package` for the package it will use, write the code, then `check_snippet` and fix what it reports before
showing the answer. When the user brings three.js code, `port_to_margo` first, once per class it uses; when they paste a Margo error, `explain_error`.

## 3. Give the assistant a project rule

Short rules in `CLAUDE.md`, `.cursor/rules` or `.github/copilot-instructions.md` stop the most common mistakes:

```md
This project uses Margo Engine (WebGPU). Docs for AI: https://margoengine.com/llms.txt
- Core (`@margoengine/core`) and the stage (`margoengine`) are small; every feature is a separate optional package.
  Find it with the margoengine MCP tool `list_packages` and import only what you use.
- `margoengine/<name>` and `@margoengine/<name>` are the same module.
- Units are metres and glTF conventions (Y up, right-handed).
- Anything that loads or waits takes an `AbortSignal`; errors carry a `code` (branch on it, not the message).
- Run the margoengine `check_snippet` tool on Margo code before presenting it.
```

## What the tools cannot do

- **Render without a GPU binding or a browser page.** `render_snippet` draws in Node through the `webgpu` binding,
  so it needs that package and a GPU (or a software adapter through `gpuFlags`). Code that needs a page (DOM input,
  `createStage('#canvas')`, a frame loop) does not run there: write the snippet against the stage it is given.
- **Run your code by default.** `check_snippet` only compiles; `render_snippet`, which runs code, is offered only when
  the server is started with `--render`.
- **Port by meaning.** `port_to_margo` matches the words and name parts of the matrix rows. A class the matrix does not
  list gets no row; the answer says so and points at `search_docs`.
- **Watch the docs change.** Resources come from the snapshot the package was built with, so there are no
  subscriptions or change notifications; update `@margoengine/mcp` to get newer docs.
- **Know a package you have not installed.** `check_snippet` resolves imports from your `node_modules`; an import of a
  package that is not installed is reported as an error, which is the right answer for an app that does not have it.

## Keeping it current

| File | Made by | Checked by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `site/llms.txt`, `site/llms-full.txt` | `node scripts/build-llms.mjs` | `tests/llms.test.js` (in `npm run verify`) and `node scripts/build-llms.mjs --check` |
| `margoengine.com/llms/...` pages | `scripts/build-site.js` | `npm run site:check` |
| `@margoengine/mcp` corpus | `packages/mcp/scripts/build-corpus.mjs`, at package build | `packages/mcp/tests/` |

=== @margoengine/stage (packages/stage/README.md) ===

# @margoengine/stage

You normally use this package as [`margoengine`](../margoengine/README.md): `import {createStage} from 'margoengine'` is this package. The packages are not on npm yet; see the [Install](../../README.md#install) section for the routes that work today.

High-level setup for Margo Engine. Mount a canvas, enable orbit/pan/zoom, start rendering and create a spinning orb in five lines. The stage creates a WebGPU engine. Pass `fallback` from the optional `@margoengine/webgl2-compat/preview` when a browser has no WebGPU; without it, creation rejects with `WebGPU unavailable`. Core handles resize and automatically recovers a lost WebGPU device. A lost WebGL2 context reports through `onError` and stops rendering; dispose and recreate the stage to resume.

This package is built from source alongside the engine. See the [package catalog](../../docs/README.md) for npm availability. Run `npm run build:packages` in the repository, or install its local tarball and `@margoengine/core`. The only dependency is `@margoengine/core`. `@margoengine/gltf`, `@margoengine/creative`, `@margoengine/sky`, `@margoengine/gltf/pbr`, `@margoengine/environment`, `@margoengine/studio`, `@margoengine/shadows`, `@margoengine/tonemap`, `@margoengine/xr`, `@margoengine/physics` (its solver comes inside it), `@margoengine/save`, `@margoengine/animation`, `@margoengine/clustered`, `@margoengine/labels` and `@margoengine/selection` are optional peers, used only by the feature entries below. The root entry imports none of them, not even lazily, so any bundler (Vite, Rollup, esbuild, webpack, Turbopack) builds an app that installs only this package and core. Each feature entry imports its package on the first call and rejects with `Install <package>` when it is absent, which keeps that code out of the initial scene.

Apps using Stage load this facade and its shared core, then only the feature entries they use and those features' required dependencies. Apps using the Engine API directly can load core without Stage. Choose specific feature imports and load heavier features on demand; keep one matching core version across the app.

The build requires the combined core and stage facade, with every base export retained, to stay strictly below 25,000 bytes gzip. It writes measurements to `test-results/modern-bundle-sizes.json`; `npm run measure:size` repeats the gate against the built artifacts. Lazy features and application bootstrap/chunk overhead are measured separately; this is not the complete page download size.

Give the container a height, for example `<div id="scene" style="height:400px"></div>`:

```ts
import {createStage} from 'margoengine';
const app = await createStage('#scene', {background: '#202024'});
const orb = app.sphere({color: '#84d6bd', roughness: 0.25, scale: [1, 0.85, 1]});
app.onTick(delta => {orb.rotation.z += delta;});
window.addEventListener('pagehide', () => app.dispose(), {once: true});
```

Use a selector, an HTMLElement container or an existing canvas. The wrapper appends its own accessible canvas to containers. `app.dispose()` stops rendering, aborts active imports, removes controls and removes an owned canvas. Existing canvases and their styles remain available after disposal. Call disposal when your page or component unmounts. `onTick` returns an unsubscribe function.

`createStage(target, options)` accepts core camera/backend/capacity options and `controls`, `autoStart`, `label`, `onError` and `background`. Controls and rendering start by default. Use `autoStart: false` for manual rendering through `app.engine`. Camera validation and initial rendering finish before creation resolves.

| API | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| `app.sphere({radius, segments, ...options})` | Creates an orb with the same material/transform options as boxes |
| `app.box({size, color, roughness, metalness, position, rotation, scale, parent, name})` | Creates a box and returns the existing mutable mesh handle |
| `app.mesh(geometry, options)` | Attaches existing or custom geometry with the same options |
| `app.onTick(delta => { ... })` | Runs once per frame with delta in seconds; returns an unsubscribe function |
| `app.fit()` / `app.fit(model.meshes)` | Fits visible geometry, including world transforms and hierarchy |
| `app.use(plugin)` | Attaches an existing plugin and returns it |
| `app.signal` | An `AbortSignal` that aborts when the stage is disposed; the feature entries combine it with yours |
| `app.engine` | Existing core API: camera, picking, plugins, manual render, start/stop and recovery |

### Options and defaults

`createStage(target, options)` takes every [core engine option](../core/README.md) (`backend`, `camera`, `capacity`,
`fallback`, `features`, `exactSize`, `signal`, `startupWarning`, `startupTimeout`, `powerPreference`) and five of its own:

[README continues: https://margoengine.com/llms/packages/stage.md]

=== @margoengine/core (packages/core/README.md) ===

# @margoengine/core

Import `margoengine/core` from the `margoengine` package, or `@margoengine/core` from this package alone; the two are the same module. Neither is on npm yet: the [Install](../../README.md#install) section lists the two routes that work today (run in a clone, or install local tarballs).

WebGPU rendering (WebGL2 fallback via the optional `@margoengine/webgl2-compat/preview`), a deterministic Rust/Wasm transform kernel, instanced drawing of one directional GGX light on position and normal, reversed float depth and picking. Materials are color, roughness, and metalness.

Desktop scenes use 4× MSAA with a canvas DPR cap of 1; phones use single-sample rendering with a DPR cap of 2. For slower desktop GPUs, set `globalThis.margoLow` to a pixel ratio (for example `1` or `1.5`) before creating the engine: scenes then render single-sampled with the DPR capped at that value, which on an Intel Arc 140V laptop cut the island demo's GPU frame from about 20 to 10 ms (particles off) compared with 4× MSAA. The site demos choose this light tier by measuring the GPU rather than guessing from the device. Color and depth targets follow canvas resize. Optional scene captures retain that sampling policy and expose single-sample resolved textures. CSS layout and HTML text retain native density.

`engine.pick(x, y)` updates scene state without forcing a color frame. One readback runs at a time and overlapping calls wait their turn, so a loop of picks costs one readback a point. A pick asked for during a frame starts after it, and one asked for inside a pick (a plugin's `onPreUpdate` picking for a hover) waits behind it instead of nesting. Meshes created or removed elsewhere during a readback leave its answer standing; only a mesh created after the pick started (one that took the hit slot) is answered as null; `pickMany` of `@margoengine/selection` answers many points from one. For cached forward-pass IDs, instance culling in a 3×3 micro frustum and neighbor resolution, attach the optional `Picking` plugin from `@margoengine/selection`. On a canvas without client size (an `OffscreenCanvas` in a worker) pick coordinates are canvas pixels.

Static scenes cost little per frame: the kernel recomputes only entities whose position, rotation, scale, parent, bounds or visibility changed (and their descendants); the engine reuses last frame's instance list unless the mesh set, a geometry or material assignment, a material's values or the layers changed; a mesh that culling or `visible` shows or hides moves one row of its batch (shown: the batch's next row; hidden: the batch's last row takes its place), a moved mesh rewrites its own row, and the WebGPU renderer uploads only the changed rows, one `writeBuffer` for each run of neighbouring rows. On an Intel Arc 140V laptop the kernel part made the kernel 2.6-4x cheaper and let 50,000 CAD parts orbit at 92 FPS instead of 49 (CAD measurements, before the row change). An orbiting camera no longer re-collects every frame: with 50,000 boxes and 500 culling flips a frame, the frame does 50,000 byte compares, 1,000 map lookups, 12,000 float copies and uploads 48 KB in at most 500 writes, where it did 100,000 lookups, 1.2 million float copies and a 4.8 MB upload (counted in `tests/core-instance-cache.test.js`; not timed yet). Several cameras on one scene flip most rows, and then cost what a full collection costs. Draw order among the instances of one geometry follows these row moves, so it changes after a flip; opaque pixels are the same except for two core meshes at exactly the same depth. Contract for `@margoengine/core/extension` users: the per-geometry instance buffers (`engine.geometryBuffers(geometry).instance`) belong to core and are read-only for packages (bind them, never write them, except a package that claims a batch and uploads its changed rows with `uploadRows`, see "Bulk poses and instance rows"; use your own buffer, as `@margoengine/selection`'s micro pick pass does), and `store.matrices` is kernel output (change transforms through the mesh, never by writing world matrices). GPU culling of core meshes (`@margoengine/culling`'s `CulledMeshes`) uses one hook: passes see the frame's batches as `context.batches`, and a package may set `batch.redirect = {instances, args}` for the frame; every core draw of that batch (main pass and replays) then reads the package's compacted instance records and `drawIndexedIndirect` arguments instead of core's buffer and count. Core still uploads into its own instance buffer, which stays the read-only source the package culls from. `engine.start({culling: false})` skips core's CPU frustum test in the built-in loop (as `render({culling: false})` does for one frame) when a package culls on the GPU.

[README continues: https://margoengine.com/llms/packages/core.md]

=== @margoengine/game (packages/game/README.md) ===

# @margoengine/game

Install profile. Games: models, animation, light and shadow, sky, physics, audio, input, effects.

It holds no code of its own and only re-exports its member packages: it installs only its declared domain members and forwards their original typed modules.
The root contains common exports; member subpaths expose the complete installed member APIs.
All packages release together at one version. Optional third-party peers remain app choices.

See the [kits guide](https://margoengine.com/llms/docs/guides/kits.md) for profile contents, independent installs,
model-loading entries and measured package counts.

With a `<div id="viewport" style="height:400px"></div>` in the page:

```ts
import {createStage, Shadows, OrbitControls, Input, Tween} from '@margoengine/game';

const stage = await createStage('#viewport', {controls: false});
const shadows = Shadows.attach(stage.engine, {resolution: 2048});
const ground = stage.box({size: [10, 0.2, 10], color: '#c8c8c8'});
const player = stage.box({position: [0, 1, 0], color: '#84d6bd'});
shadows.add(ground);
shadows.add(player);
const controls = new OrbitControls(stage.engine.camera, stage.engine.canvas as HTMLCanvasElement);
const input = new Input({jump: [{type: 'key', code: 'Space'}]});
const tween = new Tween();
const height = {y: 1};
stage.onTick((delta) => {
  input.update();
  if (input.state('jump').pressed) tween.to(height, 'y', 3, {duration: 0.4});
  tween.update(delta);
  player.position.y = height.y;
  controls.update(delta);
});
```

Model loading is a separate import: `import {loadGLTF} from '@margoengine/game/gltf/pbr'`.
Physics is one too: `import {Physics} from '@margoengine/game/physics'`. A game without it ships no solver Wasm.

=== margoengine (packages/margoengine/README.md) ===

# margoengine

Margo Engine in one install. The root is the stage (`createStage`, everything `@margoengine/core` exports), and every
engine package is a subpath: `margoengine/gltf`, `margoengine/shadows`, `margoengine/physics`, `margoengine/react`,
including their smaller entries (`margoengine/controls/orbit`, `margoengine/geometry/primitives`, ...).

The packages are not on npm yet: `npm i margoengine` gets only a name placeholder (0.0.1, no engine) until 1.0.0 is published. Use the clone or local-tarball routes in the [Install](../../README.md#install) section until then.

```ts
import {createStage} from 'margoengine';
import {Shadows} from 'margoengine/shadows';
import {OrbitControls} from 'margoengine/controls/orbit';

const stage = await createStage('#viewport', {controls: false});
const shadows = Shadows.attach(stage.engine, {resolution: 2048});
const ground = stage.box({size: [10, 0.2, 10], color: '#c8c8c8'});
const cube = stage.box({position: [0, 1, 0], color: '#84d6bd'});
shadows.add(ground);
shadows.add(cube);
const controls = new OrbitControls(stage.engine.camera, stage.engine.canvas as HTMLCanvasElement);
stage.onTick((delta) => {
  cube.rotation.y += delta;
  controls.update(delta);
});
```

## You load only what you import

`margoengine/<name>` is a one-line re-export of `@margoengine/<name>`, the same module with the same classes, and
every file is free of side effects. An app that imports `margoengine/shadows` bundles exactly the bytes it would bundle
from `@margoengine/shadows` (`tests/umbrella.test.js` compares the two bundles); the other packages are installed but
never loaded. `import {createStage} from 'margoengine'` is core + stage alone, 24,820 B gzip.

Use either name; they are interchangeable. Each package also has its own name (`@margoengine/shadows`) for
apps that want a smaller install.

## Short names

```ts
import * as M from 'margoengine';
import * as Physics from 'margoengine/physics';

const stage = await M.createStage('#viewport');
const mesh = stage.box({color: '#84d6bd'});
mesh.position.y = 1;
const cubes: M.Mesh[] = [mesh];          // types come along: M.Mesh, M.Vec3, Physics.PhysicsOptions
console.log(cubes.length, typeof Physics.Physics);
```

A namespace import tree-shakes like named imports in every modern bundler: only the members you use are kept.

## No bundler, served from your own origin

`dist/importmap.json` maps every entry to jsDelivr. A page served from your own origin (a dev server, a local tool, a
film or CI render) points the same entries at the install in `node_modules` with `margoengine/importmap`. It is pure
string work, so it runs in Node or in a page; the base is where your server serves the installed packages.

```ts
import {localImportMap} from 'margoengine/importmap';

// Keep margoengine, one of its entries, and every @margoengine package (the files import each other by name).
const map = await localImportMap('/node_modules/', {only: ['margoengine', 'margoengine/shadows', '@margoengine/']});
console.log(map.imports.margoengine); // /node_modules/margoengine/dist/index.js
const head = `<script type="importmap">${JSON.stringify(map)}</script>`;
console.log(head.length > 0);
```

`rebaseImportMap(map, base, {only})` does the same to an import map you already hold. `base` is `/node_modules/` or an
absolute URL; a missing closing slash is added. A bad base or an `only` entry the map lacks throws with a help link
([errors#import-map](https://margoengine.com/errors#import-map)). Third-party peers such as web-ifc are not in the map:
add them yourself.

## Third-party libraries

Three entries can use a library you install yourself, only when you use that entry. Everything else is in the one
install.

| Package | Install | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `margoengine/ifc` | `npm i web-ifc` | You pass an initialized `IfcAPI` to `parseIFC` |
| `margoengine/react` | `npm i react react-dom` | It is a React component library |
| `margoengine/ui/react` | `npm i react` | React bindings for the UI package |

`margoengine/react` holds every React binding but five groups, each its own entry: `margoengine/react/gltf`
(`Model`, `Gltf`), `/fbx`, `/animation`, `/materials` and `/physics`. The first four reach the Draco and Basis decoders,
and Vite copies a decoder's Wasm into the build as soon as it reads the module, used or not. A page that imports none
of them builds with no Wasm of theirs:

```tsx
import { Canvas, Mesh, BoxGeometry } from 'margoengine/react';
import { Model } from 'margoengine/react/gltf'; // only on a page that loads a model
```

The kits `margoengine/game`, `/web` and `/viz` include `loadGLTF`, so their builds hold the decoder files; the browser
fetches them only for a file that uses Draco or KTX2.

Without them nothing else changes; the package that needs one says which to install when you use it.

=== @margoengine/math (packages/math/README.md) ===

# @margoengine/math

Import `margoengine/math` from the `margoengine` package, or `@margoengine/math` from this package alone; the two are the same module. Neither is on npm yet: the [Install](../../README.md#install) section lists the two routes that work today (run in a clone, or install local tarballs).

Vector2, Vector3, Vector4, Quaternion, Euler, Matrix3, Matrix4, Color, Box3, OBB, Line3, Triangle, Capsule, Sphere, Plane, Ray, Frustum, Spherical, Cylindrical, SH3, MathUtils and the project functions. Methods write into `this` (chainable) or an `out` argument instead of returning new objects; only `clone()` and `toArray()` with no target return new ones.

```ts
import {Vector3, Quaternion, Euler, Color} from 'margoengine/math';
import {Engine} from 'margoengine/core';
import {createMesh} from 'margoengine/materials';
import {box} from 'margoengine/core';
const engine = await Engine.create(document.querySelector('canvas')!);
const mesh = engine.createMesh().setGeometry(box());
const position = new Vector3(0, 1, 0).addScaledVector(new Vector3(1, 0, 0), 2);
mesh.setPosition(position.toArray()).setQuaternion(new Quaternion().setFromEuler(new Euler(0, Math.PI / 4, 0)).toArray());
engine.camera.position = new Vector3().copy(mesh.position).add(new Vector3(0, 2, 5)).toArray();
new Color('#ff8800').toArray(mesh.material.data); // linear RGB, recolors in place
```

Each type is its own module: `import {Vector3} from '@margoengine/math/vector3'` (or from the root, which tree-shakes the same) ships about 1.4 kB min+gzip. The whole package is about 20.6 kB min+gzip ([entry-sizes.json](../../examples/package-benchmarks/results/entry-sizes.json)).

Array helpers: the other Margo packages work on plain arrays (`number[]`, `Float32Array`, `Float64Array`) rather than these classes, and share one copy of those helpers from here, each bundled into the package that uses it. `@margoengine/math/mat4`: `multiplyMatrices(a, b, out)`, `invertMatrix(m, out)` (cofactors), `invertMatrixStable(m, out, workspace?)` (pivoted, rejects non-finite input and Float32 overflow; `out` may be `m`) and `composeMatrix(t, q, s, out)`, column-major like `camera.matrix`, float64 arithmetic; the inverses return null (`out` untouched) when they fail. `@margoengine/math/quat`: `eulerToQuaternion(x, y, z)` (XYZ, like `Mesh.setRotation`), `multiplyQuaternions(a, b)`, `axisAngleToQuaternion(axis, angle)`, `conjugateQuaternion(q)`, `normalizeQuaternion(q)` and `rotateByQuaternion(v, q)`, returning new arrays, and `rotationToQuaternion(m, out?, sx?, sy?, sz?)`: the rotation of a column-major 3x3 or 4x4 (columns divided by the given scales; a negative `sx` undoes a mirror), the one conversion every package uses.

[README continues: https://margoengine.com/llms/packages/math.md]

=== @margoengine/quality (packages/quality/README.md) ===

# @margoengine/quality

Import `margoengine/quality` from the `margoengine` package, or `@margoengine/quality` from this package alone; the two are the same module. Neither is on npm yet: the [Install](../../README.md#install) section lists the two routes that work today (run in a clone, or install local tarballs).

Measured quality tiers. Desktops start on a light tier (single-sampled, pixel ratio capped, paced to an even rate of at
least 60 FPS) and read the real GPU time of each frame by timestamp queries; a page under the limit gets the full 4× MSAA tier
from its next load. No PC is first shown the 4× tier or reloaded by the probe (the light tier's own frame rate depends on
the GPU), and no rule based on device names is involved.

```ts
import {applyQualityTier, paceEngine, watchQuality} from 'margoengine/quality';
import {Engine} from 'margoengine/core';
const canvas = document.querySelector('canvas')!;

applyQualityTier();                       // before creating the engine
const engine = await Engine.create(canvas, {backend: 'webgpu'});
paceEngine(engine);                       // light tier: an even rate of at least 60 FPS
// ...build the scene and start rendering, then:
watchQuality();
```

- `applyQualityTier()` returns `'light'`, `'high'` or `'phone'`. Phones are single-sampled with the pixel ratio capped
  at 1 (`globalThis.margoLow = 1`), even with `?quality=high` or `?scale=2`. It sets core's `globalThis.margoLow`, which
  core reads when it builds pipelines and sizes the canvas, so it must run before the engine is created.
- `watchQuality()` reads 120 frames on the light tier and, when the 90th percentile of the time a frame's GPU passes cover (passes that run side by side count once) is under
  `FAST_GPU_MS` (8 ms), remembers `'high'` for this page in `localStorage['margoQuality:' + location.pathname]`. One key
  per page, because the result says what this page's scene costs: a light scene must not mark a weak PC high for a heavy
  one. A slow reading remembers nothing, so one bad session cannot hold a browser on the light tier: the next load
  measures again. On the full tier, five consecutive seconds under 55 FPS remember that for good (`'held'`) and reload
  once (a machine that slowed down, for example on battery).
- Timestamps: `applyQualityTier()` adds `timestamp-query` to the devices this page asks for, only while the page is still
  to be measured, until `watchQuality()` starts. The reading is its own small chunk, downloaded only by a page that reads. During the reading (about 4 s at 60 FPS, 10 s at most) `submit` and
  `createCommandEncoder` are wrapped and every pass gets timestamp writes; then all of it is put back and its GPU objects
  destroyed, so nothing runs after the reading. Without `timestamp-query` the page stays light and stores nothing. A frame
  whose passes the page times itself is not counted. Copies between passes, presenting and other work between passes are
  not in the number.
- `onReading(milliseconds)` on `watchQuality` reports the reading when it ends, undefined when there is none.
- For testing: `?quality=high` or `?quality=low` forces a tier without remembering it; `?scale=1.5` sets the light
  tier's pixel ratio (1 to 2). `localStorage.removeItem('margoQuality:' + location.pathname)` measures again.
- `paceEngine(engine)` sets core's `engine.pace` hook on the light tier so `engine.start()` renders at an even rate of
  at least 60 FPS instead of swinging between 120 and 40 FPS on a slow GPU. Each frame spans the most whole refreshes that
  still reach 60, so the rate depends on the display:

  | Display | 60 Hz | 75 Hz | 90 Hz | 100 Hz | 120 Hz | 144 Hz | 165 Hz | 200 Hz | 240 Hz |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | Frames per second | 60 | 75 | 90 | 100 | 60 | 72 | 83 | 67 | 60 |

  Other tiers stay uncapped. Nothing global is patched: other `requestAnimationFrame` loops on the page run at the display
  rate. An app that renders from its own loop (calling `engine.render` itself) can gate it with `frameDue`.
- `capFrameRate(engine, rate = 60)` sets the same pacing on any engine regardless of tier. It reads the display's refresh
  from the last 16 callback gaps, so it follows a page moved to another display within 16 frames.
- The light-tier reading skips the first two seconds and gives up after ten, at any refresh rate.

## Dynamic resolution

```ts
import {applyQualityTier, watchResolution} from 'margoengine/quality';
import {Engine} from 'margoengine/core';
const canvas = document.querySelector('canvas')!;
applyQualityTier(); // light or phone tier
const engine = await Engine.create(canvas, {backend: 'webgpu'});
using resolution = watchResolution({budget: 12, min: 0.6}); // restores full resolution when disposed
console.log(resolution.scale);
```
